originalRow.secondaryCondition: Post-traumatic headache (persistent, migraine or tension-type phenotype)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated DC — rated by analogy under 38 CFR § 4.20 within § 4.124a; the headache syndrome is ordinarily evaluated under DC 8100 (migraine) criteria (or tension-type criteria by analogy)
originalRow.primaryCondition: Traumatic brain injury (service-connected), with residuals
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 8045 (38 CFR § 4.124a — residuals of traumatic brain injury)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Post-traumatic headache (PTH) is a secondary headache disorder attributable to the direct and downstream effects of traumatic brain injury (TBI) on nociceptive and trigeminovascular systems. The injury cascade begins with mechanical loading of cranial and cervical structures at impact, producing axonal shearing, glial activation, and neuroinflammation in pain-modulating networks (trigeminocervical complex, thalamus, periaqueductal gray, somatosensory cortex), together with diminished descending pain inhibition and central sensitization. These changes lower the threshold for activation of the trigeminovascular system, where calcitonin gene-related peptide release, meningeal nociceptor sensitization, cortical spreading depression susceptibility, and autonomic dysregulation generate migraine-like attacks; a parallel myofascial and cervicogenic contribution arises from injury to cervical muscles and joints, producing tension-type presentations. Comorbid sleep disruption, vestibular dysfunction, and post-traumatic stress are amplifying rather than initiating factors, and medication-overuse headache can secondarily maintain the pattern. The clinical epidemiology is robust: pooled prevalence of headache after TBI is 49.3% (95% CI 44.7-53.9) across observational studies, and persistent post-traumatic headache in adult civilians is 47.1% (95% CI 34.6-59.8) with similar estimates at 3, 6, 12, and 36-plus months; in a prospective multi-center cohort, 71% of patients reported headache during the first year after injury and more than 41% still reported headache at 3, 6, and 12 months, with incidence unrelated to TBI severity (p = 0.67) but significantly related to pre-injury headache history (p < 0.001) and female sex (p < 0.01). Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a persistent headache disorder developing after a service-connected TBI is a direct-causation secondary claim, and PTH is not among the conditions listed in § 3.310(d)(1), so the nexus rests on an individual medical opinion rather than a regulatory presumption. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the TBI (with severity at the time of injury), the headache chronology relative to the injury (onset within days to weeks and persistence beyond three months), semiology consistent with the International Classification of Headache Disorders criteria for headache attributed to traumatic injury to the head, and treatment response; exclude or address primary migraine or tension-type headache predating the injury, medication-overuse headache, cervicogenic headache, and secondary causes (vascular, intracranial pressure, infection). If a pre-existing headache disorder is documented, § 3.310(b) permits service connection only for the attributable aggravation, measured against an established baseline rather than the natural progression of the pre-existing disorder.

medicalEvidence.title: Prevalence of Headache Following Traumatic Brain Injury: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Teng Y, Ge J
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (2000-2024) found a pooled prevalence of post-traumatic headache of 49.3% (95% CI 44.7-53.9) in patients with TBI, stable on sensitivity analysis; the authors note the term refers to headache reported after TBI rather than strict diagnostic-criteria cases.

medicalEvidence.title: The prevalence of persistent post-traumatic headache in adult civilian traumatic brain injury: a systematic review and meta-analysis on the past 14 years.
medicalEvidence.authors: Herrero Babiloni A, Bouferguene Y, Exposto FG, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Meta-analysis (16 studies qualitatively, 10 pooled) of adult civilian TBI estimated persistent post-traumatic headache prevalence at 47.1% (95% CI 34.6-59.8; prediction interval 10.8-85.4), similar across 3, 6, 12, and 36+ months; heterogeneity was high.

medicalEvidence.title: Natural history of headache after traumatic brain injury.
medicalEvidence.authors: Hoffman JM, Lucas S, Dikmen S, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Prospective multi-center cohort of 452 patients with TBI: 71% reported headache during the first year after injury and more than 41% still reported headache at 3, 6, and 12 months; pre-injury headache history (p < 0.001) and female sex (p < 0.01) raised risk, while incidence was not related to TBI severity (p = 0.67).

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Diabetic distal symmetric polyneuropathy (diabetic peripheral neuropathy)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated DC — rated under 38 CFR § 4.124a on the demonstrated peripheral nerve deficits (DC 8510-8530); distal lower-extremity polyneuropathy is commonly evaluated under the sciatic (DC 8520) or its branch codes (e.g., common peroneal DC 8521, posterior tibial DC 8525, femoral DC 8526), with § 4.20 analogy where the deficit does not track a single nerve trunk
originalRow.primaryCondition: Diabetes mellitus, type II (service-connected)
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 7913 (38 CFR § 4.119 — diabetes mellitus)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Type 2 diabetes produces distal symmetric polyneuropathy through chronic hyperglycemic and dyslipidemic injury to peripheral nerves and their supporting microvasculature, with a length-dependent pattern reflecting the greatest metabolic load on the longest axons. Four interdependent cascades converge: (1) increased polyol-pathway flux through aldose reductase raises intracellular sorbitol and fructose, depleting myo-inositol and NADPH and impairing Na+/K+-ATPase-dependent nerve conduction; (2) non-enzymatic glycation of proteins, lipoproteins, and nucleic acids generates advanced glycation end-products whose receptor (RAGE) signaling drives NF-kB-mediated inflammation and oxidative stress in Schwann cells, dorsal root ganglia, and endoneurial vessels; (3) activation of the hexosamine and protein kinase C pathways, mitochondrial dysfunction, and nitrosative stress amplify axonal and Schwann-cell injury; and (4) endoneurial microangiopathy (capillary basement-membrane thickening, endothelial dysfunction, impaired vasodilation, and reduced endoneurial blood flow) produces hypoxic-ischemic nerve damage that parallels diabetic retinopathy and nephropathy. The result is loss of small-fiber and then large-fiber function (pain and temperature, then vibration and proprioception), neuropathic pain, depressed reflexes, and autonomic involvement. The quantitative evidence is strong: pooled prevalence of diabetic peripheral neuropathy is 30% (95% CI 25-34) across 29 studies and 50,112 participants, higher in type 2 (31.5%) than type 1 (17.5%) diabetes; at least 50% of individuals with diabetes develop neuropathy over time; and in a 7.3-year prospective cohort the cumulative incidence was 23.5%, related to glycated hemoglobin and diabetes duration and, after adjustment, independently associated with higher total/LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, higher body-mass index, von Willebrand factor, albumin excretion rate, hypertension, and smoking. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), distal symmetric polyneuropathy developing in a veteran with service-connected type 2 diabetes is a direct-causation secondary claim. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the diabetes diagnosis, duration and glycemic control, the neuropathic examination (monofilament, vibration, pinprick, ankle reflexes, gait), and electrodiagnostic or quantitative sensory findings where needed, and address competing causes of neuropathy — vitamin B12 deficiency (including metformin-associated), alcohol use, hypothyroidism, chronic kidney disease, monoclonal gammopathy, chemotherapy, spinal stenosis or radiculopathy, and hereditary neuropathy. Where pre-existing neuropathy is documented, § 3.310(b) aggravation applies only to the attributable worsening, measured against the established baseline.

medicalEvidence.title: Prevalence of peripheral neuropathy in patients with diabetes: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Sun J, Wang Y, Zhang X, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Meta-analysis of 29 studies and 50,112 participants: pooled prevalence of diabetic peripheral neuropathy 30% (95% CI 25-34), higher in type 2 diabetes (31.5%, 95% CI 24.4-38.6) than type 1 (17.5%, 95% CI 4.8-30.2).

medicalEvidence.title: Vascular risk factors and diabetic neuropathy.
medicalEvidence.authors: Tesfaye S, Chaturvedi N, Eaton SE, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Prospective EURODIAB study of 1,172 patients with type 1 diabetes followed 7.3 years: neuropathy developed in 276 (23.5%), related to glycated hemoglobin and diabetes duration and, after adjustment, significantly associated with total and LDL cholesterol, triglycerides, body-mass index, von Willebrand factor, albumin excretion rate, hypertension, and smoking.

medicalEvidence.title: Diabetic neuropathy.
medicalEvidence.authors: Feldman EL, Callaghan BC, Pop-Busui R, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Nature Reviews Disease Primers review: diabetic neuropathy is the most prevalent complication of diabetes, with at least 50% of individuals with diabetes developing it; it begins as length-dependent sensory loss in the lower extremities and is characterized by pain and substantial morbidity, with glucose control halting progression in type 1 diabetes and showing more modest effects in type 2 diabetes.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Posterior subcapsular cataract (corticosteroid-induced)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 6027 (38 CFR § 4.79 — cataract; preoperative and pseudophakic eyes evaluated under the General Rating Formula for Diseases of the Eye; DC 6029 aphakia applies if no replacement lens is present)
originalRow.primaryCondition: Rheumatoid arthritis (service-connected), on chronic systemic corticosteroid therapy
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 5002 (38 CFR § 4.71a — multi-joint arthritis as an active process)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Systemic glucocorticoid therapy causes a characteristic posterior subcapsular cataract (PSC) through direct, receptor-mediated effects on the lens epithelium. Aqueous glucocorticoid reaches the lens and binds glucocorticoid receptors in epithelial cells at the anterior equator; the resulting changes in epithelial proliferation, migration, and differentiation disturb the orderly formation of lens fibers beneath the posterior capsule, where aberrant cells and disorganized crystallins accumulate. Biochemical correlates include altered crystallin expression and aggregation, disturbed ion and water transport with hydration of lens fibers, oxidative stress, and impaired antioxidant defenses; the opacities begin at the posterior pole, are typically bilateral, and may progress with continued exposure. Risk is related to dose, duration, and individual susceptibility (potency and route matter), and concurrent hyperglycemia may amplify lens damage. Quantitatively, in a 10-year population-based cohort of 3,654 adults with photographic lens grading, current users of oral corticosteroids had a substantially increased risk of incident posterior subcapsular cataract (odds ratio 4.11, 95% CI 1.67-10.08) and nuclear cataract (OR 3.45, 95% CI 1.26-9.43), with no increased cortical cataract risk; users of both inhaled and oral corticosteroids had an adjusted odds ratio of 4.76 (95% CI 2.59-8.74) for PSC cataract. A systematic literature review of 32 studies of long-term systemic corticosteroid exposure lists cataract (1-3% prevalence) among the common toxicities, alongside fracture (21-30%), hypertension (more than 30%), and gastrointestinal and metabolic adverse events, and notes that dose-duration risk relationships remain poorly quantified. The classic literature review documents the well-established association between corticosteroid therapy and posterior subcapsular cataract while cautioning that published series do not establish a simple dose-threshold relationship because of individual lens susceptibility. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately due to or resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so a visually significant PSC cataract developing on documented chronic systemic corticosteroid therapy for service-connected rheumatoid arthritis is a treatment-complication secondary claim; where a pre-existing cataract is documented, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the systemic corticosteroid regimen (drug, prednisone-equivalent daily dose, cumulative duration, dates), the lens findings with slit-lamp or photographic documentation and posterior subcapsular morphology, the chronology of steroid exposure relative to opacity development, and the measured visual effect; exclude or account for age-related nuclear or cortical cataract (the subtype not associated with steroids in the cohort above), diabetes, smoking, ultraviolet exposure, ocular trauma, uveitis or intraocular inflammation, and prior ocular surgery.

medicalEvidence.title: Use of inhaled and oral corticosteroids and the long-term risk of cataract.
medicalEvidence.authors: Wang JJ, Rochtchina E, Tan AG, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Population-based 10-year cohort (Blue Mountains Eye Study, 3,654 adults; photographic grading): current oral corticosteroid users had increased incident posterior subcapsular cataract (OR 4.11, 95% CI 1.67-10.08) and nuclear cataract (OR 3.45, 95% CI 1.26-9.43) but not cortical cataract; ever users of both inhaled and oral corticosteroids had adjusted OR 4.76 (95% CI 2.59-8.74) for PSC cataract.

medicalEvidence.title: Long-term Systemic Corticosteroid Exposure: A Systematic Literature Review.
medicalEvidence.authors: Rice JB, White AG, Scarpati LM, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review of 32 articles (2007-2016) on long-term systemic corticosteroid exposure: commonly cited adverse events include cataract (1-3% prevalence), bone fracture (21-30%), hypertension (more than 30%), gastrointestinal conditions (1-5%), and metabolic effects; dose- and duration-related risk remains inadequately quantified.

medicalEvidence.title: Corticosteroid-induced cataracts.
medicalEvidence.authors: Urban RC Jr, Cotlier E
medicalEvidence.summary: Classic review establishing the well-documented association between corticosteroid therapy and posterior subcapsular cataracts, describing the mechanism by which corticosteroids produce these opacities and noting that published series and individual lens susceptibility do not permit a simple dose-duration threshold.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Peripheral vestibular dysfunction (including traumatic benign paroxysmal positional vertigo)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 6204 (38 CFR § 4.87 — peripheral vestibular disorders; objective findings supporting vestibular disequilibrium are required before a compensable evaluation; DC 6205 applies where the picture meets Meniere's syndrome criteria)
originalRow.primaryCondition: Traumatic brain injury (service-connected), with residuals
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 8045 (38 CFR § 4.124a — residuals of traumatic brain injury)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Traumatic brain injury disrupts the peripheral vestibular system through mechanical and vascular injury. Impact forces transmitted to the temporal bone and labyrinth produce labyrinthine concussion with damage to the membranous labyrinth and sensory epithelia; acceleration-deceleration of the head shears the otolithic membrane and dislodges otoconia from the utricle, which migrate into a semicircular canal (most often the posterior canal) and cause positionally triggered endolymph flow — the canalithiasis mechanism of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). Additional contributions include direct injury to the vestibular nerve, hemorrhage or ischemia of the labyrinth and brainstem vestibular nuclei, and central vestibulo-ocular and vestibulospinal dysfunction that may coexist with the peripheral lesion; the clinical result is vertigo and positional dizziness, imbalance, gait instability, oscillopsia, nausea, and visual-vestibular intolerance. Severity and timing track trauma severity: in a prospective series of 117 patients with minimal, mild, or moderate head trauma examined with Dix-Hallpike and supine roll testing, 21% developed traumatic BPPV within three months (12%, 24%, and 40% across minimal, mild, and moderate trauma, respectively; p = 0.018), with nearly all onsets in the first four weeks; in a systematic review of 23 studies of non-blast TBI, BPPV was the most frequently identified peripheral vestibular deficit, diagnosed in 39.7% of 239 participants across six studies, though most data were retrospective and from tertiary centers, and a 2025 systematic review of 59 studies documents the spectrum of vestibular dysfunction after mild TBI, including dizziness, imbalance, vertigo, vestibulo-ocular dysfunction, and nystagmus, and the role of vestibular rehabilitation. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a peripheral vestibular disorder developing after a service-connected TBI is a direct-causation secondary claim; vestibular dysfunction is not among the conditions listed in § 3.310(d)(1), so an individual medical opinion is required. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the TBI, the onset and pattern of positional vertigo or imbalance relative to the injury, and objective vestibular findings (positive Dix-Hallpike or supine roll maneuver with characteristic nystagmus for BPPV; videonystagmography, video head impulse, caloric, or vestibular-evoked myogenic potential testing for non-positional deficits), and address competing causes — pre-existing or idiopathic BPPV (common in the general population, so temporal proximity to trauma is essential), vestibular migraine, Meniere's disease, medication ototoxicity, and central or cerebellar causes. Where a pre-existing vestibular disorder is documented, § 3.310(b) permits service connection only for the attributable aggravation over the established baseline.

medicalEvidence.title: Frequency of peripheral vestibular pathology following traumatic brain injury: a systematic review of literature.
medicalEvidence.authors: Šarkić B, Douglas JM, Simpson A, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review of 23 studies of adults with non-blast TBI: BPPV was the most frequently identified peripheral vestibular deficit, diagnosed in 39.7% of 239 participants across six studies; most studies were retrospective and from tertiary institutions, with the highest evidence level 2b.

medicalEvidence.title: The Risk of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo After Head Trauma.
medicalEvidence.authors: Andersson H, Jablonski GE, Nordahl SHG, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Prospective study of 117 patients with minimal, mild, or moderate head trauma examined by Dix-Hallpike and supine roll maneuvers: 21% developed traumatic BPPV within three months (12%, 24%, and 40% by increasing trauma severity; p = 0.018), with onset concentrated in the first four weeks.

medicalEvidence.title: Vestibular dysfunction after mild traumatic brain injury: A systematic review.
medicalEvidence.authors: Owens MR, Larkin E, Tenhoeve SA, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review of 59 studies: vestibular dysfunction after mild TBI commonly presents with dizziness, imbalance, vertigo, vestibulo-ocular dysfunction, postural and gait disturbance, and nystagmus; the review covers diagnostic testing and treatments including vestibular rehabilitation.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Hypopituitarism (anterior pituitary hormone deficiency following traumatic brain injury)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated DC — evaluated by analogy under 38 CFR § 4.20 to the deficient hormonal axis or residual condition within § 4.119 (for example DC 7903 hypothyroidism, DC 7911 adrenocortical insufficiency, DC 7909 diabetes insipidus); § 4.119 contains no hypopituitarism code (DC 7916 addresses hyperpituitarism only)
originalRow.primaryCondition: Traumatic brain injury (moderate or severe, service-connected), with residuals
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 8045 (38 CFR § 4.124a — residuals of traumatic brain injury)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Traumatic brain injury causes hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction through several converging mechanisms. Direct mechanical forces can fracture the skull base and sella, shear the pituitary stalk, and injure the median eminence, while rotational acceleration damages the fine hypothalamic-hypophyseal portal vasculature and the pituitary itself. Subsequent edema, hemorrhage, and hypoxic-ischemic injury (from apnea, hypotension, or raised intracranial pressure) further compromise the hypothalamic neurons and pituitary secretory cells that regulate the axes. The result is deficient synthesis or release of one or more anterior pituitary hormones: growth hormone (most commonly), gonadotropins leading to hypogonadism, thyrotropin leading to central hypothyroidism, corticotropin leading to secondary adrenal insufficiency, and less commonly antidiuretic hormone deficiency. Early post-injury abnormalities may be transient, but a substantial proportion of patients develop persistent deficits that are detectable at 12 months or later, and untreated deficiency produces fatigue, impaired quality of life, adverse metabolic profiles, and impaired recovery. The evidence base is quantitative and consistent: a systematic review pooling 19 studies of 1,137 patients found chronic-phase hypopituitarism in 27.5% (95% CI 22.8-28.9) after TBI, with higher prevalence after severe TBI; a meta-analysis of 29 studies and 2,756 participants found at least one anterior pituitary hormone dysfunction in 32% (95% CI 25-38) at 12 months or more (34% in high-quality studies); and a 2024 meta-analysis of 52 studies and 7,367 participants found any pituitary axis dysfunction in 33% (95% CI 28-37), with growth hormone deficiency 18%, gonadal deficiency 16%, ACTH deficiency 10%, and TSH deficiency 6%, and multiple affected axes in 7%. Legally, 38 CFR § 3.310(d)(1)(v) provides that diseases of hormone deficiency that result from hypothalamo-pituitary changes are presumed to be the proximate result of a service-connected TBI when they manifest within 12 months of moderate or severe TBI; where that presumption does not apply (mild TBI, or manifestation outside 12 months), § 3.310(d)(2) directs decision under generally applicable principles, i.e., a § 3.310(a) causation opinion. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the TBI and its severity using the § 3.310(d)(3) criteria (loss of consciousness, alteration of consciousness, post-traumatic amnesia, Glasgow Coma Scale, imaging), the date of manifestation of the hormone deficiency relative to the injury, and endocrinologic testing of the affected axes (morning cortisol with stimulation testing where indicated, IGF-1, LH/FSH with testosterone or estradiol, TSH with free T4, prolactin, and sodium/osmolality for diabetes insipidus), and exclude competing causes — pituitary adenoma or other sellar mass, cranial radiotherapy, hypophysitis, Sheehan's syndrome, hemochromatosis, infiltrative disease, and drug effects.

medicalEvidence.title: Hypothalamopituitary dysfunction following traumatic brain injury and aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage: a systematic review.
medicalEvidence.authors: Schneider HJ, Kreitschmann-Andermahr I, Ghigo E, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review pooling 19 studies and 1,137 patients: chronic-phase hypopituitarism prevalence was 27.5% (95% CI 22.8-28.9) after traumatic brain injury, higher after severe injury; early abnormalities were transient in some patients while hypopituitarism evolved over time in others, and affected patients showed impaired quality of life and adverse metabolic profiles.

medicalEvidence.title: Prevalence of Anterior Pituitary Dysfunction Twelve Months or More following Traumatic Brain Injury in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Emelifeonwu JA, Flower H, Loan JJ, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Meta-analysis of 29 studies and 2,756 participants: overall prevalence of at least one anterior pituitary hormone dysfunction at 12 months or more after TBI was 32% (95% CI 25-38), and 34% (95% CI 27-42) in the 12 high-quality studies; studies with a higher proportion of mild TBI had lower prevalence.

medicalEvidence.title: Acute and chronic hypopituitarism following traumatic brain injury: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Aljboor GS, Tulemat A, Al-Saedi AR, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Meta-analysis of 52 studies and 7,367 participants: pooled prevalence of any pituitary axis dysfunction after TBI was 33% (95% CI 28-37), remaining 32% (95% CI 26-38) beyond 12 months; deficiency rates were 18% for growth hormone, 16% for the gonadal axis, 10% for ACTH, and 6% for TSH, with multiple axes affected in 7%.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Migraine headache (aggravated by persistent tinnitus)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 8100 (38 CFR § 4.124a — migraine; rated by the frequency and prostration of attacks)
originalRow.primaryCondition: Tinnitus, recurrent (service-connected)
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 6260 (38 CFR § 4.87 — tinnitus, recurrent; 10% maximum, combinable where it does not support another ear rating)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Persistent tinnitus can aggravate an existing migraine diathesis through converging neurophysiological and behavioral mechanisms. Tinnitus is not a passive percept: chronic cochlear injury and deafferentation trigger maladaptive central plasticity, increased central auditory gain, and thalamocortical dysrhythmia, with limbic and salience-network modulation that attaches threat and distress to the sound; stress and sleep disruption further entrench the maladaptive state. In a brain already predisposed to migraine — a disorder of multisensory sensitization — this persistent auditory load lowers attack threshold through central sensitization, cortical hyperexcitability, and overlapping neurochemical pathways (glutamatergic excitotoxicity, neuropeptide signaling, and innate immune activation), while the distress, hypervigilance, and sleep fragmentation that accompany bothersome tinnitus amplify trigeminovascular activation and reduce habituation. The clinical literature documents the intersection: a systematic review of six studies (26,166 participants) found most studies demonstrating an association between migraine and tinnitus, with high odds and hazard ratios for tinnitus in migraine populations and migraine present in 10.1% and 22.5% of tinnitus patients in two studies; a 2026 review reports that 15-49% of migraine patients have comorbid auditory symptoms including tinnitus and that nearly two-thirds show auditory electrophysiological abnormalities; and the current authoritative tinnitus review identifies migraine, anxiety, depression, and insomnia as frequent comorbidities and describes the central-gain and thalamocortical-dysrhythmia mechanisms that plausibly drive bidirectional symptom amplification. Because most of the located evidence is cross-sectional or directionally weighted toward migraine as the exposure (migraine-to-tinnitus), this mapping is framed as aggravation under 38 CFR § 3.310(b), not as de novo causation: service connection is warranted only for the increase in migraine frequency, severity, or prostration proximately attributable to service-connected tinnitus, measured against a baseline established by medical evidence created before the aggravation or the earliest evidence between onset and current severity. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the pre-tinnitus migraine baseline (attack frequency, duration, and disability before tinnitus onset), the timing and severity of the tinnitus and its associated distress and sleep disruption, the subsequent change in migraine pattern, and effective audiologic and neurologic evaluation; exclude medication-overuse headache, new-onset primary headache, structural or vascular causes, and independent progression of the underlying migraine disorder. Where no pre-existing migraine is documented, a causation theory under § 3.310(a) may be advanced, but it requires temporal precedence of the tinnitus and an individualized opinion because the located population evidence does not establish the tinnitus-to-migraine direction.

medicalEvidence.title: Migraine associated with tinnitus and hearing loss in adults: a systematic review.
medicalEvidence.authors: Campello CP, Lemos CAA, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review (PROSPERO-registered, PRISMA) of six eligible observational studies with 26,166 participants: most studies showed an association between migraine and tinnitus, with high odds and hazard ratios for tinnitus in migraine; two investigations found migraine in 10.1% and 22.5% of tinnitus patients.

medicalEvidence.title: Migraine and auditory dysfunction: beyond comorbidity.
medicalEvidence.authors: Xu W, Zhai N, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of epidemiological, audiological, and pathophysiological data: 15-49% of migraine patients present comorbid auditory symptoms (sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, hyperacusis) and nearly two-thirds show auditory electrophysiological abnormalities; proposed mechanisms span localized microvascular ischemia, glutamate excitotoxicity, neuropeptide signaling, and innate immune activation across a peripheral-to-central sensitization continuum.

medicalEvidence.title: Tinnitus.
medicalEvidence.authors: Vanneste S, De Ridder D, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Nature Reviews Disease Primers review: tinnitus affects approximately 14% of adults (2% severe); cochlear injury and deafferentation trigger maladaptive plasticity, increased central gain, and thalamocortical dysrhythmia modulated by limbic and salience networks; migraine, anxiety, depression, and insomnia are frequent comorbidities influencing assessment and care.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (NSAID-associated)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 7206 (38 CFR § 4.114 — gastroesophageal reflux disease; rated by stricture history, dysphagia, and treatment requirements)
originalRow.primaryCondition: Osteoarthritis (service-connected), on chronic NSAID therapy
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 5003 (38 CFR § 4.71a — degenerative arthritis, other than post-traumatic)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Chronic nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) therapy injures the esophageal mucosa and promotes reflux disease through inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1-mediated prostaglandin synthesis and direct topical injury. Prostaglandins maintain mucosal blood flow, bicarbonate and mucus secretion, epithelial restitution, and mucosal immunoregulation throughout the upper gastrointestinal tract; their depletion leaves the esophageal epithelium vulnerable to acid-pepsin injury, while the weakly acidic NSAID molecule itself can cause topical injury during reflux episodes (the mechanism of action proposed in the case-control literature for NSAID-associated esophageal ulceration). Because many patients with service-connected osteoarthritis take NSAIDs continuously for years, the exposure is typically prolonged and often combined with other reflux risk factors (hiatus hernia, obesity, smoking, age), producing an additive risk profile. The population evidence is direct: a prospective case-control study of 195 patients receiving continuous NSAIDs for osteoarthritis found endoscopically diagnosed esophagitis in 41 patients (21%), with hiatus hernia (OR 3.72, 95% CI 1.63-8.49) and younger age (OR 1.79 per decade, 95% CI 1.11-2.86) increasing risk, and heartburn was reported by all esophagitis patients (OR 4.78, 95% CI 2.04-11); a meta-analysis of 102 population-based studies (460,984 subjects) found NSAID/aspirin users had modestly but significantly higher odds of gastro-oesophageal reflux symptoms (OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.10-1.88); and a mechanism review documents esophagitis among the upper gastrointestinal adverse effects of COX-1 inhibition by NSAIDs and aspirin. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately due to or resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so endoscopically documented GERD or reflux esophagitis arising on documented chronic NSAID therapy for service-connected osteoarthritis is a treatment-complication secondary claim; where reflux disease predates the NSAID exposure, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation measured against the baseline. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the specific NSAID, dose, duration, and adherence; endoscopic or clinically documented reflux disease with symptom chronology relative to NSAID initiation; and address competing causes — hiatus hernia and other anatomic factors, obesity, smoking, alcohol, pregnancy, scleroderma or other motility disorders, and proton-pump inhibitor or other acid-suppression history. Rating under DC 7206 requires the documented stricture/dysphagia and treatment picture specified by the schedule; uncomplicated reflux disease is evaluated under the applicable criteria in § 4.114 or by analogy under § 4.20.

medicalEvidence.title: Risk factors of oesophagitis in arthritic patients.
medicalEvidence.authors: Avidan B, Sonnenberg A, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Prospective case-control study of 195 patients on continuous NSAIDs for osteoarthritis: endoscopically diagnosed esophagitis in 41 patients (21%); hiatus hernia (OR 3.72, 95% CI 1.63-8.49) and younger age (OR 1.79 per decade, 95% CI 1.11-2.86) increased risk, and heartburn was present in all esophagitis patients (OR 4.78, 95% CI 2.04-11).

medicalEvidence.title: Global prevalence of, and risk factors for, gastro-oesophageal reflux symptoms: a meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Eusebi LH, Ratnakumaran R, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Meta-analysis of 102 population-based studies (460,984 subjects): weekly heartburn/regurgitation prevalence 13.3% (95% CI 12.0-14.6); NSAID/aspirin users had significantly higher odds of reflux symptoms (OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.10-1.88), alongside age 50+ (OR 1.32), smoking (OR 1.26), and obesity (OR 1.73).

medicalEvidence.title: Nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs and cyclooxygenase inhibition in the gastrointestinal tract: a trip from peptic ulcer to colon cancer.
medicalEvidence.authors: Lanas A
medicalEvidence.summary: Mechanistic review: COX-1 inhibition by NSAIDs and aspirin is linked to upper gastrointestinal adverse effects including esophagitis, peptic ulcer, and ulcer complications; the review describes the prostaglandin-dependent mucosal defense pathways whose blockade produces the injury.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Seizure disorder (post-traumatic epilepsy, unprovoked seizures)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 8910-8914 (38 CFR § 4.124a — epilepsy: grand mal 8910, petit mal 8911, Jacksonian/focal 8912, diencephalic 8913, psychomotor 8914; rated under the major- and minor-seizure formulas)
originalRow.primaryCondition: Traumatic brain injury (moderate or severe, service-connected), with residuals
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 8045 (38 CFR § 4.124a — residuals of traumatic brain injury)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Traumatic brain injury produces epilepsy through a well-characterized epileptogenic cascade. Focal cortical contusion, subdural and subarachnoid hemorrhage, and shearing of white-matter tracts create a structural lesion with hemosiderin deposition, blood-brain-barrier disruption, and reactive gliosis; injured neurons and glia release glutamate and inflammatory mediators that produce excitotoxic injury, while loss of inhibitory interneurons and aberrant axonal sprouting (mossy fiber reorganization) establish a hyperexcitable network capable of spontaneous seizure generation. The latent period between injury and the first unprovoked seizure reflects this progressive epileptogenesis, and lesional features visible on imaging (cortical contusion, subdural hematoma) are among the most consistently reported risk factors. The epidemiological evidence is strong and severity-dependent: a population-based cohort of 4,541 patients with TBI (Olmsted County, 1935-1984) found an overall standardized incidence ratio of 3.1 (95% CI 2.5-3.8), with SIR 1.5 after mild injury (no increase beyond five years), 2.9 after moderate injury, and 17.0 after severe injury; a Danish population-based cohort of 1,605,216 people found relative risks of 2.22 (95% CI 2.07-2.38) after mild injury, 7.40 (6.16-8.89) after severe injury, and 2.17 (1.73-2.71) after skull fracture, with risk still elevated more than 10 years later (severe injury RR 4.29, 95% CI 2.04-9.00) and especially high in those injured after age 15 (severe injury RR 12.24, 95% CI 8.52-17.57); and a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies (242,803 patients) found a pooled post-traumatic seizure incidence of 7.2% (95% CI 5.4-9.3), with severe TBI, subdural hematoma, cortical contusions, and older age the most consistently reported risk factors in individual studies. Legally, 38 CFR § 3.310(d)(1)(ii) provides that unprovoked seizures following moderate or severe TBI are held to be the proximate result of the service-connected TBI absent clear evidence to the contrary; where the injury was mild or the claim falls outside the presumption, § 3.310(d)(2) routes the claim to generally applicable principles and a § 3.310(a) opinion. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the TBI and its severity using the § 3.310(d)(3) criteria, the imaging findings (contusion, hemorrhage, encephalomalacia), the seizure semiology with a witness account and the date of first unprovoked seizure relative to the injury, and the electroencephalographic and neurologic workup; exclude competing causes — pre-existing epilepsy, alcohol withdrawal, metabolic derangements, medication or drug effects, central nervous system infection, tumor, and syncope or non-epileptic events misclassified as seizures. Where seizures predate the injury, only attributable worsening is service-connected under § 3.310(b).

medicalEvidence.title: A population-based study of seizures after traumatic brain injuries.
medicalEvidence.authors: Annegers JF, Hauser WA, Coan SP, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Population-based cohort of 4,541 patients with TBI: overall standardized incidence ratio for unprovoked seizures 3.1 (95% CI 2.5-3.8), rising with injury severity (mild 1.5 with no increase beyond five years, moderate 2.9, severe 17.0); significant risk factors included brain contusion with subdural hematoma, skull fracture, loss of consciousness or amnesia for more than one day, and age 65 or older.

medicalEvidence.title: Long-term risk of epilepsy after traumatic brain injury in children and young adults: a population-based cohort study.
medicalEvidence.authors: Christensen J, Pedersen MG, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Nationwide Danish cohort of 1,605,216 people: relative risk of epilepsy was 2.22 (95% CI 2.07-2.38) after mild TBI, 7.40 (6.16-8.89) after severe TBI, and 2.17 (1.73-2.71) after skull fracture, with risk still elevated more than 10 years later (severe TBI RR 4.29) and highest in those injured after age 15 (mild RR 3.51; severe RR 12.24).

medicalEvidence.title: Clinical risk factors for post-traumatic seizures: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Viaroli E, Gillespie C, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies and 242,803 adults with TBI: pooled incidence of post-traumatic seizures 7.2% (95% CI 5.4-9.3); the most consistently reported risk factors on multivariable analysis were severe TBI or lower Glasgow Coma Scale score, subdural hematoma, cortical contusions, and age, although pooled estimates were limited by heterogeneity.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Dementia / major neurocognitive disorder (TBI-associated)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 9304 (38 CFR § 4.130 — major or mild neurocognitive disorder due to traumatic brain injury); phenotype-specific codes include 9312 (due to Alzheimer's disease) and 9310 (unspecified); 9305 (vascular) is not on the § 3.310(d)(1)(iii) presumption list
originalRow.primaryCondition: Traumatic brain injury (moderate or severe, service-connected), with residuals
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 8045 (38 CFR § 4.124a — residuals of traumatic brain injury)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Traumatic brain injury increases the long-term risk of dementia through injury-driven neurodegenerative and vascular mechanisms. Focal contusions, diffuse axonal injury, and microhemorrhages initiate persistent neuroinflammation (microglial and astrocytic activation), blood-brain-barrier disruption, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired protein clearance, promoting accumulation of amyloid-beta and hyperphosphorylated tau; these proteinopathies, together with synaptic loss and reduced cognitive reserve, are the leading hypotheses linking TBI to Alzheimer-type and related dementias. Injury to small vessels and repeated episodes of impaired perfusion contribute an additional vascular burden. Several features support a causal rather than coincidental relationship: risk is dose-dependent (increasing with the number and severity of injuries), persists over decades, and is present when TBI is compared both with uninjured people and with people who sustained non-head trauma. Quantitatively, a Danish nationwide cohort of 2,794,852 people (27.6 million person-years; 132,093 with at least one TBI) found a fully adjusted hazard ratio for all-cause dementia of 1.24 (95% CI 1.21-1.27) and for Alzheimer's disease 1.16 (1.12-1.22), with the highest risk in the first six months after injury (HR 4.06, 3.79-4.34) and a graded increase with the number of TBIs (HR 1.22 after one, rising to 2.83 after five or more); a meta-analysis of 32 studies found a pooled risk ratio of 1.66 (95% CI 1.42-1.93) for dementia after TBI, with the population attributable risk among U.S. veterans twice that of the general population; and a veteran-specific meta-analysis of 13 cohorts (more than 7.1 million observations) found all-cause dementia HR 1.95 (95% CI 1.55-2.45) and vascular dementia HR 2.02 (1.46-2.80), with higher risk after severe or penetrating injury (HR 3.35) than after moderate (2.82) or mild (1.91) injury, while the association with Alzheimer's disease alone was not statistically significant (HR 1.30, 0.88-1.91). Legally, 38 CFR § 3.310(d)(1)(iii) provides that presenile dementia of the Alzheimer type, frontotemporal dementia, and dementia with Lewy bodies are held to be the proximate result of a service-connected TBI if they manifest within 15 years following moderate or severe TBI; the presumption is diagnosis- and timing-specific, and dementias outside that list (including vascular dementia) are decided under § 3.310(d)(2) on generally applicable principles with a § 3.310(a) opinion. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the TBI and its severity under § 3.310(d)(3), the dementia phenotype with formal neurocognitive testing and the date of manifestation relative to the injury, and the neurologic, psychiatric, and laboratory workup; exclude competing causes — Alzheimer's disease occurring independently of trauma, vascular dementia from hypertension or stroke, Parkinson's disease and Lewy body disease occurring independently, alcohol-related cognitive impairment, medication effects, depression with cognitive symptoms, thyroid disease, vitamin B12 deficiency, and normal-pressure hydrocephalus. Where cognitive decline predates the injury or arises from another established cause, only attributable aggravation can be service-connected under § 3.310(b).

medicalEvidence.title: Long-term risk of dementia among people with traumatic brain injury in Denmark: a population-based observational cohort study.
medicalEvidence.authors: Fann JR, Ribe AR, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Nationwide Danish cohort of 2,794,852 people (27,632,020 person-years): fully adjusted hazard ratio for all-cause dementia after TBI 1.24 (95% CI 1.21-1.27) and for Alzheimer's disease 1.16 (1.12-1.22); risk was highest in the first six months (HR 4.06) and increased with the number of TBIs (1.22 after one to 2.83 after five or more).

medicalEvidence.title: Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Population Attributable Risk of Dementia Associated with Traumatic Brain Injury in Civilians and Veterans.
medicalEvidence.authors: Gardner RC, Bahorik A, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Meta-analysis of 32 studies: pooled risk ratio for dementia after TBI 1.66 (95% CI 1.42-1.93), with higher risk at younger age and in men; the population attributable risk of dementia due to TBI among U.S. veterans was twice that of the general U.S. population because of the high prevalence of TBI in the veteran population.

medicalEvidence.title: Traumatic brain injuries among veterans and the risk of incident dementia: A systematic review & meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Leung KK, Carr FM, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Meta-analysis of 13 veteran cohorts (over 7.1 million observations): TBI associated with all-cause dementia (HR 1.95, 95% CI 1.55-2.45) and vascular dementia (HR 2.02, 95% CI 1.46-2.80), with severe or penetrating injuries carrying higher risk (HR 3.35) than moderate (2.82) or mild (1.91); the association with Alzheimer's disease alone was not statistically significant (HR 1.30, 95% CI 0.88-1.91).

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Anorgasmia (orgasmic dysfunction)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated DC — evaluated by analogy under 38 CFR § 4.20 to the disability picture, within the § 4.115b genitourinary framework (erectile dysfunction, DC 7522, is the closest content-matched schedule entry for the male analog); § 4.116 applies where the presentation is gynecological in character
originalRow.primaryCondition: Major depressive disorder (service-connected), on SSRI therapy
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 9434 (38 CFR § 4.130 — major depressive disorder; PTSD under DC 9411 and the other SSRI-treated anxiety and trauma disorders follow the same treatment pathway)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) cause orgasmic dysfunction primarily through serotonergic modulation of the neural circuits governing sexual response. Increased synaptic serotonin at 5-HT2 and related receptors inhibits the mesolimbic dopaminergic reward pathway and the medial preoptic area that mediate sexual desire, arousal, and the orgasmic reflex; serotonergic effects on the spinal ejaculation generator and on genital sensory processing increase the latency to orgasm and can abolish it entirely, while prolactin elevation and altered nitric-oxide-mediated genital vasocongestion contribute to impaired arousal. Orgasmic dysfunction is the most serotonergic-specific of the sexual side effects and typically appears shortly after drug initiation or dose escalation, persists for the duration of treatment, and resolves after discontinuation (the emerging literature on post-SSRI sexual dysfunction describes a subset with persisting symptoms after drug cessation). The evidence is quantitative and of high certainty: a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials in adults with depression found SSRI use significantly increased the risk of orgasmic dysfunction (RR 3.28, 95% CI 2.33-4.60, I2 = 8%, high certainty) and reduced sexual satisfaction (RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.11-1.32); a prospective multicenter study of 1,022 outpatients with previously normal sexual function found an overall sexual-dysfunction incidence of 59.1%, ranging from 57.7% (fluoxetine) to 72.7% (citalopram) among SSRIs, with orgasm among the assessed domains; and a management review documents that SSRIs can cause all types of sexual side effects (libido, arousal, orgasm, and ejaculation) and that up to 80% of patients may report sexual side effects, in a class prescribed for major depressive disorder, PTSD, panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately due to or resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so anorgasmia developing on documented SSRI therapy for service-connected major depressive disorder (or PTSD) is a treatment-complication secondary claim; where orgasmic dysfunction predated the medication, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the SSRI agent, dose, start date, and any dose changes with the chronology of orgasmic symptoms relative to initiation; the pre-treatment sexual history and baseline function (ideally documented contemporaneously); the effect on the relationship and distress; and address competing causes — depression itself (which independently reduces sexual function), relationship and psychosocial factors, age and menopause or hypogonadism, diabetes and other neuropathy, pelvic surgery or radiation, alcohol and other drugs, and concomitant medications (other serotonergic agents, antipsychotics, beta blockers, opioids). A trial of dose reduction, switching, or augmentation is helpful evidence where medically appropriate, and the rating proceeds by analogy under § 4.20 because no diagnostic code specifically addresses orgasmic disorder.

medicalEvidence.title: Sexual dysfunction associated with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors in adults with depression: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Dagostin Ferraz S, Kuyunga L, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 randomized controlled trials in adults with depression: SSRIs significantly increased the risk of orgasmic dysfunction (RR 3.28, 95% CI 2.33-4.60, I2 = 8%) and reduced sexual satisfaction (RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.11-1.32); GRADE assessment indicated high certainty for orgasmic dysfunction and moderate certainty for sexual satisfaction.

medicalEvidence.title: Incidence of sexual dysfunction associated with antidepressant agents: a prospective multicenter study of 1022 outpatients. Spanish Working Group for the Study of Psychotropic-Related Sexual Dysfunction.
medicalEvidence.authors: Montejo AL, Llorca G, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Prospective multicenter study of 1,022 outpatients with previously normal sexual function: overall incidence of sexual dysfunction 59.1% across antidepressants, with SSRI/venlafaxine rates of 57.7% (fluoxetine) to 72.7% (citalopram); sexual dysfunction was assessed by questionnaire across libido, orgasm, ejaculation, erectile function, and satisfaction domains.

medicalEvidence.title: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor-Induced Sexual Dysfunction: Current Management Perspectives.
medicalEvidence.authors: Atmaca M
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of SSRI-induced sexual dysfunction: SSRIs can cause all types of sexual side effects, including arousal, libido, orgasm, and ejaculation problems, and up to 80% of patients may report sexual side effects; the class is prescribed for major depressive disorder, PTSD, panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Hepatic steatosis (non-alcoholic fatty liver disease / metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated DC — rated by analogy under 38 CFR § 4.20 within § 4.114; where the documented picture meets them, DC 7345 (chronic liver disease without cirrhosis) criteria apply, and DC 7312 (cirrhosis of the liver) applies if cirrhosis develops
originalRow.primaryCondition: Diabetes mellitus, type II (service-connected)
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 7913 (38 CFR § 4.119 — diabetes mellitus)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Type 2 diabetes drives hepatic steatosis and its progression through the same insulin-resistance physiology that defines the diabetes. Chronic hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance in adipose tissue increase free fatty-acid flux to the liver while hepatic de novo lipogenesis is upregulated (SREBP-1c and ChREBP activation), and impaired fatty-acid oxidation plus very-low-density lipoprotein export failure cause triglyceride accumulation in hepatocytes. Glucotoxicity and lipotoxicity then promote lipotoxic injury, mitochondrial dysfunction, endoplasmic-reticulum stress, and inflammasome activation; adipose-tissue and gut-derived inflammatory signals drive the transition from simple steatosis to steatohepatitis, and activation of hepatic stellate cells produces progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Because type 2 diabetes also accelerates fibrosis once steatosis is present, it is one of the strongest risk factors for progression rather than merely a co-traveler. The quantitative evidence is direct and large: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of 156 studies and 1,832,125 patients found NAFLD prevalence of 65.04% (95% CI 61.79-68.15) and NASH prevalence of 31.55% in people with type 2 diabetes, with clinically significant fibrosis (F2-F4) in 35.54% and advanced fibrosis (F3-F4) in 14.95% of those with NAFLD; and a prospective cohort of 501 adults with type 2 diabetes systematically assessed by MRI-PDFF and elastography found NAFLD in 65%, advanced fibrosis in 14%, and cirrhosis in 6%, with obesity and insulin use associated with advanced fibrosis. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), fatty liver disease developing in a veteran with service-connected type 2 diabetes is a direct-causation secondary claim, and the evidence recited above — a majority prevalence of steatosis among people with type 2 diabetes together with a shared causal physiology and a demonstrated progression gradient with diabetes severity — supports the conclusion that steatotic liver disease is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected diabetes. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the diabetes (duration, control, treatment), the hepatic findings (imaging or biopsy demonstrating steatosis, and staging of fibrosis where available), and the chronology, and address competing causes — alcohol use (which may co-exist and is excluded only by a reliable history), other causes of chronic liver disease (viral hepatitis, autoimmune and drug-induced hepatitis, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency), medications (corticosteroids, methotrexate, tamoxifen, amiodarone), and other metabolic contributors (obesity, dyslipidemia, hypothyroidism). Rating follows the documented severity under DC 7345/7312 criteria or by analogy under § 4.20; where the pre-existing hepatic disease is documented, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation.

medicalEvidence.title: Global prevalence of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease in type 2 diabetes mellitus: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: En Li Cho E, Ang CZ, Quek J, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Meta-analysis of 156 studies and 1,832,125 patients: NAFLD prevalence in type 2 diabetes 65.04% (95% CI 61.79-68.15) and NASH prevalence 31.55%; among those with NAFLD, clinically significant fibrosis (F2-F4) was present in 35.54% and advanced fibrosis (F3-F4) in 14.95%.

medicalEvidence.title: The complex link between NAFLD and type 2 diabetes mellitus - mechanisms and treatments.
medicalEvidence.authors: Targher G, Corey KE, Byrne CD, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Nature Reviews Gastroenterology & Hepatology review: NAFLD and type 2 diabetes frequently coexist and act synergistically to increase adverse hepatic and extra-hepatic outcomes; type 2 diabetes is one of the strongest risk factors for faster progression of NAFLD to steatohepatitis, advanced fibrosis, or cirrhosis, and the review describes the shared insulin-resistance, lipotoxicity, and inflammatory mechanisms.

medicalEvidence.title: A prospective study on the prevalence of NAFLD, advanced fibrosis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma in people with type 2 diabetes.
medicalEvidence.authors: Ajmera V, Cepin S, Tesfai K, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Prospective cohort of 501 adults with type 2 diabetes systematically assessed with MRI-proton density fat fraction and elastography: NAFLD prevalence 65%, advanced fibrosis 14%, cirrhosis 6%; obesity and insulin use were associated with increased odds of advanced fibrosis (OR 2.50 and 2.71, respectively).

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Osteopenia (glucocorticoid-induced bone loss)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated DC — evaluated by analogy under 38 CFR § 4.20 to DC 5013 (osteoporosis, residuals of) within § 4.71a, per the note to DCs 5013-5024
originalRow.primaryCondition: Rheumatoid arthritis (service-connected), on chronic systemic corticosteroid therapy
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 5002 (38 CFR § 4.71a — multi-joint arthritis, active process)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Systemic glucocorticoids produce bone loss through direct effects on bone cells and bone vascularity, and the risk appears early in treatment. Glucocorticoids reduce the lifespan and function of osteoblasts and osteocytes, shift bone remodeling toward resorption, suppress gonadal and growth-hormone axes, and reduce bone vascularity, so that bone strength falls more than bone mineral density alone would predict; trabecular-rich sites such as the vertebrae and femoral neck are affected disproportionately, and bone loss is fastest in the first months of therapy. The fracture risk is dose-dependent and detectable even at low doses and with short courses, which matters for veterans treated with repeated steroid bursts for a service-connected inflammatory condition. Quantitatively, a cohort of 244,235 oral corticosteroid users matched to 244,235 controls found dose-dependent fracture risk: relative rate of hip fracture 0.99 (95% CI 0.82-1.20) at prednisolone doses under 2.5 mg/day, rising to 1.77 (1.55-2.02) at 2.5-7.5 mg/day and 2.27 (1.94-2.66) at 7.5 mg/day or more; vertebral fracture rates rose in parallel from 1.55 to 2.59 to 5.18; and a nationwide cohort of 1,548,945 adults found that 21.1% received short-term oral corticosteroids and that fracture risk was increased within 30 days of initiation (incidence rate ratio 1.87, 95% CI 1.69-2.07), persisting at prednisone-equivalent doses below 20 mg/day. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately due to or resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so glucocorticoid-induced osteopenia (reduced bone mineral density and/or fragility fracture) developing on documented systemic corticosteroid therapy for service-connected rheumatoid arthritis is a treatment-complication secondary claim; where reduced bone density predates the steroid exposure, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the steroid regimen (drug, prednisone-equivalent dose, duration, cumulative exposure, dates), dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry results with T-scores and dates, fracture history with imaging, and the chronology of exposure relative to bone loss; and address competing causes — postmenopausal and age-related bone loss, hypogonadism, hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D and calcium deficiency, malabsorption, chronic kidney disease, smoking, alcohol, other medications (proton-pump inhibitors, anticonvulsants, aromatase inhibitors), and immobilization. The rating proceeds by analogy under § 4.20 to DC 5013 because no code specifically addresses osteopenia.

medicalEvidence.title: Use of oral corticosteroids and risk of fractures.
medicalEvidence.authors: Van Staa TP, Leufkens HG, Abenhaim L, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Retrospective cohort of 244,235 oral corticosteroid users matched to 244,235 controls: dose-dependent fracture risk — hip fracture relative rate 0.99 (95% CI 0.82-1.20) below 2.5 mg/day prednisolone, 1.77 (1.55-2.02) at 2.5-7.5 mg/day, and 2.27 (1.94-2.66) at 7.5 mg/day or more; vertebral fracture rates 1.55, 2.59, and 5.18 respectively.

medicalEvidence.title: Short term use of oral corticosteroids and related harms among adults in the United States: population based cohort study.
medicalEvidence.authors: Waljee AK, Rogers MA, Lin P, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Nationwide cohort of 1,548,945 adults: 21.1% received at least one short-term oral corticosteroid prescription; within 30 days of initiation, fracture incidence rate ratio was 1.87 (95% CI 1.69-2.07), with increased risk persisting at prednisone-equivalent doses below 20 mg/day.

medicalEvidence.title: Glucocorticoid-Induced Osteoporosis: New Insights into the Pathophysiology and Treatments.
medicalEvidence.authors: Lane NE
medicalEvidence.summary: Mechanistic review: glucocorticoids reduce osteoblast and osteocyte lifespan and activity and reduce bone vascularity, which together explain why bone strength declines more than bone mineral density; the review summarizes the resulting fracture risk and treatment approaches.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve entrapment neuropathy)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 8515 (38 CFR § 4.124a — median nerve; rated by the degree of incomplete paralysis and, where applicable, neuritis criteria)
originalRow.primaryCondition: Hypothyroidism (service-connected)
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 7903 (38 CFR § 4.119 — hypothyroidism; residual effects rated under the appropriate body-system codes)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Hypothyroidism can produce or aggravate median-nerve compression at the wrist through deposition of mucopolysaccharide-rich ground substance (myxedema) in the flexor retinaculum, subsynovial connective tissue, and tendon sheaths, which increases carpal tunnel contents and pressure; reduced nerve tolerance to compression and slowed nerve conduction in hypothyroid nerve also lower the threshold at which entrapment becomes symptomatic. The mechanism predicts the observed clinical pattern: bilateral symptoms, a high prevalence of hypothyroidism among carpal tunnel populations, and improvement of symptoms with restoration of euthyroidism in some patients. The epidemiologic evidence is real but modest and must be presented honestly: a meta-analysis of 18 studies found hypothyroidism associated with carpal tunnel syndrome with an effect size of 2.15 (95% CI 1.64-2.83) in unadjusted analyses, attenuating to 1.44 (95% CI 1.27-1.63) in studies controlling for confounders, with evidence of publication bias; a Mendelian randomization study using genome-wide association data found hypothyroidism increased the risk of carpal tunnel syndrome (inverse-variance-weighted OR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01-1.08, p = 0.017) with no detected pleiotropy; and a hospital series of 422 patients undergoing carpal tunnel release found hypothyroidism in 13.8% and subclinical hypothyroidism in 5%, with more than two-thirds of those cases previously asymptomatic. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), carpal tunnel syndrome developing in a veteran with service-connected hypothyroidism is a direct-causation secondary claim, but because the adjusted association is modest, an 'at least as likely as not' opinion requires more than the two diagnoses: document the thyroid disease and its duration and treatment status (thyroid-stimulating hormone and free T4 with dates), the electrodiagnostic confirmation and severity of median neuropathy at the wrist, the chronology of thyroid disease relative to symptom onset, and improvement or persistence with thyroid replacement; and exclude the common competing causes — repetitive occupational or biomechanical exposure, diabetes, obesity, pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory arthropathies, amyloidosis, acromegaly, renal failure, ganglion cysts and other space-occupying lesions (the corpus already authors routes from those primaries), and idiopathic carpal tunnel syndrome. Where carpal tunnel syndrome is documented before the thyroid disease, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation.

medicalEvidence.title: Hypothyroidism and carpal tunnel syndrome: a meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Shiri R
medicalEvidence.summary: Meta-analysis of 18 studies: hypothyroidism associated with carpal tunnel syndrome with effect size 2.15 (95% CI 1.64-2.83) in unadjusted analyses, attenuating to 1.44 (95% CI 1.27-1.63) in confounder-controlled analyses, with evidence of publication bias; the author concludes the association is modest.

medicalEvidence.title: The causal relationship between thyroid dysfunction and carpal tunnel syndrome: A Mendelian randomization study.
medicalEvidence.authors: Zhang F, Cui R, Yin L, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Mendelian randomization using genome-wide association data found both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism increase carpal tunnel syndrome risk (hypothyroidism inverse-variance-weighted OR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01-1.08, p = 0.017; hyperthyroidism OR 1.08, 95% CI 1.05-1.12), with no pleiotropy detected in sensitivity analyses.

medicalEvidence.title: Prevalence of Hypothyroidism Among Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Patients at a Hospital in Saudi Arabia.
medicalEvidence.authors: Aldaghri F, Algahtani MS, Almutairi TA, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Retrospective series of 422 patients who underwent carpal tunnel release: 13.8% had hypothyroidism and 5% subclinical hypothyroidism; more than two-thirds of those with hypothyroidism had been asymptomatic, and body-mass index was significantly associated with hypothyroidism (p = 0.001).

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Hypogonadism (opioid-induced androgen deficiency)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated DC — evaluated by analogy under 38 CFR § 4.20; the closest content-matched schedule entry is DC 7523 (testis, atrophy complete) within the § 4.115b genitourinary framework, with the § 4.119 endocrine framework applying where a specific hormone-deficiency axis is rated
originalRow.primaryCondition: Degenerative disc disease of the spine (service-connected), on long-term opioid therapy
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 5242 (38 CFR § 4.71a — degenerative arthritis, degenerative disc disease other than intervertebral disc syndrome)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Long-term opioid therapy suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and produces androgen deficiency primarily by inhibiting gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) synthesis and secretion, reducing pituitary luteinizing hormone pulsatility and downstream testicular testosterone production; the suppression is opioid-receptor-mediated and occurs at analgesic doses used for chronic pain, not only in opioid dependence. The clinical picture combines low morning testosterone, low or inappropriately normal LH/FSH (hypogonadotropic pattern), and symptoms including libido and erectile dysfunction, fatigue, depressed mood, loss of muscle mass and strength, increased fat mass, and reduced bone mineral density; the effect is dose- and duration-related, varies with the specific opioid (long-acting and higher-potency agents suppress more), and reverses after opioid discontinuation in many patients. The evidence is quantitative: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 studies and 2,769 participants (800 opioid users, 1,969 controls) found mean testosterone in men was 164.78 ng/dL lower with regular opioid use (95% CI -245.47 to -84.08, p < 0.0001), regardless of opioid type, while testosterone levels in women were not significantly affected; a retrospective cohort of 1,159 men on stable single-opioid therapy for chronic non-cancer pain found androgen deficiency more likely with fentanyl (OR 25.7, 95% CI 2.82-234.97), methadone (OR 7.33, 95% CI 3.29-16.33), and oxycodone (OR 3.15, 95% CI 1.87-5.33) than with hydrocodone, with dose effects; and a focused review reports a prevalence of opioid-induced androgen deficiency in men of 20-80% depending on opioid type, duration, age, and the testosterone threshold used, with GnRH suppression as the principal mechanism and testosterone therapy improving libido, body composition, and some quality-of-life domains. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), androgen deficiency proximately resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so hypogonadism developing on documented long-term opioid therapy for service-connected degenerative disc disease is a treatment-complication secondary claim; where hypogonadism or a low baseline testosterone is documented before opioid therapy, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the opioid regimen (agent, morphine-equivalent daily dose, duration, dates), at least two morning serum testosterone measurements with LH/FSH and prolactin, symptoms and their chronology relative to opioid initiation, and any response to dose reduction or discontinuation; and exclude competing causes — primary testicular failure (elevated LH/FSH), pituitary or hypothalamic disease, hemochromatosis, obesity and metabolic syndrome, obstructive sleep apnea, thyroid disease, chronic illness, alcohol, anabolic steroid or other drug use, and age-related decline. Because no diagnostic code specifically addresses hypogonadism, the rating proceeds by analogy under § 4.20.

medicalEvidence.title: Testosterone suppression in opioid users: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Bawor M, Bami H, Dennis BB, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 studies and 2,769 participants (800 opioid users and 1,969 controls): mean testosterone in men was significantly lower with opioid use (mean difference -164.78 ng/dL, 95% CI -245.47 to -84.08, p < 0.0001) regardless of opioid type, while testosterone in women was not significantly affected.

medicalEvidence.title: Association Between Commonly Prescribed Opioids and Androgen Deficiency in Men: A Retrospective Cohort Analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Rubinstein AL, Carpenter DM
medicalEvidence.summary: Retrospective cohort of 1,159 men on stable single-opioid therapy for chronic non-cancer pain with morning testosterone measurement: androgen deficiency was more likely with fentanyl (OR 25.7, 95% CI 2.82-234.97), methadone (OR 7.33, 95% CI 3.29-16.33), and oxycodone (OR 3.15, 95% CI 1.87-5.33) than with hydrocodone, and increased with hydrocodone and oxycodone dose.

medicalEvidence.title: Opioid-induced androgen deficiency in men: Prevalence, pathophysiology, and efficacy of testosterone therapy.
medicalEvidence.authors: Kafel H, Braga-Basaria M, Basaria S
medicalEvidence.summary: Focused review: opioid-induced androgen deficiency in men has a prevalence of 20-80% depending on opioid type, duration of exposure, age, and testosterone threshold; opioids suppress the gonadal axis mainly by inhibiting GnRH synthesis and secretion, and limited trial data show testosterone therapy improves libido, body composition, and some quality-of-life domains.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Insomnia disorder (chronic, post-traumatic)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated DC — evaluated under the 38 CFR § 4.130 General Rating Formula for Mental Disorders by analogy to the listed mental disorders, with § 4.14 prohibiting duplicate evaluation where insomnia is a symptom of an already service-connected mental disorder
originalRow.primaryCondition: Traumatic brain injury (service-connected), with residuals
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 8045 (38 CFR § 4.124a — residuals of traumatic brain injury)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Traumatic brain injury produces chronic insomnia through structural and functional injury to the sleep-wake regulatory system rather than through pain or psychological factors alone. The ascending arousal system (brainstem cholinergic and monoaminergic nuclei), the hypothalamic sleep-wake switch including orexin/hypocretin neurons, the suprachiasmatic nucleus and its light-entrainment input, and the thalamocortical circuits that generate sleep spindles are all vulnerable to shearing, contusion, and hypoxic-ischemic injury; diffuse axonal injury and neuroinflammation (microglial activation with cytokine release, including interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor) further disturb sleep homeostasis and circadian timing. Clinically this produces sleep-onset and sleep-maintenance insomnia, fragmentation, and non-restorative sleep, often with excessive daytime sleepiness, and the disturbance can persist for years after the injury and impede rehabilitation. The epidemiologic evidence is substantial: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 studies (19 meta-analyzed, n = 95,195) found pooled prevalence of post-mild-TBI insomnia disorder of 27.0% (95% CI 6.49-54.68) and insomnia symptoms of 71.7% (95% CI 60.31-81.85), significantly higher than general-population estimates, though heterogeneity was high; a second, larger synthesis of 69 studies found adults with prior mild TBI reported worse subjective sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index elevations) at every recovery phase from under a week to one year and beyond, while objective sleep-stage differences were less robust after bias adjustment; and a mechanistic review documents the neural-network, neuroendocrine, sleep-wake-regulator, and immune-inflammatory pathways implicated in post-TBI sleep-wake disturbance. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a chronic insomnia disorder developing after a service-connected TBI is a direct-causation secondary claim; insomnia is not among the conditions listed in § 3.310(d)(1), so an individual medical opinion is required. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the TBI and its severity using the § 3.310(d)(3) criteria, the sleep history with onset relative to the injury and persistence over time (sleep diary, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index or insomnia severity measures, and polysomnography where indicated), and the treatment history; exclude or account for competing causes — obstructive and central sleep apnea, restless legs syndrome and periodic limb movements, circadian rhythm disorders, pain, post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety and depression, substance and medication effects (including stimulants and sedatives), and primary insomnia predating the injury. Where pre-existing insomnia is documented, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation, and where insomnia is a symptom of an already service-connected mental disorder, § 4.14 prohibits duplicate evaluation.

medicalEvidence.title: Prevalence of insomnia and insomnia symptoms following mild-traumatic brain injury: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Montgomery MC, Baylan S, Gardani M
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 studies (19 pooled, n = 95,195): pooled prevalence of post-mild-TBI insomnia disorder was 27.0% (95% CI 6.49-54.68) and of insomnia symptoms 71.7% (95% CI 60.31-81.85), significantly higher than general-population estimates, with high heterogeneity and methodological differences among studies.

medicalEvidence.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of sleep following mild traumatic brain injury: A synthesis of the literature according to age and time-since-injury.
medicalEvidence.authors: Roberts SSH, Owen PJ, Warmington SA, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 69 studies comparing sleep after mild TBI with controls: adults with prior mild TBI reported worse subjective sleep quality (higher Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores) at every recovery phase from under one week to one year and beyond (mean differences 2.26-2.86 points); objective sleep-stage differences were largely not robust after removing studies with selection bias.

medicalEvidence.title: Characteristics and Neural Mechanisms of Sleep-Wake Disturbances After Traumatic Brain Injury.
medicalEvidence.authors: Yan G, Wei Y, Wang D, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Mechanistic review: sleep-wake disturbances are among the most common complaints after TBI and include insomnia, excessive daytime sleepiness, hypersomnia, obstructive sleep apnea, and circadian rhythm disorders; implicated pathways include abnormal neural network function, neuroendocrine changes, disturbance of sleep-wake regulators, and immune-inflammatory responses related to the structural brain injury.
