originalRow.secondaryCondition: Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis of bone, glucocorticoid-associated)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated DC — evaluated by analogy under 38 CFR § 4.20; where the affected joint's function is impaired, residuals are evaluated under the applicable § 4.71a joint-schedule code and § 4.40 (functional loss), with post-surgical residuals rated under the appropriate codes
originalRow.primaryCondition: Asthma, bronchial (service-connected), on chronic or recurrent systemic corticosteroid therapy
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 6602 (38 CFR § 4.97 — asthma, bronchial; the schedule expressly contemplates daily systemic corticosteroids and intermittent courses of at least three per year)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Systemic glucocorticoids cause osteonecrosis of bone — most often the femoral head, but also the humeral head, knee, and talus — through a sequence of direct cell toxicity and vascular compromise. Glucocorticoids induce apoptosis of osteocytes and osteoblasts, suppress osteogenesis, and shift marrow stromal differentiation toward adipocytes, which expands the fatty marrow and raises intraosseous pressure; fat microemboli and thrombi further occlude the subchondral microvasculature, producing ischemia of the femoral head, subchondral fracture, and collapse of the articular surface with secondary joint degeneration. The risk is corticosteroid-dose-dependent and appears early in treatment rather than requiring years of exposure; the affected joint is often painful and disabling even before radiographic collapse, and magnetic resonance imaging detects the lesion before plain films. The quantitative evidence is strong: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 35 studies and 11,356 patients with systemic lupus erythematosus found that pulse steroid therapy (OR 2.02, P < 0.00001), an initial dose greater than 60 mg/day (OR 4.19, P < 0.0001), and a maximum daily dose greater than 50 mg significantly increased the risk of osteonecrosis of the femoral head, while cumulative glucocorticoid dose showed no significant association — identifying short-term high-dose exposure, not cumulative burden, as the core medication-related risk; a nationally representative survey of 30,030 Chinese adults found a non-traumatic femoral-head osteonecrosis prevalence of 0.725% (218 cases; an estimated 8.12 million affected nationally) with glucocorticoid intake among the significant independent risk factors; and the ARCO international consensus classification recognizes glucocorticoid-associated osteonecrosis as a distinct etiologic category with its own diagnostic criteria. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately due to or resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so glucocorticoid-associated osteonecrosis developing after systemic corticosteroid therapy for service-connected asthma is a treatment-complication secondary claim — the analysis does not require that the veteran have been on steroids continuously, because the evidence identifies high-dose pulse and initial-dose exposure as sufficient; where pre-existing osteonecrosis or an established alternative cause is documented, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the corticosteroid regimen (drug, route, prednisone-equivalent dose including initial and pulse doses, dates), the imaging (MRI, which is the most sensitive, or radiographs with staging), the chronology of steroid exposure relative to symptom onset, and the functional loss; and exclude competing causes — alcohol abuse, prior trauma, sickle cell disease and other hemoglobinopathies, decompression sickness, Gaucher disease, coagulation disorders, radiation, and idiopathic osteonecrosis. Because no diagnostic code specifically addresses osteonecrosis, the rating proceeds by analogy under § 4.20 to the § 4.71a joint-schedule entries for the affected joint's residual functional loss.

medicalEvidence.title: Population characteristics, glucocorticoid dosage, and risk factors for osteonecrosis of the femoral head in systemic lupus erythematosus: a Systematic Review and meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Zhang J, Zhang J, Dong Y, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 35 studies and 11,356 patients: pulse steroid therapy (OR 2.02, P < 0.00001), an initial glucocorticoid dose greater than 60 mg/day (OR 4.19, P < 0.0001), a maximum daily dose greater than 50 mg (SMD 0.42, P = 0.0002), and higher average daily intake (SMD 0.32, P = 0.004) significantly increased osteonecrosis risk, while cumulative dose did not (P = 0.14) — short-term high-dose exposure, not cumulative burden, is the core medication-related risk.

medicalEvidence.title: Prevalence of Nontraumatic Osteonecrosis of the Femoral Head and its Associated Risk Factors in the Chinese Population: Results from a Nationally Representative Survey.
medicalEvidence.authors: Zhao DW, Yu M, Hu K, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Nationally representative survey of 30,030 adults: non-traumatic femoral-head osteonecrosis was diagnosed in 218 subjects (0.725%; an estimated 8.12 million cases), and multivariate regression showed glucocorticoid intake — along with a family history of osteonecrosis, heavy smoking, alcohol abuse, and metabolic factors — was significantly associated with increased risk.

medicalEvidence.title: Etiologic Classification Criteria of ARCO on Femoral Head Osteonecrosis Part 1: Glucocorticoid-Associated Osteonecrosis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Yoon BH, Jones LC, Chen CH, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: International consensus (ARCO) etiologic classification criteria establishing glucocorticoid-associated osteonecrosis of the femoral head as a distinct diagnostic category with defined criteria — the clinical standard under which a steroid-exposed patient is classified.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Diabetic gastroparesis (delayed gastric emptying due to diabetic autonomic neuropathy)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 7356 (38 CFR § 4.114 — gastrointestinal dysmotility syndrome; the schedule entry whose criteria address poor gastric emptying, with DC 7319 reserved for irritable bowel syndrome)
originalRow.primaryCondition: Diabetes mellitus, type II (service-connected)
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 7913 (38 CFR § 4.119 — diabetes mellitus)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Type 2 diabetes causes gastroparesis through chronic hyperglycemic injury to the autonomic and enteric nervous systems that regulate the stomach. Sustained hyperglycemia drives oxidative stress, advanced glycation end-product accumulation, and microvascular disease in the vagus nerve and gastric myenteric plexus; the resulting vagal neuropathy, loss of interstitial cells of Cajal (the gastric pacemaker cells), and depletion of neuronal nitric oxide synthase impair fundal accommodation and antral contractility and cause pyloric spasm, so gastric contents empty too slowly. The clinical picture is early satiety, prolonged postprandial fullness, bloating, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, and the condition is a complication of long-standing diabetes; it is associated with increased mortality and complicates glycemic control because of unpredictable absorption of food and medication. The epidemiologic evidence is direct: a systematic review and meta-analysis found the pooled prevalence of gastroparesis among patients with diabetes to be 9.3%, with the highest subgroup prevalence in type 2 diabetes at 12.5% (95% CI 7.7-17.3), and a large US epidemiological study of 82.6 million patients identified type 2 diabetes as the single most common cause of gastroparesis (51.7% of cases) — ahead of postsurgical effects, medication effects, and idiopathic cases. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), gastroparesis developing in a veteran with service-connected type 2 diabetes is a direct-causation secondary claim: the diabetes is the proximate cause through diabetic autonomic neuropathy, and no new injury is required. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the diabetes (duration, control, complications), the gastric-emptying study (scintigraphy or a validated breath test) or the clinical diagnosis with exclusion of obstruction by endoscopy, the symptom chronology relative to diabetes duration, and treatment response; and exclude competing causes — medication effects (opioids, GLP-1 receptor agonists, anticholinergics), prior gastric or esophageal surgery, hypothyroidism, Parkinson disease and other neurological disease, connective tissue disease, amyloidosis, and viral injury. Where pre-existing gastroparesis is documented, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. Because gastric dysmotility in diabetes is evaluated under DC 7356, the requirement for a diagnostic code is met directly rather than by analogy.

medicalEvidence.title: Prevalence of gastroparesis in diabetic patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Li L, Wang L, Long R, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis: the pooled prevalence of gastroparesis in patients with diabetes was 9.3%, with a significantly higher prevalence in type 2 diabetes (12.5%, 95% CI 7.7-17.3) than type 1 diabetes (8.3%); women and patients under 60 had higher estimates, and the authors report high heterogeneity and limited robustness (an erratum was subsequently published).

medicalEvidence.title: Gastroparesis: A Review.
medicalEvidence.authors: Camilleri M
medicalEvidence.summary: JAMA review of gastroparesis: the condition is caused by reduced contractions of the distal stomach or abnormal pyloric relaxation; in a large US epidemiological study of 82.6 million patients, the most common cause was type 2 diabetes (51.7%), followed by postsurgical effects (15%), medication-induced cases (11.8%), and idiopathic cases (11.3%); prevalence of definite gastroparesis was 21.5 per 100,000 persons.

medicalEvidence.title: Diabetic gastroparesis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Koch KL, Calles-Escandón J
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of diabetic gastroparesis as a complication of long-standing type 1 and type 2 diabetes, with symptoms of early satiety, prolonged postprandial fullness, bloating, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain; a subset of patients has pylorospasm producing obstructive gastroparesis, and mortality is increased in patients with diabetic gastroparesis.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Obstructive sleep apnea (sleep apnea syndromes)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 6847 (38 CFR § 4.97 — sleep apnea syndromes, obstructive, central, mixed; rated from 0 to 100 percent, with the 50-percent level assigned for use of a breathing assistance device such as CPAP)
originalRow.primaryCondition: Hypothyroidism (service-connected)
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 7903 (38 CFR § 4.119 — hypothyroidism; residual effects rated under the appropriate body-system codes)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Hypothyroidism causes or aggravates obstructive sleep apnea through deposition of mucopolysaccharide-rich ground substance (myxedema) in the soft tissues of the upper airway — the tongue (macroglossia), pharyngeal walls, soft palate, and larynx — which narrows the pharyngeal lumen and increases collapsibility during sleep; hypothyroid myopathy of the pharyngeal dilator muscles and blunted ventilatory drive further promote obstruction and hypoventilation. Because hypothyroidism is treatable, the mechanism has a therapeutic prediction: restoration of euthyroidism reduces apnea severity in many patients, which supports the causal direction. The clinical evidence is consistent: a meta-analysis of 12 studies and 5 case reports (192 hypothyroid OSA patients vs 1,423 euthyroid OSA patients) found the prevalence of clinical hypothyroidism among OSA patients was 8.12 ± 7.13% and subclinical hypothyroidism 11.07 ± 8.49%, with higher apnea-hypopnea index, more time with oxygen desaturation below 90%, and higher Epworth sleepiness scores in the hypothyroid group at diagnosis; a US population study (NHANES 2007-2008, 5,515 adults) found hypothyroidism associated with sleep apnea after adjustment for demographics, body-mass index, and comorbidities (OR 1.88, 95% CI 1.24-2.84, P < 0.01); and a cross-sectional study of 100 hypothyroid patients found obstructive sleep apnea (AHI at least 5) in 74% — with 85.3% prevalence among treatment-naive patients versus 66.1% among those on thyroid replacement (P = 0.030), and 40.5% of cases severe. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), obstructive sleep apnea developing in a veteran with service-connected hypothyroidism is a direct-causation secondary claim. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the thyroid disease and its treatment status (TSH and free T4 with dates), the sleep study with the apnea-hypopnea index and severity, the chronology of thyroid disease relative to sleep symptoms, and any change in apnea severity with thyroid replacement; and address competing causes — obesity (the dominant confounder, which must be documented and weighed rather than assumed), acromegaly, nasal obstruction and deviated septum, tonsillar hypertrophy and craniofacial anomalies, sedative, alcohol, and opioid effects, and age. Where pre-existing sleep apnea or an established alternative cause is documented, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation.

medicalEvidence.title: Role of hypothyroidism in obstructive sleep apnea: a meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Zhang M, Zhang W, Tan J, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Meta-analysis of 12 studies and 5 case reports comparing 192 hypothyroid OSA patients with 1,423 euthyroid OSA patients: prevalence of clinical hypothyroidism among OSA patients was 8.12 ± 7.13% (subclinical 11.07 ± 8.49%), and the hypothyroid group had significantly higher apnea-hypopnea index, more desaturation time below 90%, and higher Epworth sleepiness scores at diagnosis.

medicalEvidence.title: Hypothyroidism and Its Association With Sleep Apnea Among Adults in the United States: NHANES 2007-2008.
medicalEvidence.authors: Thavaraputta S, Dennis JA, Laoveeravat P, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Cross-sectional analysis of 5,515 US adults (NHANES 2007-2008): hypothyroidism prevalence was 9.47%, and multivariate logistic regression adjusted for demographics, health care access, body-mass index, socioeconomic factors, alcohol, smoking, and comorbidities showed a significant association between hypothyroidism and sleep apnea (OR 1.88, 95% CI 1.24-2.84, P < 0.01).

medicalEvidence.title: Obstructive sleep apnea in hypothyroidism.
medicalEvidence.authors: Pancholi C, Chaudhary SC, Gupta KK, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Cross-sectional study of 100 hypothyroidism patients: 74% had obstructive sleep apnea on polysomnography (AHI at least 5), with 40.5% of those severe; treatment-naive patients had significantly higher OSA prevalence (85.3%) than patients on thyroid replacement (66.1%, P = 0.030), supporting both the association and an effect of treating the hypothyroidism.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Peptic ulcer disease (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug-associated gastroduodenal ulcer)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 7304 (38 CFR § 4.114 — peptic ulcer disease, including the post-operative, recurrent pain with anemia, and medication-managed episode criteria, with a 0-percent level for an endoscopic or imaging-documented history)
originalRow.primaryCondition: Osteoarthritis (service-connected), on chronic nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug therapy
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 5003 (38 CFR § 4.71a — degenerative arthritis)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs cause peptic ulcers by inhibiting cyclooxygenase-1 and thereby depleting the prostaglandins that protect the gastroduodenal mucosa: prostaglandin E2 and prostacyclin normally stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion, increase mucosal blood flow, and drive epithelial repair, so their loss leaves the mucosa vulnerable to acid and pepsin; NSAIDs are also weak acids that trap in parietal cells and cause direct topical injury, and both mechanisms together produce erosions and ulcers, most often in the stomach and duodenum. Importantly for claims, the injury occurs at therapeutic analgesic doses used for musculoskeletal pain, can occur without warning symptoms, and is the leading medication-related cause of ulcer bleeding. The quantitative evidence is strong: a meta-analysis of 25 studies found uncomplicated peptic-ulcer disease significantly more common in NSAID takers than in controls (35.8% vs 8.3%), with NSAID use increasing the risk of peptic ulcer approximately 3.55-fold and of ulcer bleeding 4.85-fold, and a synergistic interaction when Helicobacter pylori infection coexists; a separate meta-analysis of peptic-ulcer risk factors attributed 24% of peptic-ulcer disease in the general population to NSAIDs; and current Cochrane evidence frames the entire class of NSAID-induced ulcers as a recognized, preventable entity for which proton-pump inhibitors are the standard protective therapy. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately due to or resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so peptic ulcer disease developing on documented chronic NSAID therapy for service-connected osteoarthritis is a treatment-complication secondary claim; where pre-existing ulcer disease is documented, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the NSAID regimen (agent, dose, duration, dates, over-the-counter use), the endoscopic or imaging diagnosis (DC 7304 requires endoscopic or imaging documentation where rated at 0 percent, and the evaluation above that level follows symptom burden), the chronology of NSAID exposure relative to ulcer diagnosis, and treatment; and exclude competing causes — Helicobacter pylori infection (test and treat), alcohol and smoking, physiologic stress and critical illness, corticosteroid co-therapy, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and gastric malignancy (with ulcer symptoms requiring biopsy at endoscopy where indicated). Where the veteran also has service-connected GERD evaluated under DC 7206, § 4.14 bars using the same signs and symptoms under both codes.

medicalEvidence.title: Role of Helicobacter pylori infection and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs in peptic-ulcer disease: a meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Huang JQ, Sridhar S, Hunt RH
medicalEvidence.summary: Lancet meta-analysis of 25 studies: peptic-ulcer disease was significantly more common in NSAID takers than controls (138/385, 35.8% vs 23/276, 8.3%) irrespective of H. pylori infection; NSAID use increased ulcer risk approximately 3.55-fold and ulcer-bleeding risk 4.85-fold, with synergy when H. pylori infection coexisted.

medicalEvidence.title: Meta-analysis of risk factors for peptic ulcer. Nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, Helicobacter pylori, and smoking.
medicalEvidence.authors: Kurata JH, Nogawa AN
medicalEvidence.summary: Meta-analysis of attributable risk models for peptic ulcer and serious upper-GI events: the population attributable risk percent for NSAIDs was 24% (H. pylori 48%, smoking 23%), and in the no-interaction model these three factors accounted for the overwhelming majority of peptic-ulcer-related risk.

medicalEvidence.title: Proton pump inhibitors for the prevention of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug-induced ulcers and dyspepsia.
medicalEvidence.authors: Garegnani L, Oltra G, Burgos MA, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Cochrane review stating that chronic NSAID consumption increases the risk of gastrointestinal toxicity ranging from mild dyspepsia to serious ulcer complications such as bleeding, obstruction, and perforation, and assessing proton-pump inhibitors for prevention of NSAID-induced ulcers and dyspepsia — the clinical standard confirming NSAID-induced ulceration as a recognized, preventable entity.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Glaucoma (corticosteroid-induced ocular hypertension progressing to secondary open-angle glaucoma)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 6013 (38 CFR § 4.79 — open-angle glaucoma; evaluated under the General Rating Formula for Diseases of the Eye with a minimum 10-percent evaluation if continuous medication is required; DC 6012 for angle-closure glaucoma if the mechanism is documented as angle closure)
originalRow.primaryCondition: Rheumatoid arthritis (service-connected), on chronic corticosteroid therapy (systemic, topical ocular, periocular, or inhaled)
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 5002 (38 CFR § 4.71a — multi-joint arthritis, active process)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Corticosteroids raise intraocular pressure and produce secondary open-angle glaucoma by increasing resistance to aqueous humor outflow through the conventional pathway — the trabecular meshwork, the juxtacanalicular connective tissue, and the inner wall of the Schlemm canal. Glucocorticoids induce extracellular matrix deposition (including myocilin and fibronectin) and cytoskeletal changes in trabecular meshwork cells that reduce outflow facility, so intraocular pressure rises; in susceptible individuals the steroid response progresses from asymptomatic ocular hypertension to sustained pressure elevation, glaucomatous optic neuropathy, and irreversible visual-field loss if the elevation is unrecognized or continues. The effect is a class property of corticosteroids rather than of any one drug or route: it has been recognized since the 1950s after systemic ACTH and both topical and systemic corticosteroids, risk increases with prolonged use, higher frequency, higher anti-inflammatory potency, and greater ocular penetrance (and is greater in children and in known steroid responders), and reducing the molecule's intrinsic steroid activity (as with loteprednol etabonate) demonstrably reduces the intraocular pressure effect. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately due to or resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so corticosteroid-induced ocular hypertension and glaucomatous damage developing on documented corticosteroid therapy for service-connected rheumatoid arthritis is a treatment-complication secondary claim; where pre-existing open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension is documented before steroid exposure, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the corticosteroid regimen (drug, route, potency, frequency, duration, dates — including topical ocular and periocular injections, which carry the highest ocular risk), serial intraocular pressure measurements and optic-nerve and visual-field examinations with dates, the chronology of pressure rise relative to steroid exposure, and the response to steroid withdrawal or pressure-lowering therapy; and address competing causes — primary open-angle glaucoma (family history, age, myopia, African ancestry, diabetes), angle-closure mechanisms, uveitis and other intraocular inflammation, pseudoexfoliation, and pigment dispersion. Because the diagnosis is open-angle glaucoma unless the mechanism is angle closure, the claim is evaluated under DC 6013 (or DC 6012 for angle closure) — the requirement for a diagnostic code is met directly rather than by analogy.

medicalEvidence.title: Steroid-Induced Glaucoma.
medicalEvidence.authors: Zeppieri M, Capobianco M, Khazaeni L
medicalEvidence.summary: StatPearls clinical review: corticosteroid-induced ocular hypertension and glaucoma are among the most clinically relevant ocular adverse effects of a very widely prescribed drug class; steroid-induced glaucoma is a form of secondary open-angle glaucoma in which intraocular pressure rises because of increased resistance to aqueous humor outflow at the trabecular meshwork, juxtacanalicular tissue, and Schlemm canal, and it progresses from the steroid response and ocular hypertension to glaucomatous optic neuropathy and visual-field loss when the elevation is sustained or unrecognized.

medicalEvidence.title: Risk of intraocular pressure elevation after topical steroids in children and adults: A systematic review.
medicalEvidence.authors: Musleh MG, Bokre D, Dahlmann-Noor AH
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review of randomized trials of topical corticosteroids: topical steroids induce rises in intraocular pressure, and the risk increases with prolonged use, high frequency of administration, young age, higher ocular penetrance, and higher anti-inflammatory potency.

medicalEvidence.title: Impact of the Topical Ophthalmic Corticosteroid Loteprednol Etabonate on Intraocular Pressure.
medicalEvidence.authors: Sheppard JD, Comstock TL, Cavet ME
medicalEvidence.summary: Review establishing that topical ophthalmic corticosteroids carry an inherent class risk of elevated intraocular pressure — a risk factor for glaucoma — and that loteprednol etabonate's ester structure minimizes this effect, demonstrating that the pressure response is attributable to the corticosteroid moiety itself.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Barrett's esophagus (intestinal metaplasia of the distal esophagus)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 7207 (38 CFR § 4.114 — Barrett's esophagus; with esophageal stricture rated as DC 7203, without stricture 30 percent with high-grade dysplasia and 10 percent with low-grade dysplasia)
originalRow.primaryCondition: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (service-connected)
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 7206 (38 CFR § 4.114 — gastroesophageal reflux disease)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Chronic gastroesophageal reflux causes Barrett's esophagus by driving reparative metaplasia of the distal esophageal epithelium: repeated exposure of the squamous mucosa to gastric acid and pepsin (and, where present, bile) produces chronic epithelial injury, and in genetically susceptible individuals the healing response replaces the damaged squamous epithelium with intestinalized columnar mucosa — the metaplastic change that defines Barrett's esophagus and that carries the risk of progression through low-grade and high-grade dysplasia to esophageal adenocarcinoma. The risk is not binary: longer duration and greater frequency of reflux symptoms, male sex, older age, central obesity, smoking, and family history all raise the probability of the metaplastic transformation, and screening guidelines treat GERD as the cardinal clinical criterion. The quantitative evidence is direct: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 43 studies (12,883 patients with GERD and 51,350 without) found Barrett's esophagus prevalence of 7% (95% CI 5.8-8.5%) in patients with GERD versus 2.2% (95% CI 1.6-3%) in those without, with an odds ratio for Barrett's esophagus of 2.91 (95% CI 2.06-4.11) and 4.17 (95% CI 1.78-9.77) for long-segment disease; a systematic review and meta-analysis of 49 studies and 307,273 individuals found Barrett's prevalence rising from 0.8% in the low-risk general population to 3% with GERD and 12.2% with GERD plus any additional risk factor, with a positive linear relationship between the number of risk factors and prevalence; and the JAMA scientific review of the reflux-Barrett's-adenocarcinoma sequence documents that Barrett's esophagus — metaplasia from squamous to intestinalized columnar mucosa — is associated with chronic reflux and is the pathway through which adenocarcinoma develops. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), Barrett's esophagus developing in a veteran with service-connected GERD is a direct-causation secondary claim. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the GERD diagnosis (duration, symptom frequency and severity, endoscopic and, where performed, ambulatory pH findings), the upper endoscopy with biopsy demonstrating intestinal metaplasia and any dysplasia grade, and the chronology of chronic reflux relative to the metaplastic change; and address competing contributors — obesity and central adiposity, smoking, age and male sex as susceptibility factors rather than alternative diagnoses, and the known inverse association with Helicobacter pylori. Where Barrett's esophagus or dysplasia is documented before the service-connected reflux disease, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. Where the veteran's GERD itself is evaluated under DC 7206, § 4.14 prohibits using the same stricture or dysphagia findings to evaluate both the GERD and the Barrett's esophagus.

medicalEvidence.title: Prevalence of Barrett's Esophagus and Esophageal Adenocarcinoma With and Without Gastroesophageal Reflux: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Saha B, Vantanasiri K, Mohan BP, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 43 studies (12,883 patients with GERD; 51,350 without): Barrett's esophagus prevalence was 7% (95% CI 5.8-8.5%) with GERD versus 2.2% (95% CI 1.6-3%) without, with odds ratios of 2.91 (95% CI 2.06-4.11) for Barrett's esophagus and 4.17 (95% CI 1.78-9.77) for long-segment disease in patients with GERD.

medicalEvidence.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prevalence and risk factors for Barrett's esophagus.
medicalEvidence.authors: Qumseya BJ, Bukannan A, Gendy S, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 49 studies and 307,273 individuals: Barrett's esophagus prevalence was 0.8% (95% CI 0.6-1.1%) in the low-risk general population, 3% (95% CI 2.3-4%) with GERD, and 12.2% (95% CI 10.2-14.6%) with GERD plus any additional risk factor, with a positive linear relationship between the number of risk factors and prevalence.

medicalEvidence.title: Gastroesophageal reflux, barrett esophagus, and esophageal cancer: scientific review.
medicalEvidence.authors: Shaheen N, Ransohoff DF
medicalEvidence.summary: JAMA scientific review: GERD is a risk factor for esophageal adenocarcinoma, which may develop from Barrett's esophagus — a metaplastic change of the esophageal epithelium from squamous to intestinalized columnar mucosa associated with chronic reflux — establishing the clinical-standard etiologic sequence from chronic reflux to metaplasia.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Peripheral neuropathy (chronic alcohol-related axonal polyneuropathy)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 8520 (38 CFR § 4.124a — sciatic nerve) as the usual schedule entry for a symmetric lower-extremity axonal neuropathy, with evaluation keyed to the degree of incomplete paralysis; other § 4.124a peripheral-nerve codes apply according to the documented distribution and severity
originalRow.primaryCondition: Alcohol use disorder (service-connected)
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated DC — alcohol use disorder is evaluated under the 38 CFR § 4.130 General Rating Formula for Mental Disorders (the schedule's code list at 9201-9440 contains no substance-specific entry), with § 4.14 prohibiting duplicate evaluation where a substance-induced disorder is already evaluated
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Chronic heavy alcohol use produces a length-dependent axonal polyneuropathy through two converging mechanisms: direct neurotoxicity from ethanol and its metabolite acetaldehyde, which generate oxidative stress and activate protein kinase C epsilon signaling in peripheral nerve, and the nutritional deficiencies that commonly accompany sustained heavy drinking — most importantly thiamine, but also folate, B12, and other vitamins — which impair axonal energy metabolism and repair. The result is axonal degeneration with reduced density of both small and large fibers, a stockings-and-gloves sensory loss with hyperalgesia and weakness, reduced sensory nerve action potential amplitudes with mild conduction slowing on electrodiagnostic testing, and greater vulnerability in women at a given lifetime dose. The quantitative evidence is consistent: a systematic review and meta-analysis (87 articles) found the prevalence of peripheral neuropathy among chronic alcohol abusers to be 46.3% (95% CI 35.7-57.3%), with the review detailing the toxic and nutritional pathogenetic mechanisms; a clinical-electroneurographic study of 62 chronic alcoholics found clinical and/or subclinical neuropathy — mostly axonal — in 67.7% (65.9% of men and 72.2% of women), with women showing significantly greater lifetime alcohol exposure effects at lower cumulative doses; and a mechanistic review documents axonal degeneration, reduced small and large fiber density, direct ethanol and acetaldehyde neurotoxicity, oxidative stress, and the contribution of dietary vitamin deficiency in the pathogenesis. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), peripheral neuropathy developing in a veteran with service-connected alcohol use disorder is a direct-causation secondary claim. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the alcohol use disorder with a quantified drinking history (dose, duration, pattern), the neurologic examination and electrodiagnostic findings (nerve conduction studies and electromyography demonstrating an axonal, length-dependent pattern), and the exclusion of competing causes — diabetes mellitus (the most common competing cause and one with its own documented route to neuropathy), hypothyroidism, vitamin B12 and folate deficiency and other nutritional states, uremia and chronic kidney disease, HIV and chemotherapy agents, monoclonal gammopathy and paraproteinemia, inherited neuropathies such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, and idiopathic neuropathy. The claim runs from the diagnosis of alcohol use disorder as marking sustained heavy exposure; where a specific documented drinking history is inconsistent with the diagnosis or with the neuropathy's chronology, the individual opinion must reconcile them rather than rely on the label alone. Where pre-existing neuropathy is documented, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation.

medicalEvidence.title: Alcohol-related peripheral neuropathy: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Julian T, Glascow N, Syeed R, Zis P
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review of 87 articles (29 case-control, 52 cohort, 2 randomized trials, and population-based studies): the prevalence of peripheral neuropathy among chronic alcohol abusers was 46.3% (95% CI 35.7-57.3%), with toxic and nutritional mechanisms discussed and management strategies identified.

medicalEvidence.title: Gender and peripheral neuropathy in chronic alcoholism: a clinical-electroneurographic study.
medicalEvidence.authors: Ammendola A, Gemini D, Iannaccone S, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Consecutive sample of 62 chronic alcoholics (18 women, 44 men): clinical and/or subclinical neuropathy — mostly axonal — was present in 67.7% (65.9% of men, 72.2% of women), and women showed significantly greater effects of total lifetime ethanol dose and disease duration on nerve findings than men.

medicalEvidence.title: Peripheral systems: neuropathy.
medicalEvidence.authors: Maiya RP, Messing RO
medicalEvidence.summary: Mechanistic review: long-term excessive alcohol consumption produces a peripheral neuropathy characterized by axonal degeneration with reduced small and large fiber density; ethanol exerts direct neurotoxic effects via acetaldehyde and oxidative stress and activates protein kinase C epsilon signaling, while dietary vitamin deficiency associated with chronic alcoholism contributes to pathogenesis.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Diabetic nephropathy (renal involvement in diabetes mellitus, diabetic kidney disease)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 7541 (38 CFR § 4.115b — renal involvement in diabetes mellitus type I or II), rated as renal dysfunction under the § 4.115a criteria (100/80/60/30/0 levels keyed to glomerular filtration rate and albumin-creatinine ratio measured over at least 3 consecutive months)
originalRow.primaryCondition: Diabetes mellitus, type II (service-connected)
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 7913 (38 CFR § 4.119 — diabetes mellitus)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Type 2 diabetes causes diabetic nephropathy through chronic hyperglycemic injury to the glomerulus. Hyperglycemia drives glomerular hyperfiltration and intraglomerular hypertension, non-enzymatic glycation of proteins, and activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and of pro-fibrotic growth factors; the resulting mesangial matrix expansion, glomerular basement membrane thickening, and podocyte injury progressively impair the filtration barrier, which appears clinically first as microalbuminuria and then as macroalbuminuria with declining glomerular filtration rate. Hypertension and smoking accelerate the same process, and glycemic control slows it — the therapeutic prediction that anchors the causal direction. The evidence is direct and interventional: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 studies across 13 countries found a pooled prevalence of chronic kidney disease among type 2 diabetes patients of 27% (95% CI 21-33%), identifying diabetes as the leading cause of chronic kidney disease; the UK Prospective Diabetes Study randomized trial (3,867 newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes patients followed for 10 years) found that intensive blood-glucose control produced a 25% risk reduction (95% CI 7-40, p = 0.0099) in microvascular endpoints, including the renal manifestations of diabetes; and a longitudinal cohort of 694 type 2 diabetes patients followed 4.5 years documented the natural history — 36.6% with microalbuminuria and 2.4% with macroalbuminuria at baseline, 9.9% progressing albuminuria stage, and 32.5% deteriorating in renal function. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), diabetic nephropathy developing in a veteran with service-connected type 2 diabetes is a direct-causation secondary claim. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the diabetes (onset, duration, control with glycated hemoglobin history), the renal findings (serial urine albumin-creatinine ratios and estimated glomerular filtration rates with dates, and renal imaging where performed), and the chronology of albuminuria relative to diabetes duration; and address competing causes — hypertensive nephrosclerosis (which commonly coexists and is rated under § 4.115 principles regarding the close interrelationships of cardiovascular and renal disability), glomerulonephritis, toxic nephropathy from nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or other agents (DC 7535), interstitial and gouty nephropathy (DC 7537), multiple myeloma and amyloidosis, and viral nephropathies (DC 7544). Where pre-existing renal disease is documented, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. Because the schedule has a dedicated code for renal involvement in diabetes, the requirement for a diagnostic code is met directly rather than by analogy.

medicalEvidence.title: Prevalence and predictors of chronic kidney disease among type 2 diabetic patients worldwide, systematic review and meta-analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Fenta ET, Eshetu HB, Kebede N, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 studies across 13 countries: the pooled prevalence of chronic kidney disease among type 2 diabetes patients was 27% (95% CI 21-33%), and diabetes is identified as the leading cause of chronic kidney disease.

medicalEvidence.title: Intensive blood-glucose control with sulphonylureas or insulin compared with conventional treatment and risk of complications in patients with type 2 diabetes (UKPDS 33). UK Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS) Group.
medicalEvidence.authors: UK Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS) Group
medicalEvidence.summary: Randomized controlled trial of 3,867 newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes patients followed 10 years: intensive blood-glucose control (achieved HbA1c 7.0% vs 7.9%) produced a 25% risk reduction (95% CI 7-40, p = 0.0099) in microvascular endpoints, establishing that glycemic control causally modifies microvascular complication risk including the renal pathway.

medicalEvidence.title: Longitudinal Trajectories of Albuminuria and eGFR in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: Natural Progression of Diabetic Kidney Disease.
medicalEvidence.authors: Qiao X, Cai Q, Luo Y, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Longitudinal cohort of 694 type 2 diabetes patients followed 4.5 years: baseline albuminuria was normoalbuminuric in 61.3%, microalbuminuric in 36.6%, and macroalbuminuric in 2.4%; 9.9% progressed albuminuria stage and 32.5% deteriorated in renal function, documenting the natural progression of diabetic kidney disease.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Hypertensive retinopathy (retinal arteriolar and microvascular changes of chronic hypertension)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated DC — evaluated under the 38 CFR § 4.79 General Rating Formula for Diseases of the Eye, with DC 6006 (retinopathy or maculopathy not otherwise specified) available for the retinopathy findings and visual impairment evaluated under §§ 4.75-4.78 and the 6061-6091 visual-acuity and field codes where present
originalRow.primaryCondition: Hypertension (service-connected)
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 7101 (38 CFR § 4.104 — hypertensive vascular disease; hypertension and isolated systolic hypertension, with a minimum 10-percent evaluation for a history of diastolic pressure predominantly 100 or more who requires continuous medication for control)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Chronic elevated blood pressure damages the retinal microvasculature in a stereotyped sequence. The retinal arterioles first respond to pressure elevation with autoregulatory vasoconstriction, producing generalized and focal arteriolar narrowing; sustained hypertension then drives arteriolosclerosis — intimal thickening, medial hyperplasia, and hyaline degeneration — visible as arteriovenous nicking and altered vessel light reflexes; with further pressure elevation and endothelial dysfunction the blood-retinal barrier fails, producing flame and dot-blot hemorrhages, microaneurysms, cotton-wool spots, and hard exudates; and in accelerated or malignant hypertension, optic disc and macular edema develop. Because the retinal circulation is a directly visible microvascular bed, these changes track the severity and duration of blood pressure elevation, correlate with other end-organ damage such as left ventricular hypertrophy and renal impairment, and predict stroke and cardiovascular events — and blood pressure control prevents their progression. The clinical evidence is substantial: the Bhaktapur Retina population-based study of 643 elderly subjects with hypertension found hypertensive retinopathy in 12.6% (more frequent in diabetics at 16.49% and in those with body-mass index at or above 25); the classic review of how hypertension affects the eye documents the full spectrum of signs (generalized and focal arteriolar narrowing, arteriovenous nicking, hemorrhages, microaneurysms, and optic disc and macular edema in severe cases) and notes that mild hypertensive retinopathy signs appear in nearly 10% of the general adult non-diabetic population and associate with left ventricular hypertrophy and renal impairment; and the Nature Reviews Disease Primers review of hypertensive eye disease establishes the current clinical-standard framework for the spectrum and its systemic significance. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), hypertensive retinopathy developing in a veteran with service-connected hypertension is a direct-causation secondary claim. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document serial blood pressure readings (the schedule requires values confirmed by readings taken two or more times on at least three different days), the fundoscopic findings with their severity or grading, and any visual impairment with acuity and field testing; and exclude competing causes — diabetic retinopathy (which has its own dedicated code and commonly coexists, so the presence of diabetes must be documented and its contribution weighed), retinal vein occlusion, hematologic disorders and coagulopathies, and other retinopathies. Where pre-existing retinopathy or a separate established retinal disease is documented before the hypertension, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation.

medicalEvidence.title: Prevalence, Associated Factors and Awareness of Hypertensive Retinopathy among an Elderly Population with Hypertension in Nepal: The Bhaktapur Retina Study.
medicalEvidence.authors: Thapa R, Khanal S, Tan HS, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Population-based cross-sectional study of 1,860 elderly subjects (643 with hypertension): hypertensive retinopathy was found in 81 hypertensive subjects (12.6%), more frequently in diabetics (16.49%), males (13.25%), and those with body-mass index at or above 25 kg/m2.

medicalEvidence.title: How does hypertension affect your eyes?
medicalEvidence.authors: Bhargava M, Ikram MK, Wong TY
medicalEvidence.summary: Review documenting that elevated blood pressure produces hypertensive retinopathy through generalized and focal retinal arteriolar narrowing, arteriovenous nicking, retinal hemorrhages, microaneurysms, and — in severe cases — optic disc and macular edema; mild signs appear in nearly 10% of the general adult non-diabetic population and associate with other end-organ damage such as left ventricular hypertrophy and renal impairment.

medicalEvidence.title: Hypertensive eye disease.
medicalEvidence.authors: Cheung CY, Biousse V, Keane PA, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Nature Reviews Disease Primers review of hypertensive eye disease characterizing the spectrum of pathological changes in which hypertensive retinopathy is the best-known manifestation, providing the current clinical-standard framework for diagnosis and systemic risk implications.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Gout (diuretic-associated hyperuricemic crystal arthropathy)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated gout DC — evaluated by analogy under 38 CFR § 4.20 to the § 4.71a joint-schedule entries, such as DC 5002 (arthritis, multi-joint, active process) for active gouty arthritis and DC 5003 for chronic residual arthritic change, with acute attacks and tophaceous disease evaluated under the entry that best reflects the predominant disability picture
originalRow.primaryCondition: Hypertension (service-connected), on chronic thiazide or loop diuretic therapy
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 7101 (38 CFR § 4.104 — hypertensive vascular disease; hypertension and isolated systolic hypertension, with a minimum 10-percent evaluation for a history of diastolic pressure predominantly 100 or more who requires continuous medication for control)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Thiazide and loop diuretics raise serum uric acid and precipitate gout through a renal transport mechanism: volume depletion and reduced tubular flow increase proximal tubular urate reabsorption (net urate retention), and the resulting hyperuricemia is the direct precursor of gout — when serum urate exceeds its solubility, monosodium urate crystals deposit in joints and periarticular tissues and trigger the intense interleukin-1-driven inflammatory response of an acute gout flare, with recurrent attacks producing chronic gouty arthropathy and tophi. The effect is drug-class-specific (potassium-sparing diuretics do not show it), dose- and duration-related, persists during therapy, and is mediated by the change in serum urate — a mechanism confirmed by the observation that adjusting for urate level eliminates the association. The quantitative evidence is strong: a population-based case-control study of 91,530 incident gout cases and matched controls found adjusted odds ratios for current diuretic use of 2.64 (95% CI 2.47-2.83) for loop diuretics, 1.70 (95% CI 1.62-1.79) for thiazide diuretics, and 2.30 (95% CI 1.95-2.70) for thiazide-like diuretics, with combined loop and thiazide use carrying the highest risk (OR 4.65, 95% CI 3.51-6.16) and potassium-sparing agents showing no association (OR 1.06, 95% CI 0.91-1.23); the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities cohort (5,789 adults with hypertension, 37% on diuretics) found any diuretic associated with incident gout (HR 1.48, 95% CI 1.11-1.98), with thiazide HR 1.44 (1.00-2.10) and loop HR 2.31 (1.36-3.91), a longitudinal serum urate increase of 0.72 mg/dL in those starting diuretics (P < 0.001), and the association becoming null after adjustment for urate — establishing mediation; and a population-based cohort of gout-naive hypertensive adults matched 4,045 to 4,045 found that thiazide initiation carried sustained higher risks of subsequently being prescribed antigout medication (adjusted hazard ratios 2.23, 2.07, and 2.41 for under 30 days, 31-180 days, and over 180 days). Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately due to or resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so gout developing on documented chronic thiazide or loop diuretic therapy for service-connected hypertension is a treatment-complication secondary claim; where pre-existing gout or hyperuricemia is documented before diuretic exposure, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the diuretic regimen (agent, dose, duration, dates, and any dose changes), serial serum urate values before and during therapy, the gout diagnosis (monosodium urate crystals on joint aspiration, or validated clinical/imaging criteria such as ultrasound double-contour sign or dual-energy CT), the joint distribution and attack frequency, and the chronology of attacks relative to diuretic initiation; and address competing causes — alcohol use (which has its own route to gout and must be documented), chronic kidney disease with impaired urate excretion, obesity and metabolic syndrome, purine-rich diet and fructose intake, family history, myeloproliferative and lymphoproliferative disorders, psoriasis, and other drugs such as low-dose aspirin and calcineurin inhibitors. Because no diagnostic code specifically addresses gout, the rating proceeds by analogy under § 4.20 to the § 4.71a joint-schedule entries.

medicalEvidence.title: Use of diuretics and risk of incident gout: a population-based case-control study.
medicalEvidence.authors: Bruderer S, Bodmer M, Jick SS, Meier CR
medicalEvidence.summary: Population-based case-control study of 91,530 incident gout cases and matched controls: adjusted odds ratios for current use were 2.64 (95% CI 2.47-2.83) for loop diuretics, 1.70 (95% CI 1.62-1.79) for thiazide diuretics, 2.30 (95% CI 1.95-2.70) for thiazide-like diuretics, and 1.06 (95% CI 0.91-1.23) for potassium-sparing agents, with combined loop and thiazide use at OR 4.65 (95% CI 3.51-6.16).

medicalEvidence.title: Diuretic use, increased serum urate levels, and risk of incident gout in a population-based study of adults with hypertension: the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities cohort study.
medicalEvidence.authors: McAdams DeMarco MA, Maynard JW, Baer AN, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Prospective cohort of 5,789 adults with hypertension: any diuretic use was associated with incident gout (HR 1.48, 95% CI 1.11-1.98; thiazide HR 1.44, 1.00-2.10; loop HR 2.31, 1.36-3.91); serum urate rose 0.72 mg/dL in those starting a diuretic (P < 0.001), and the association became null after adjusting for urate level — establishing mediation by serum urate.

medicalEvidence.title: Prescribing cascades of antigout medications from thiazide diuretics in gout-naïve hypertensive adults receiving first-line pharmacological management.
medicalEvidence.authors: Lu SY, Hsu HY, Hsieh YW, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Population-based retrospective cohort (thiazide group n = 4,192 vs non-thiazide 81,083; 4,045 matched per group after propensity scoring): in gout-naive hypertensive adults, thiazide initiation was associated with sustained higher risk of subsequently being prescribed antigout medications (adjusted hazard ratios 2.23, 2.07, and 2.41 for under 30 days, 31-180 days, and over 180 days).

originalRow.secondaryCondition: L5/S1 lumbosacral radiculopathy with sciatic-distribution impairment
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8520 (sciatic nerve); DC 8620 for neuritis or 8720 for neuralgia when that phenotype is the appropriate rating basis
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected lumbar degenerative disc disease with a clinically concordant herniation or foraminal/lateral-recess stenosis
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5242 for degenerative disc disease other than intervertebral disc syndrome; DC 5243 only when disc herniation compresses and/or irritates the adjacent nerve root
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Anatomical causal sequence: lumbar disc degeneration and a concordant herniation or stenotic lesion can compromise a spinal nerve root in the lateral recess, neural foramen, or extraforaminal region. A paracentral L4-L5 herniation commonly affects the traversing L5 root, whereas a paracentral L5-S1 herniation commonly affects S1; a foraminal lesion can affect the exiting root instead. Root dysfunction may produce radiating neuropathic pain, sensory change, myotomal weakness, and reflex abnormalities. These are nerve-root findings, not proof of a distal sciatic-nerve lesion; the sciatic rating family is selected for the resulting functional distribution. Berry et al. (PMID 31788391) describes compression by disc bulging/herniation and degenerative narrowing, clinical localization, MRI, and electrodiagnostic differentiation. The NASS guideline (PMID 24239490) provides a systematic-review-based diagnostic and management framework for symptomatic lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy. Mechanical compression is the central established pathway. A secondary chemical contribution from exposed disc material and local inflammatory mediators is plausible, but Goupille et al. (PMID 9726337) explicitly states that the role of the identified mediators in producing human radicular pain was not proven and may be transient. Do not convert that mechanistic hypothesis into a proven TNF-alpha-mediated cause in an individual claim.

Required individual evidence: identify the service-connected lumbar segment and review dated pre-onset records, the side and root distribution of symptoms, motor and sensory examination, reflexes, and an anatomically concordant MRI or CT myelogram. EMG/nerve-conduction testing can help when imaging and symptoms disagree or a peripheral neuropathy is suspected; it is not an obligatory positive test in every clinical radiculopathy and can be nondiagnostic in sensory-predominant disease. Incidental disc degeneration, axial back pain alone, and nonspecific leg pain do not establish this relationship. Competing causes include diabetic or other length-dependent neuropathy, common-peroneal entrapment, plexopathy, hip disease, vascular claudication, and a separate nonservice-connected spinal lesion. A selective root-block response can corroborate localization but is not independently dispositive. New bladder dysfunction, saddle sensory loss, or rapidly progressive weakness requires urgent assessment rather than routine nexus processing.

Legal theory: this is secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a) when the service-connected disc lesion produces the documented radiculopathy; it is not a medication side effect. If a separate radiculopathy already existed and the service-connected lesion increased its severity, analyze aggravation under § 3.310(b) separately, documenting the prior baseline, attributable increment, and natural progression. An examiner may conclude that the relationship is 'at least as likely as not' only after explaining why the veteran's anatomical concordance, chronology, and competing-cause assessment place the positive and negative evidence at least in approximate balance. No individual probability is asserted by this population-level mapping.

Rating and graph controls: § 4.71a's General Rating Formula Note (1) directs separate evaluation of associated objective neurologic abnormalities under the appropriate code; § 4.14 prohibits counting the same manifestation twice. DC 5243's incapacitating-episode method is an alternative to the combined General Formula approach, not an automatic extra award, and requires physician-prescribed bed rest. Select sciatic versus femoral or other nerve codes from documented function rather than coding every lumbar root as sciatic. The repository already has degenerative-disc-disease → radiculopathy; this anatomically scoped radiculopathy-sciatic proposal must be reconciled with that generic edge, not added as a duplicate recommendation.

medicalEvidence.title: A Review of Lumbar Radiculopathy, Diagnosis, and Treatment
medicalEvidence.authors: James A Berry; Christopher Elia; Harneel S Saini; Dan E Miulli
medicalEvidence.summary: Clinical review describing degenerative and disc-related nerve-root compression, dermatomal/myotomal examination, MRI, and the role and limitations of electrodiagnostic testing. Supports the anatomical pathway and diagnostic safeguards; it does not establish a veteran-specific nexus or an individual probability.

medicalEvidence.title: An evidence-based clinical guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy
medicalEvidence.authors: D Scott Kreiner; Steven W Hwang; John E Easa; et al.; North American Spine Society
medicalEvidence.summary: NASS systematic review and evidence-based guideline addressing 29 clinical questions using graded evidence and explicitly identified consensus statements. Provides a clinical standard for diagnosing and treating symptomatic disc herniation with radiculopathy, not proof that incidental degeneration explains every leg complaint.

medicalEvidence.title: The role of inflammation in disk herniation-associated radiculopathy
medicalEvidence.authors: P Goupille; M I Jayson; J P Valat; A J Freemont
medicalEvidence.summary: Review identifies inflammatory mediators in herniated disc material but expressly concludes that their role in radiculopathy was not proven and that inflammation may be transient. Included as a mechanistic limitation: biochemical plausibility supplements, rather than replaces, anatomical and clinical evidence.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Cervical radiculopathy affecting an upper-extremity radicular group
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8510 (upper radicular group), 8511 (middle), 8512 (lower), or 8513 (all groups), selected by documented distribution; corresponding 8610-8613 neuritis or 8710-8713 neuralgia codes when appropriate
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected cervical degenerative disc disease with disc herniation or spondylotic foraminal stenosis
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5242; DC 5243 only for disc herniation with compression and/or irritation of the adjacent nerve root; DC 5238 when spinal stenosis is the diagnosed rating basis
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Anatomical causal sequence: a cervical disc herniation can impinge the adjacent nerve root, while degenerative loss of disc height and uncinate/facet hypertrophy can narrow the neural foramen even without a large soft-disc extrusion. Iyer and Kim (PMID 27250042; full text PMC4958381) describes disc-height loss, increased loading of the intervertebral joints, bony hypertrophy, foraminal narrowing, and nerve-root compression. Compression can disturb local perfusion and neural conduction, with local inflammatory sensitization contributing to pain; neither cytokine levels nor a specific biochemical cascade must be demonstrated in order to diagnose a clinically concordant compressive radiculopathy. Caridi et al. (PMID 23024624) identifies spondylosis and disc herniation as common causes and describes dermatomal pain/paresthesias with possible weakness. Abbed and Coumans (PMID 17204882) specifically identifies cervical disc herniation and spondylosis as frequent causes of root compression and inflammation.

Localization matters: C5-C6 pathology commonly affects C6, C6-C7 affects C7, and C7-T1 affects C8. The examiner should map pain, sensory findings, myotomal weakness, and reflexes against the actual lesion and side; for example, C6 may involve the radial forearm/thumb with biceps or wrist-extension weakness, whereas C7 may involve the middle finger and triceps. These clinical root distributions guide examination but do not automatically dictate one VA radicular-group code. MRI must be interpreted with the examination because common age-related degenerative findings can be incidental. CT may better define bony stenosis, and EMG/nerve-conduction studies can help distinguish root disease from distal entrapment when needed. A normal or nondiagnostic EMG does not by itself exclude radiculopathy. Progressive motor deficits, gait change, hyperreflexia, or other myelopathic signs require timely spine evaluation; myelopathy is not interchangeable with an isolated radiculopathy.

Competing explanations include median or ulnar entrapment, shoulder pathology, brachial plexopathy/Parsonage-Turner syndrome, generalized neuropathy, and neoplasm or another independent spinal process. Coexisting distal entrapment and root disease may both be present; a 'double-crush' label cannot substitute for identifying each lesion. Neck pain alone or hand tingling without root concordance is insufficient. Surgical decompression or targeted-treatment response can corroborate but does not independently prove the origin or service connection of the cervical disease.

Legal theory: secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), provided the cervical pathology is itself service connected or supported through a separately established chain. Service-connected lumbar degeneration does not automatically establish service connection for cervical degeneration. If cervical disease worsens a pre-existing nonservice-connected root disorder instead of originating it, address § 3.310(b) aggravation independently with baseline findings and an attributable increase beyond natural progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion must integrate a compatible timeline, lesion-to-root concordance, and competing causes; neither radiographic prevalence nor the general causal mechanism establishes the probability in an individual veteran.

Rating and graph controls: evaluate objective neurologic abnormalities separately under § 4.71a Note (1) when warranted, record affected side and dominant versus nondominant arm, and apply § 4.14 to avoid rating the same weakness or sensory deficit under overlapping group and distal-nerve codes. Use DC 8513 only when all radicular groups are actually involved, not as a default. Project to radiculopathy-upper-extremity; reconcile this specific identity with the existing generic degenerative-disc-disease → radiculopathy edge before authoring.

medicalEvidence.title: Cervical radiculopathy
medicalEvidence.authors: Sravisht Iyer; Han Jo Kim
medicalEvidence.summary: Review covers disc herniation and spondylotic foraminal narrowing, root-localizing clinical findings, MRI/CT, electrodiagnostic limitations, natural history, and management. Its full text explicitly describes disc-height loss and uncinate hypertrophy as mechanisms of foraminal stenosis. Does not establish causation from an incidental scan alone.

medicalEvidence.title: Cervical radiculopathy: a review
medicalEvidence.authors: John M Caridi; Matthias Pumberger; Alexander P Hughes
medicalEvidence.summary: Clinical review identifies facet spondylosis and intervertebral disc herniation as common causes of cervical nerve-root compression and links the syndrome to dermatomal pain/paresthesias and possible weakness. Supports clinical, imaging, and electrophysiologic correlation rather than automatic inference from degeneration.

medicalEvidence.title: Cervical radiculopathy: pathophysiology, presentation, and clinical evaluation
medicalEvidence.authors: Khalid M Abbed; Jean-Valéry C E Coumans
medicalEvidence.summary: Review describes compression and inflammation of cervical roots in the neural foramen, frequently from cervical disc herniation or spondylosis, and warns that entrapment neuropathies can mimic or coexist with the syndrome. Supports the causal anatomy and differential-diagnosis requirements.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Benign peptic esophageal stricture
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7203 (esophageal stricture)
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected gastroesophageal reflux disease with chronic reflux esophagitis
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7206 (gastroesophageal reflux disease)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Injury-repair causal sequence: repeated reflux exposure can cause esophagitis and ulcerative injury; healing of sustained injury can produce fibrotic scar and a fixed luminal narrowing, usually distal in a peptic stricture. The resulting mechanical resistance to bolus passage causes dysphagia and may require repeated dilation. This is a GERD → reflux esophagitis → peptic stricture pathway, not a claim that every episode of heartburn causes irreversible fibrosis. Pregun et al. (PMID 19439958) identifies peptic stricture as a consequence of GERD, emphasizes exclusion of malignancy, and explains why healing coexistent esophagitis and effective acid suppression reduce repeated dilation. In the 366-patient randomized trial by Smith et al. (PMID 7926495), omeprazole versus ranitidine after dilation reduced the proportion needing redilation at 12 months from 46% to 30% among the reported evaluable groups. This intervention evidence supports an ongoing acid-dependent contribution to recurrence; it does not prove the cause of all benign strictures or estimate an individual nexus probability. The ACG guideline (PMID 34807007) supplies an evidence-based GERD evaluation and management standard.

Required individual evidence: establish documented GERD before the fibrotic lesion, retrieve serial endoscopy reports with stricture location, caliber and associated erosive findings, obtain biopsies as clinically indicated to exclude cancer and eosinophilic disease, and review barium imaging, dilation history, reflux-treatment history, and symptoms. A prior clinical diagnosis of GERD without objective or persuasive longitudinal support is not enough to label a new narrowing 'peptic.' Competing causes in the differential include esophageal malignancy, eosinophilic esophagitis, caustic ingestion, radiation injury, anastomotic narrowing, and pill-induced injury. Achalasia and other motility disorders can cause dysphagia without a peptic fixed narrowing. A short distal scar with prior erosive reflux and an appropriate treatment history supports the route, whereas a proximal or multifocal lesion, eosinophilic histology, cancer, or a relevant alternative exposure may favor a different etiology.

Legal theory: when service-connected GERD produces the documented peptic stricture, the connection is causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), not a medication side effect. If an independently caused stricture predates GERD, any reflux-related increase in recurrent narrowing or dysphagia belongs to an independently reasoned § 3.310(b) aggravation analysis. Record baseline caliber, dilation frequency, diet tolerance, and clinical severity from pre-aggravation or qualifying earliest records, and distinguish natural progression of the original lesion. An 'at least as likely as not' conclusion requires the veteran-specific temporal, endoscopic, histologic, and differential evidence to be at least approximately balanced; population evidence and treatment response alone cannot supply that conclusion.

Rating and graph controls: current DC 7203 requires documented stricture findings and grades dysphagia/treatment burden; DC 7206 also uses stricture-related criteria. Establishing a distinct diagnosis does not automatically permit two ratings for the same dysphagia, dilation burden, or nutritional impairment under § 4.14. Claim-period-specific criteria must be checked rather than applying obsolete GERD-by-hiatal-hernia coding to every claim. The repository already carries esophagitis → esophageal-stricture → dysphagia. Preserve that intermediate-node physiology and perform a redundancy review before adding a direct GERD → stricture shortcut; source PMID 19439958 is already registered and requires provenance-aware reuse rather than a duplicate source entity.

medicalEvidence.title: Peptic esophageal stricture: medical treatment
medicalEvidence.authors: István Pregun; István Hritz; Zsolt Tulassay; László Herszényi
medicalEvidence.summary: Review identifies peptic stricture as a consequence of GERD, requires diagnostic exclusion of malignancy, and describes acid suppression, dilation and surgery. Healing coexistent esophagitis is important to outcome; proton-pump inhibitors can reduce repeated dilation. The route is scoped to confirmed peptic strictures, not all dysphagia.

medicalEvidence.title: A comparison of omeprazole and ranitidine in the prevention of recurrence of benign esophageal stricture. Restore Investigator Group
medicalEvidence.authors: P M Smith; G D Kerr; R Cockel; B A Ross; C M Bate; P Brown; M W Dronfield; J R Green; W S Hislop; A Theodossi
medicalEvidence.summary: Double-blind randomized trial enrolled 366 patients after dilation. At 12 months, redilation was needed in 43/143 (30%) on omeprazole versus 66/143 (46%) on ranitidine, P<0.01. Supports acid suppression reducing recurrence in the studied population, not automatic veteran-specific causation or a present-day recommendation to use ranitidine.

medicalEvidence.title: ACG Clinical Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease
medicalEvidence.authors: Philip O Katz; Kerry B Dunbar; Felice H Schnoll-Sussman; Katarina B Greer; Rena Yadlapati; Stuart Jon Spechler
medicalEvidence.summary: GRADE-based clinical guideline provides evidence-based evaluation and management of GERD, including pharmacologic, lifestyle, endoscopic, and surgical approaches. Supports appropriate confirmation and management of the upstream disease; it is a clinical standard, not a stricture-specific causation trial.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Drug-induced parkinsonism from dopamine-receptor-blocking antipsychotic exposure
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated drug-induced-parkinsonism DC is listed. 38 CFR §§ 4.20 and 4.27 permit a clinically justified analogous code; DC 8004 (paralysis agitans) under § 4.124a is a candidate analogy only, not an automatic diagnosis or award; qualified-human rating review required
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected schizophrenia treated with a dopamine-receptor-blocking antipsychotic
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.130, DC 9201 (schizophrenia); DC 9203 is removed and must not be substituted
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Pharmacological causal sequence: an antipsychotic prescribed for service-connected schizophrenia can block postsynaptic striatal D2 receptors. In the basal-ganglia motor circuit, D2 blockade disinhibits the indirect-pathway striatal output, increasing downstream inhibitory output to thalamocortical motor systems and producing bradykinesia and rigidity, with tremor or impaired gait in some patients. Shin and Chung (PMID 22523509; full text PMC3325428) describes this circuit and distinguishes postsynaptic blockade from the presynaptic nigrostriatal degeneration typical of idiopathic Parkinson disease. The proximate exposure is the documented medication, not schizophrenia itself. Feldman et al. (PMID 36573102) reviews culprit drugs, differential diagnosis, and management. Ali et al. (PMID 34506552) supplies a systematic review/meta-analysis of observational studies, with pooled antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism prevalence of 20% (95% CI 11-28%). That pooled prevalence quantifies a recognized adverse effect across heterogeneous exposed populations; it is neither a 20% probability that a particular veteran's syndrome is drug-caused nor proof of permanent neurodegeneration.

Required individual evidence: identify the exact antipsychotic, indication, starting date, dose changes, adherence, and concurrent dopamine-blocking medications. Compare dated baseline neurologic findings with the onset of bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor and functional impairment. A compatible onset after initiation or dose escalation and improvement after a clinician-supervised reduction or substitution support attribution, but deliberate rechallenge is not required and medication changes must be coordinated with psychiatry to avoid relapse. Persistence after withdrawal does not exclude a drug contribution; it can reflect prolonged drug effects or unmasking of underlying neurodegenerative disease. Symmetry alone is not diagnostic because drug-induced cases can be asymmetric. Neurologic review should distinguish competing causes, including idiopathic Parkinson disease, vascular parkinsonism, essential tremor, depressive/psychotic psychomotor slowing, tardive dyskinesia, akathisia, and other toxidromes. DAT imaging, when clinically appropriate, may help distinguish presynaptic degeneration from pure postsynaptic blockade but is not a universal required test. Do not relabel tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, or serotonin syndrome as this identity.

Legal theory: 'Medication Side Effect' is the requested packet label. In 38 CFR § 3.310(a) it is a treatment-mediated secondary-causation theory: service-connected schizophrenia → medically documented antipsychotic exposure → drug-induced parkinsonism. It is not a fourth repository nexusClassification enum arm, and no negligence allegation is necessary to describe this secondary-service-connection mechanism. If a pre-existing Parkinson syndrome was instead worsened by necessary antipsychotic treatment, evaluate § 3.310(b) aggravation with a documented baseline and an attributable increase beyond its natural course; do not assert that the drug created the underlying neurodegenerative disease. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion needs the actual exposure chronology, movement-disorder examination, medication response where safely observed, and reasoned consideration of alternatives. No patient-specific probability is asserted here.

Rating and governance controls: schizophrenia uses current DC 9201. Drug-induced parkinsonism has no dedicated code; DC 8004 is identified only as an analogous-rating candidate requiring review of affected function, anatomical localization and symptomatology under §§ 4.20 and 4.27. Do not apply its minimum rating automatically, equate this syndrome with idiopathic Parkinson disease, or duplicate the same manifestations under § 4.14. The repository's batch-95 deferral and ME-29 held-evidence adjudication remain active. This newly located independent systematic-review anchor is presented for human reassessment, not an automatic lifting of that hold; reserved PMIDs 30695288 and 34652577 are not reused in this proposal.

medicalEvidence.title: Drug-induced parkinsonism
medicalEvidence.authors: Hae-Won Shin; Sun Ju Chung
medicalEvidence.summary: Review explains basal-ganglia motor-circuit effects of dopamine-receptor blockade, culprit drugs, clinical overlap with Parkinson disease, and DAT imaging. Notes that asymmetry can occur and deficits may persist after stopping the drug. Supports treatment causation while rejecting an automatic equation with neurodegeneration.

medicalEvidence.title: Updated Perspectives on the Management of Drug-Induced Parkinsonism (DIP): Insights from the Clinic
medicalEvidence.authors: Matthew Feldman; Sarah Marmol; Jason Margolesky
medicalEvidence.summary: Clinical review differentiates secondary/iatrogenic parkinsonism from idiopathic Parkinson disease, describes motor and nonmotor diagnostic clues, identifies culprit medications, and discusses management. Supports individualized exposure and differential assessment rather than diagnosis from an antipsychotic prescription alone.

medicalEvidence.title: Antipsychotic-induced extrapyramidal side effects: A systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies
medicalEvidence.authors: Tilahun Ali; Mekonnen Sisay; Mandaras Tariku; Abraham Nigussie Mekuria; Assefa Desalew
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review/meta-analysis included 15 original articles and reported pooled antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism prevalence of 20% (95% CI 11-28%). Provides a non-case-report anchor for adverse-effect burden. Heterogeneous observational prevalence does not establish individual causality or satisfy a VA probability threshold by itself.
