originalRow.secondaryCondition: Pre-existing restless legs syndrome worsened in advanced chronic kidney disease
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated restless-legs-syndrome DC is listed. 38 CFR §§ 4.20 and 4.27 require an appropriate analogous rating; DC 8103 (convulsive tic) under § 4.124a is a possible comparator only when functions and symptomatology are sufficiently analogous, not a diagnosis of a tic disorder or an automatic rating
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected advanced chronic kidney disease requiring regular dialysis
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.115b, DC 7530 (chronic renal disease requiring regular dialysis), evaluated as renal dysfunction under § 4.115a; use the actual etiology-specific renal code if regular dialysis is not present
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Scope and proposed mechanism: this mapping addresses documented restless legs syndrome (RLS) that existed before advanced service-connected kidney disease and subsequently became more severe. It does not infer de novo causation from the fact that kidney disease and RLS coexist. The characteristic syndrome is an urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensations, provoked by rest, relieved by movement, and worse in the evening/night, after excluding mimics. Uremic illness and disordered iron availability can contribute to the sensorimotor syndrome in a susceptible person, but a single established biochemical cascade from reduced filtration to RLS has not been demonstrated. Brain-iron regulation, genetic susceptibility and altered neurotransmission are implicated in RLS generally; renal anemia is not interchangeable with proven brain-iron deficiency. Safarpour et al. (PMID 37008995) reports that most dialysis studies found RLS prevalence of 15-30% versus 5-10% in the general population, while correlations with iron, ferritin, electrolytes and parathyroid hormone were inconsistent. Trenkwalder et al. (PMID 26944272) specifically warns that the labels 'primary' and 'secondary' RLS can suggest an inappropriate causal relation and describes a genetic-environmental spectrum. Those cautions must remain in the mapping.

Clinical-standard anchor: the current AASM guideline (PMID 39324694; full text PMC11701286) recognizes an end-stage-renal-disease subgroup, recommends regular ferritin/transferrin-saturation assessment in clinically significant RLS, and conditionally supports IV iron sucrose in the ESRD subgroup with ferritin <200 ng/mL and transferrin saturation <20%. A treatment recommendation and clinical improvement after iron replacement support a modifiable contributor in selected patients, not proof that every case is caused by kidney disease. The guideline also stresses untreated sleep apnea and serotonergic, antihistaminergic, or antidopaminergic medications as exacerbating factors and cautions against standard long-term dopamine-agonist use because of augmentation. Do not repeat the older review's description of gabapentin/pregabalin as calcium-channel blockers: they are alpha2-delta ligands. No medication or iron dosing is prescribed by this mapping.

Required individual evidence: establish RLS with clinical criteria rather than diagnosing it from periodic movements on a sleep study alone; retrieve baseline symptom frequency, duration, onset time, sleep/function impact, treatment requirements and, where available, International RLS Severity Scale scores. Align subsequent worsening with renal progression/dialysis history, iron studies and medication changes. Distinguish actual RLS from dialysis-associated cramps, uremic neuropathy, positional discomfort, edema and akathisia. Assess nonrenal iron loss, longstanding familial RLS, pregnancy where relevant, untreated sleep apnea, caffeine/alcohol exposure, antidepressant or dopamine-blocker effects, and dopamine-agonist augmentation as alternate causes of the increased burden. Kidney severity or a high population prevalence alone is insufficient.

Legal theory: 38 CFR § 3.310(b) applies only to an attributable increase beyond the pre-existing RLS course and natural progression. Baseline must be supported by evidence predating aggravation or the qualifying earliest evidence between onset of aggravation and evidence of current severity; the rating activity determines baseline/current severity and the compensable increment. An examiner should separately address whether the worsening is 'at least as likely as not' due to service-connected CKD, using chronology, repeated clinical assessments, documented renal/iron changes, and comparison with competing explanations. Do not require permanent worsening as an added threshold, but do identify an actual attributable increase rather than diagnostic overlap. Without these individual data, the appropriate conclusion is that aggravation is a medically plausible, evidence-supported proposal, not an established patient nexus; the schema probability remains NOT_ASSERTED. If RLS began only after CKD, a separate causation analysis under § 3.310(a) is needed rather than inventing a pre-existing baseline.

Rating and graph controls: DC 7530 is specific to regular dialysis, not a universal CKD code. RLS is unlisted; the potential DC 8103 analogy requires qualified review rather than asserting that RLS is a convulsive tic. Avoid duplicating the same sleep or leg manifestations under § 4.14. Project to restless-leg-syndrome with an AGGRAVATION arm only if baselineProgression and aggravatingFactor are separately authored and clinically supportable; absent that evidence, retain association-only status instead of forcing this proposal into an established causal edge.

medicalEvidence.title: Restless Legs Syndrome in Chronic Kidney Disease- a Systematic Review
medicalEvidence.authors: Yasaman Safarpour; Nosratola D Vaziri; Bahman Jabbari
medicalEvidence.summary: Review found 175 articles and examined 111 clinical-trial/cross-sectional reports; most dialysis studies reported RLS prevalence of 15-30% compared with 5-10% in the general population. Correlations with iron/ferritin and other laboratory factors were inconsistent. Supports the renal-disease association and possible contributors, not universal causation or individual aggravation.

medicalEvidence.title: Restless legs syndrome associated with major diseases: A systematic review and new concept
medicalEvidence.authors: Claudia Trenkwalder; Richard Allen; Birgit Högl; Walter Paulus; Juliane Winkelmann
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review identifies increased RLS prevalence in iron deficiency and kidney disease but cautions that primary/secondary labels can imply an inappropriate causal relationship. Describes overlapping genetic and environmental contributions and potential reduction of symptoms after treating underlying disease. Included as an explicit limit on causal and aggravation inference.

medicalEvidence.title: Treatment of restless legs syndrome and periodic limb movement disorder: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline
medicalEvidence.authors: John W Winkelman; J Andrew Berkowski; Lourdes M DelRosso; Brian B Koo; Matthew T Scharf; Denise Sharon; Rochelle S Zak; Uzma Kazmi; Yngve Falck-Ytter; Anita V Shelgikar; Lynn Marie Trotti; Arthur S Walters
medicalEvidence.summary: GRADE-based guideline gives iron-assessment and exacerbating-factor guidance and ESRD-specific conditional recommendations, including IV iron sucrose for ferritin <200 ng/mL with transferrin saturation <20%. Highlights mimics and dopamine-agonist augmentation. These are clinical care standards; they do not establish a veteran's CKD-attributable aggravation without baseline and longitudinal evidence.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Clinically diagnosed oral candidiasis associated with inhaled corticosteroid exposure
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated oral-candidiasis DC is listed in 38 CFR Part 4. Select a clinically justified analogous code under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 based on actual localization, symptoms and impaired function; § 4.150 does not supply a dedicated thrush code. Qualified-human rating review required; no specific analogy is asserted without findings
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected bronchial asthma treated with an inhaled corticosteroid
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.97, DC 6602 (bronchial asthma)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Treatment-mediated sequence: service-connected asthma → documented inhaled corticosteroid exposure → a locally permissive oral/oropharyngeal environment → symptomatic mucosal Candida infection. The relevant exposure is corticosteroid deposited locally during inhalation, not asthma itself infecting the mouth. Local glucocorticoid effects can weaken mucosal antifungal defenses and permit Candida overgrowth; the precise cellular contribution is a mechanistic explanation, not a patient-specific assay or quantified mediator. Rachelefsky et al. (PMID 17378253) supplies the direct adverse-event anchor: 23 studies comprising 59 drug arms found increased oral candidiasis versus placebo, with dose dependence. The metered-dose-inhaler OR of 5.40 and dry-powder-inhaler OR of 3.24 are each comparisons with their corresponding placebo, NOT a randomized head-to-head comparison between devices. The review includes older formulations, limiting extrapolation to every current device. Its finding that mouth rinsing or a spacer may reduce local adverse events is consistent with reducing local exposure; spacer suitability is device-specific and is not assumed for a dry-powder inhaler.

Temporal corroboration: van Boven et al. (PMID 23516006) found increased oral-candidiasis medication dispensing after ICS initiation, greatest in the first three months; higher daily ICS dose and concurrent oral steroids were predictive factors. This prescription-sequence design uses antifungal dispensing as a proxy, not uniform clinical or microbiological confirmation. Pappas et al. (PMID 26679628; PMC4725385, section XVI) recognizes steroid exposure among mucosal-candidiasis risk settings and distinguishes management of oropharyngeal from esophageal disease. Positive Candida culture alone can reflect colonization and is not clinical thrush; establish compatible lesions, symptoms and clinician diagnosis, with microscopy/culture when indicated for uncertainty or refractory disease. Do not infer candidemia, esophageal candidiasis, dysphagia, or permanent taste loss from oral colonization.

Individual evidence and competing causes: retrieve the asthma treatment indication, exact drug/device, dose, start/escalation dates, inhalation technique, local preventive measures, prior oral examinations, lesion documentation, symptoms, recurrence and response to clinician-directed antifungal treatment or exposure modification. Consider diabetes, recent antibiotics, systemic corticosteroids, dentures, xerostomia, HIV or other immunosuppression, cancer treatment and noncandidal oral lesions. A compatible onset after ICS initiation/escalation and recurrent exposure-related episodes can support attribution; response to antifungal therapy supports infection but does not alone identify the upstream cause. Do not discontinue necessary asthma treatment merely to demonstrate a nexus.

Legal and rating analysis: the packet label 'Medication Side Effect' projects to treatment-mediated causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a). If candidiasis already existed and ICS increased its severity or recurrence, use a separately reasoned § 3.310(b) aggravation opinion: establish the qualifying baseline from pre-aggravation or earliest permissible records, identify the attributable increment and distinguish natural progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion requires a reasoned assessment of the individual's exposure chronology, confirmed disease and competing causes placing the positive and negative evidence at least in approximate balance; neither an odds ratio nor mechanistic plausibility establishes that probability alone. No individual probability is asserted here. DC 6602 distinguishes inhalational from systemic corticosteroid treatment; local thrush does not convert an inhaled regimen into a systemic-steroid rating tier. Oral candidiasis is unlisted: do not substitute dental bone-loss, neoplasm, skin, or esophageal-stricture criteria without a justified functional analogy. Apply § 4.14 to overlapping manifestations and check claim-period criteria. This incoming treatment route does not upgrade the repository's existing oral-candidiasis → ageusia association or reopen its withheld esophageal-extension route.

medicalEvidence.title: Impact of inhaled corticosteroid-induced oropharyngeal adverse events: results from a meta-analysis
medicalEvidence.authors: Gary S Rachelefsky; Yuning Liao; Rab Faruqi
medicalEvidence.summary: Meta-analysis of 23 studies/59 drug arms found increased oral candidiasis with ICS versus placebo and a dose effect. MDI OR 5.40 and DPI OR 3.24 refer to separate placebo comparisons, not direct device superiority. Mouth rinsing or a suitable spacer may reduce local adverse events. Older formulations and trial heterogeneity limit universal extrapolation; the findings do not establish an individual nexus probability.

medicalEvidence.title: Inhaled corticosteroids and the occurrence of oral candidiasis: a prescription sequence symmetry analysis
medicalEvidence.authors: Job F M van Boven; Lolkje T W de Jong-van den Berg; Stefan Vegter
medicalEvidence.summary: Among 52,279 incident ICS users, the oral-antifungal prescription sequence ratio was 1.94 (95% CI 1.71-2.21), highest in the first three months at 2.72 (2.19-3.38). Higher ICS doses and concomitant oral steroids predicted the outcome. Supports temporal adverse-effect attribution, but antifungal dispensing is a proxy and residual confounding remains.

medicalEvidence.title: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Candidiasis: 2016 Update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America
medicalEvidence.authors: Peter G Pappas; Carol A Kauffman; David R Andes; Cornelius J Clancy; Kieren A Marr; Luis Ostrosky-Zeichner; Annette C Reboli; Mindy G Schuster; Jose A Vazquez; Thomas J Walsh; Theoklis E Zaoutis; Jack D Sobel
medicalEvidence.summary: GRADE-based clinical standard. Full-text section XVI recognizes steroid exposure, diabetes, antimicrobial therapy, immunosuppression and dentures among mucosal-candidiasis settings and provides severity-specific oropharyngeal management. Esophageal candidiasis is addressed separately. This guideline is not an ICS-specific causation trial and does not make culture positivity alone equivalent to symptomatic thrush.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Achilles tendinopathy or Achilles tendon rupture associated with systemic fluoroquinolone exposure
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5024 for diagnosed tendinitis, tendinosis or tendinopathy, evaluated on limitation of motion of affected parts; DC 5271 when ankle limitation is the rating basis. No dedicated Achilles-rupture DC; residual-function review under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 may consider § 4.73, DC 5311 only as a justified Muscle Group XI analogy, not an automatic muscle-injury diagnosis
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected chronic bacterial prostatitis for which a systemic fluoroquinolone was actually prescribed
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.115b, DC 7525 (includes chronic prostatitis), evaluated as urinary tract infection under § 4.115a
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Treatment-mediated sequence: service-connected chronic bacterial prostatitis → documented systemic fluoroquinolone course → drug-associated tendon injury → clinically confirmed Achilles tendinopathy and, in some cases, rupture. Prostatitis itself is not asserted to mechanically damage the Achilles tendon, and this route does not presume that every prostatitis/pelvic-pain presentation warrants antibiotics. Establish the actual indication, bacterial evidence where available and prescription rather than assuming treatment from the diagnostic label. Grace K Kim's review (PMID 20725547; PMC2921747) describes experimental evidence for disrupted type-I collagen synthesis/degradation and extracellular-matrix injury, with metal-ion chelation proposed as a contributor. The exact human molecular mechanism remains unresolved. These mechanisms provide biological plausibility; they do not prove a particular patient's tendon failed through a measured collagen or metalloproteinase pathway. The review describes onset during or after exposure and vulnerability associated with age, corticosteroids, renal impairment and prior tendon disease. Its older case-based estimates should not displace modern cohort findings.

Quantified support and counter-evidence: Morales et al. (PMID 30465300) found current fluoroquinolone exposure associated with Achilles rupture, aIRR 3.14 (95% CI 2.11-4.65), with an elevated-risk window persisting for 60 days and a larger association with concurrent oral corticosteroids. This is not a prostatitis-specific trial, and rupture estimates cannot be treated as identical estimates for nonruptured tendinopathy. Baik et al. (PMID 33371012) found no elevated class-wide rupture risk in 1,009,925 Medicare beneficiaries; levofloxacin had an Achilles signal within 30 days, while ciprofloxacin and moxifloxacin did not show increased combined rupture risk. Cephalexin signals and confounding by indication challenged a simple class-wide causal interpretation. Carry this disagreement explicitly; do not claim every agent has the same demonstrated risk or convert an epidemiological relative risk greater than two into an individual probability greater than 50%.

Individual evidence and competing causes: obtain the exact agent, dose, dates, duration, renal function and concurrent systemic steroid exposure; establish pre-exposure tendon symptoms and the date and circumstances of new pain, swelling or rupture. Orthopedic examination, ultrasound/MRI and operative findings as available distinguish tendinopathy from partial/complete rupture and document laterality and residual function. Review athletic loading, acute trauma, chronic degenerative tendon disease, prior rupture/surgery, age, diabetes, inflammatory disease and other relevant drug exposures. Symptoms beginning after an appropriate exposure interval without a persuasive traumatic explanation favor attribution; symptoms long predating exposure or a substantial independent injury may favor another cause. Rupture after cessation is not automatically excluded, but latency still requires explanation. Do not deliberately rechallenge or independently alter antibiotic treatment to test causation.

Legal and rating analysis: 'Medication Side Effect' is treatment-mediated secondary causation under § 3.310(a), conditional on the service-connected indication and individualized attribution. For pre-existing tendinopathy worsened by treatment, separately analyze § 3.310(b): document baseline pain, imaging and function, the attributable increase or supervening rupture, and natural progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion must explain how the veteran's exposure, compatible chronology, confirmed lesion and alternatives balance the conflicting research. No individual probability is asserted here. DC 5024 directly lists tendinopathy but does not automatically code a healed rupture as arthritis. Rate actual residual limitation or other justified function; DC 5311 is only a possible analogous comparator for impaired plantar flexion/propulsion and needs human review. Do not stack overlapping ankle limitation and muscle-function ratings under § 4.14 or apply wound-based muscle severity without justification. The proposed graph direction is prostatitis/treatment → achilles-tendinopathy-rupture, not tendon injury → antibiotic use.

medicalEvidence.title: Relative and Absolute Risk of Tendon Rupture with Fluoroquinolone and Concomitant Fluoroquinolone/Corticosteroid Therapy: Population-Based Nested Case-Control Study
medicalEvidence.authors: Daniel R Morales; Jim Slattery; Alexandra Pacurariu; Luis Pinheiro; Patricia McGettigan; Xavier Kurz
medicalEvidence.summary: UK primary-care nested case-control study found an Achilles-rupture aIRR of 3.14 (95% CI 2.11-4.65) with current fluoroquinolone exposure and elevated risk persisting for 60 days. Concurrent oral corticosteroids markedly increased the association. Observational exposure-risk evidence, not a prostatitis-specific causal trial or an individual probability determination.

medicalEvidence.title: The Risk of Fluoroquinolone-induced Tendinopathy and Tendon Rupture: What Does The Clinician Need To Know?
medicalEvidence.authors: Grace K Kim
medicalEvidence.summary: Narrative clinical review describes recognized tendon adverse effects, variable latency including post-cessation events, clinical evaluation and risk modifiers. Full text reviews experimental collagen/ECM injury and proposed chelation mechanisms while acknowledging that the exact human mechanism is elusive. Supports plausibility and safeguards, not a proven molecular pathway in a specific veteran.

medicalEvidence.title: Association between tendon ruptures and use of fluoroquinolone, and other oral antibiotics: a 10-year retrospective study of 1 million US senior Medicare beneficiaries
medicalEvidence.authors: Seo Baik; Jason Lau; Vojtech Huser; Clement J McDonald
medicalEvidence.summary: Counter-evidence from 1,009,925 beneficiaries: no elevated class-wide rupture association, but levofloxacin showed an Achilles HR of 2.20 (95% CI 1.50-3.24) within 30 days. Ciprofloxacin/moxifloxacin did not show increased combined rupture risk; cephalexin signals raised confounding-by-indication concerns. Requires agent-specific, chronology-based assessment rather than blanket causal attribution.

cfrCitations: 38 CFR § 4.73, DC 5311 (conditional analogous comparator for rupture residuals only)

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Sensorineural hearing loss associated with cisplatin ototoxicity
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR Part 4, DC 6100, evaluated under § 4.85; apply § 4.86 only when its exceptional-pattern criteria are met. Also establish hearing-loss disability under § 3.385; extended-high-frequency changes alone do not establish those VA criteria
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected testicular germ-cell malignancy treated with cisplatin-based chemotherapy
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.115b, DC 7528 (malignant neoplasms of the genitourinary system); evaluate post-treatment status and residuals according to the code's note rather than assuming an indefinite active-cancer rating
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Treatment-mediated sequence: service-connected testicular cancer → documented cisplatin exposure → cochlear injury → sensorineural hearing loss. Paken et al. (PMID 28115933; PMC5223030) describes reactive-oxygen-species generation, depletion of antioxidant defenses and apoptotic injury, most prominently involving outer hair cells in the basal cochlear turn; supporting cells, stria vascularis and spiral-ganglion structures can also be affected. Basal-turn vulnerability explains why high-frequency thresholds may deteriorate first, with lower-frequency involvement as injury increases. These molecular pathways draw partly on experimental research and are not biomarkers proving an individual nexus. The typical pattern is bilateral high-frequency sensorineural impairment, often with tinnitus, but perfect symmetry is not required and an atypical pattern requires a careful differential. This is a treatment effect, not a claim that the testicular tumor directly invades the cochlea.

Human evidence: Frisina et al. (PMID 27354478) studied 488 male germ-cell-tumor survivors and found a dose-response relationship: each additional 100 mg/m² of cumulative cisplatin was associated with 3.2 dB worse age-adjusted thresholds across 4-12 kHz. This survivor analysis does not supply a pretreatment audiogram for each participant and its ASHA-defined severity is not a VA rating. Haugnes et al. (PMID 29384420) provides longitudinal pretreatment/follow-up data in 46 treated testicular-cancer survivors with 46 untreated matched survivors. Age and dose mattered; at 8 kHz each additional 100 mg of cumulative dose was associated with 3.6 dB deterioration as reported in that abstract. Do not replace its dose unit with mg/m². The ASHA-defined follow-up case/control difference was nonsignificant (70% versus 65%, P=.66), while a four-frequency definition differed (13% versus 2.2%, P=.049). This definitional counterweight prevents exaggerating attributable clinical disability.

Individual evidence and competing causes: obtain cancer treatment records, cumulative cisplatin dose and dates, baseline and serial air/bone-conduction audiograms, speech results, tympanometry, tinnitus history and functional reports. Extended-frequency monitoring can detect early ototoxic change but does not replace conventional VA testing. Consider pre-existing military/occupational/recreational noise exposure, presbycusis, familial loss, middle-ear disease, vestibular schwannoma or another asymmetric lesion, renal impairment, and other ototoxic drugs. Renal impairment may modify exposure risk but does not independently prove attribution. Serial threshold changes during or after treatment and a compatible cochlear pattern support the chain; absence of baseline testing creates uncertainty, not an automatic positive or negative opinion.

Legal and rating analysis: the packet's 'Medication Side Effect' label represents § 3.310(a) treatment-mediated causation when service-connected cancer treatment produces the impairment. If hearing loss predated chemotherapy, separately address § 3.310(b) aggravation, comparing the qualifying baseline with current severity and separating an attributable treatment increment from natural age/noise-related progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion needs veteran-specific chronology, audiometric change and a reasoned competing-cause assessment placing evidence at least in approximate balance; general ototoxicity or cohort prevalence alone is insufficient. No individual probability is asserted here. § 3.385 requires a threshold of at least 40 dB at any of 500/1000/2000/3000/4000 Hz, at least 26 dB at three of those frequencies, or Maryland CNC recognition below 94%. § 4.85 requires state-licensed audiology, appropriate puretone and Maryland CNC testing without hearing aids, and a 1000/2000/3000/4000-Hz average, subject to its stated exceptions. A change confined to 8-12 kHz can be medically important without meeting VA disability or compensable-rating criteria. Keep service connection, disability definition and rating percentage separate; avoid duplicate manifestations under § 4.14. Author this incoming route from the oncology/exposure side, respecting the hearing-loss file's direction guard.

medicalEvidence.title: Comprehensive Audiometric Analysis of Hearing Impairment and Tinnitus After Cisplatin-Based Chemotherapy in Survivors of Adult-Onset Cancer
medicalEvidence.authors: Robert D Frisina; Heather E Wheeler; Sophie D Fossa; Sarah L Kerns; Chunkit Fung; Howard D Sesso; Patrick O Monahan; Darren R Feldman; Robert Hamilton; David J Vaughn; Clair J Beard; Amy Budnick; Eileen M Johnson; Shirin Ardeshir-Rouhani-Fard; Lawrence H Einhorn; Steven E Lipshultz; M Eileen Dolan; Lois B Travis
medicalEvidence.summary: Audiometric study of 488 male germ-cell-tumor survivors found increasing cumulative cisplatin dose associated with worse 4-12-kHz thresholds; each 100 mg/m² corresponded to 3.2 dB impairment. Eighteen percent had ASHA-defined severe/profound loss. Middle-ear deficits were not dose-associated. Cross-sectional survivor findings and ASHA definitions cannot substitute for individual baseline data or VA criteria.

medicalEvidence.title: Hearing loss before and after cisplatin-based chemotherapy in testicular cancer survivors: a longitudinal study
medicalEvidence.authors: Hege S Haugnes; Niels Christian Stenklev; Marianne Brydøy; Olav Dahl; Tom Wilsgaard; Einar Laukli; Sophie D Fosså
medicalEvidence.summary: Forty-six treated survivors had pretreatment and median-ten-year audiograms; 46 matched survivors without cisplatin were controls. Age and dose predicted deterioration, especially at high frequencies. ASHA-defined case/control prevalence was not significantly different, whereas the four-frequency measure differed. Supports dose/chronology analysis while showing that aging and outcome definitions materially affect attribution.

medicalEvidence.title: Cisplatin-Associated Ototoxicity: A Review for the Health Professional
medicalEvidence.authors: Jessica Paken; Cyril D Govender; Mershen Pillay; Vikash Sewram
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of 79 articles and two books describes cochlear oxidative/apoptotic injury, basal-turn outer-hair-cell damage, high-frequency sensorineural presentation, susceptibility factors and audiologic monitoring. Cellular mechanisms include experimental evidence. Its treatment-prevention statements reflect literature through July 2015 and are not presented as a current universal prevention standard.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Hydronephrosis attributable to documented benign-prostatic-hyperplasia-related bladder outlet obstruction
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.115b, DC 7509 (hydronephrosis); severe hydronephrosis is evaluated as renal dysfunction under § 4.115a. Imaging dilation alone does not establish the severity criteria or a compensable rating
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected benign prostatic hyperplasia with demonstrated bladder outlet obstruction and high-risk retention physiology
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.115b, DC 7527 (includes prostate hypertrophy and bladder outlet obstruction), rated as voiding dysfunction or urinary tract infection, whichever predominates, under § 4.115a
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Mechanical causal sequence: prostatic enlargement attributable to BPH can obstruct the bladder outlet; in a patient with sustained high-pressure retention or adverse bladder compliance, pressure can be transmitted to the upper urinary tract and produce hydroureter/hydronephrosis. The proximal cause is demonstrated outlet obstruction/retention physiology, while hydronephrosis describes collecting-system dilation. It is not synonymous with obstruction, obstructive nephropathy, or chronic kidney disease. The AUA 2026 evaluation guideline (Goueli et al., PMID 42095481) defines BPH as glandular/stromal proliferation in the transition zone and cautions that LUTS can arise from bladder, prostate, urethral or other pathology. That guideline abstract supports upstream evaluation, not a quantified BPH-to-hydronephrosis effect or proof that prostate size alone establishes obstructive pressure.

Direction-specific support: George et al. (PMID 6407564; PMC1548028) prospectively evaluated 21 selected patients with high-pressure chronic retention, urodynamic/renographic/operative assessment and bilateral hydroureter/hydronephrosis; the syndrome included a tense bladder and progressive renal impairment, sometimes without conventional obstructive symptoms. Recovery after appropriately managed transurethral resection supported reversibility of the outlet-related process. This small 1983 series is a physiological anchor, not a modern incidence estimate for all BPH. Stoffel et al. (PMID 28163030) classifies imaging hydronephrosis as a high-risk feature of nonneurogenic chronic retention. Its consensus definition of chronic retention uses postvoid residual >300 mL for at least six months on at least two occasions; this research/management definition neither proves high-pressure obstruction from residual volume alone nor requires waiting six months before assessing threatened kidneys.

Individual evidence and competing causes: establish the service-connected BPH diagnosis and dated onset of retention; review repeated residuals, bladder/renal ultrasound or CT, laterality, bladder distension, renal function, catheter history and urologic assessment. Uroflow and pressure-flow/urodynamic evaluation when clinically appropriate help distinguish outlet obstruction from detrusor underactivity or neurogenic dysfunction. Improvement of upper-tract dilation after drainage or outlet treatment can corroborate the pathway but is not indispensable and does not guarantee renal recovery. Investigate ureteral stone, ureteral/urethral stricture, pelvic or urinary malignancy, retroperitoneal fibrosis, reflux, prior reconstructed urinary anatomy and nonobstructive dilation. Unilateral dilation without a fitting lower-tract mechanism warrants especially careful upper-tract evaluation. A large prostate, LUTS, residual urine or incidental hydronephrosis alone is insufficient. Infected obstruction, acute retention with renal threat or deteriorating renal function requires timely clinical evaluation, not delayed evidence collection for a claim.

Legal and rating analysis: § 3.310(a) causation is appropriate when the service-connected BPH produces documented outlet obstruction that explains the collecting-system dilation. If another disorder caused pre-existing hydronephrosis and BPH-related obstruction increased its burden, analyze § 3.310(b) aggravation separately with qualifying baseline imaging/function, the attributable increase and natural progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion must integrate the individual's obstruction physiology, imaging chronology, decompression response if available and alternative causes so that evidence is at least approximately balanced; general co-occurrence does not meet the standard. No individual probability is asserted here. DC 7509 uses specific colic/infection/drainage/function findings, with severe cases referred to renal dysfunction; do not infer a rating from a radiology label. DC 7527 and § 4.115a require predominant-function and overlap review: distinct nonoverlapping disability may be separately evaluated, but do not count the same urinary or renal manifestation twice under § 4.14. The proposed direction is BPH/outlet obstruction → hydronephrosis. It does not revive the withdrawn hydronephrosis → CKD edge; any renal injury must be attributed to the actual obstructive disorder and reconciled with the existing BPH → CKD route.

medicalEvidence.title: AUA White Paper on Nonneurogenic Chronic Urinary Retention: Consensus Definition, Treatment Algorithm, and Outcome End Points
medicalEvidence.authors: John T Stoffel; Andrew C Peterson; Jaspreet S Sandhu; Anne M Suskind; John T Wei; Deborah J Lightner
medicalEvidence.summary: Literature review/expert consensus defines chronic retention and identifies hydronephrosis, stage 3 CKD or recurrent culture-proven UTI/urosepsis as high-risk features. Provides risk-stratified assessment and outcome monitoring. A postvoid-residual threshold alone does not establish high-pressure BPH obstruction, and the six-month definition is not a reason to delay urgent evaluation.

medicalEvidence.title: High pressure chronic retention
medicalEvidence.authors: N J George; P H O'Reilly; R J Barnard; N J Blacklock
medicalEvidence.summary: Prospective physiological/clinical series of 21 selected patients describes high-pressure retention with bilateral hydroureter/hydronephrosis and renal impairment, sometimes without classic obstructive symptoms, and recovery after appropriately managed transurethral resection. Supports the pressure-mediated direction but cannot quantify frequency or prove that every enlarged prostate causes upper-tract dilation.

medicalEvidence.title: Management of Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms Attributed to Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: AUA Guideline (2026) Part I: Presentation and Evaluation
medicalEvidence.authors: Ramy Goueli; Gopal H Badlani; Charles Welliver; Paul D Anderson; Scott R Bauer; Tracy Dana; Rodrigo Donalisio da Silva; Rebecca Holmes; Sennett K Kim; Erin Kirkby; Bradley C Gill; Steven Maislos; Timothy McClure; Nicole L Miller; Iraj Roshan; Stephen J Summers; Annette Totten; Jaspreet S Sandhu
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic-review-informed guideline with searches updated in December 2025 addresses presentation, evaluation and initial management of LUTS/BPH. Emphasizes that LUTS may arise from bladder, prostate, urethral or other pathology. Used as an upstream evaluation standard, not as a hydronephrosis-specific causal trial or evidence that symptoms/prostate size alone demonstrate obstruction.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Contiguous foot osteomyelitis arising from an infected diabetes-related foot ulcer
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5000 (acute, subacute or chronic osteomyelitis), subject to its activity, recurrence, constitutional-symptom and post-resection notes; no automatic percentage from diabetes or ulcer status alone
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus with documented diabetes-related foot vulnerability and a clinically infected foot ulcer
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7913 (diabetes mellitus), including Note (1) on evaluation of compensable complications
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Multi-hop infectious sequence: service-connected diabetes → documented diabetes-related neuropathic/vascular and healing vulnerability where present → skin breakdown/foot ulcer → tissue infection → contiguous spread into adjacent bone. Diabetes does not itself introduce bacteria into bone, and diabetic status alone cannot establish osteomyelitis. The IWGDF/IDSA 2023 guideline (Senneville et al., PMID 37779323) explains that foot infections most often follow a break in the skin, commonly an ulcer in a person with peripheral neuropathy and frequently PAD. Neuropathy diminishes protective warning from pressure or injury; associated deformity/loading can promote skin breakdown. PAD impairs perfusion and worsens healing/infection outcomes, while diabetes-related immune dysfunction, including neutrophil dysfunction, can increase susceptibility. Not every patient has every mediator, and PAD should not be attributed to diabetes without assessing other vascular causes. Microorganisms invading soft tissue can spread contiguously through the foot compartments to tendons, joints and bone. Lipsky and Uçkay (PMID 33916055; PMC8066570) expressly describes this wound-to-bone route; it is not a default hematogenous-infection theory.

Clinical confirmation: distinguish bacterial wound colonization from clinical infection, and infection confined to soft tissue from actual bone involvement. The current IWGDF/IDSA standard recommends a combination of probe-to-bone testing, plain radiographs and inflammatory markers initially; MRI is recommended when doubt persists despite clinical, radiographic and laboratory assessment. When osteomyelitis is suspected and sampling is appropriate, aseptically obtained bone rather than superficial soft-tissue specimens are the microbiological standard in its conditional recommendation. Giurato et al. (PMID 28465790; PMC5394733) reviews these diagnostic issues and describes variable probe-to-bone performance across populations. No single bedside test, normal white count, swab culture or nonspecific MRI marrow edema should be treated as universally dispositive. Charcot neuroarthropathy, recent surgery and trauma can complicate imaging interpretation; Charcot alone is not bacterial osteomyelitis, although the two may coexist.

Individual evidence and competing causes: retrieve the diabetes chronology and control history, neuropathy examinations, deformity/loading history, perfusion studies where relevant, dated wound location/depth/duration, clinical infection findings, serial imaging, bone cultures/histology if obtained, and operative/debridement reports. Establish anatomical continuity between the infected ulcer and involved bone and document the actual diabetes-related contribution to the wound. Consider an independent penetrating injury, postoperative/hardware infection, hematogenous seeding from another source, non-diabetic vascular insufficiency, pressure injury from another cause, and sterile Charcot/traumatic/inflammatory changes. Lack of fever or pain does not exclude a neuropathic foot infection, but neither absence of symptoms nor diabetes alone proves it. Severe infection, gangrene, deep abscess or significant ischemia requires urgent multidisciplinary clinical assessment. This packet is not an antimicrobial prescription.

Legal and rating analysis: § 3.310(a) can support the full treatment-independent causal chain when service-connected diabetes materially contributes to the documented wound and contiguous bone infection. If osteomyelitis arose independently and diabetes instead worsened severity or impaired healing, separately reason under § 3.310(b), documenting the qualifying baseline, attributable increase and expected natural course. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion must explain the veteran-specific wound-to-bone continuity, diabetes-related contribution and competing causes so evidence is at least approximately balanced; general diabetic-foot prevalence is not an individual nexus probability. No individual probability is asserted here. DC 5000 distinguishes active, recurrent, inactive and systemic patterns; its historical ratings have recurrence prerequisites, and its note precludes an osteomyelitis rating following cure by removal/radical resection of the affected bone. Review actual residuals rather than assuming persistent infection after amputation. DC 7913 Note (1) addresses separate compensable complications unless part of the criteria supporting a 100-percent diabetes evaluation; § 4.14 still forbids duplicate manifestations. The catalog lacks a dedicated diabetic-foot-ulcer identity in the selection scan. Preserve the clinical intermediate in the narrative, do not invent an ID or substitute decubitus-ulcers, and require identity/governance review before landing a shortcut or new multi-hop graph chain.

medicalEvidence.title: IWGDF/IDSA guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of diabetes-related foot infections (IWGDF/IDSA 2023)
medicalEvidence.authors: Éric Senneville; Zaina Albalawi; Suzanne A van Asten; Zulfiqarali G Abbas; Geneve Allison; Javier Aragón-Sánchez; John M Embil; Lawrence A Lavery; Majdi Alhasan; Orhan Oz; Ilker Uçkay; Vilma Urbančič-Rovan; Zhang-Rong Xu; Edgar J G Peters
medicalEvidence.summary: GRADE-based guideline incorporating 149 studies, including 62 newly identified studies. Full text supports skin-break/infection/contiguous-bone spread, distinguishes colonization from infection, and gives probe-to-bone/radiograph/marker, MRI and aseptic bone-sampling recommendations with stated certainty levels. Diabetes alone, a surface culture or sterile Charcot change does not establish the causal chain.

medicalEvidence.title: Treating Diabetic Foot Osteomyelitis: A Practical State-of-the-Art Update
medicalEvidence.authors: Benjamin A Lipsky; İlker Uçkay
medicalEvidence.summary: Narrative review, emphasizing recent treatment studies and clinical experience, explicitly states that diabetic foot osteomyelitis usually develops by contiguous spread from an open infected wound into bone, often with neuropathy and sometimes PAD/deformity. Discusses the greater reliability of properly obtained bone specimens and contamination/antibiotic-related culture limitations. Does not establish that every diabetic ulcer progresses to bone infection.

medicalEvidence.title: Osteomyelitis in diabetic foot: A comprehensive overview
medicalEvidence.authors: Laura Giurato; Marco Meloni; Valentina Izzo; Luigi Uccioli
medicalEvidence.summary: Clinical review covers foot-osteomyelitis presentation, diagnostic testing and medical/surgical management. Reports population-dependent probe-to-bone performance and the importance of combining clinical, imaging and microbiological evidence. Used for diagnostic context, not as an independent causal cohort; the newer IWGDF/IDSA guideline controls the current clinical-standard discussion.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Complex regional pain syndrome (post-stroke shoulder-hand syndrome phenotype)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated complex-regional-pain-syndrome DC is listed in 38 CFR Part 4. Select a clinically justified analogous code under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 based on documented distribution, pain, vasomotor/sudomotor/trophic findings and functional loss; the word 'causalgia' appears in § 4.124a only as descriptive language inside DC 8525 (posterior tibial nerve) and is not asserted as an automatic comparator. Qualified-human rating review required
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected residual neurologic deficit after ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke (status post cerebrovascular accident)
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8007 (embolism), DC 8008 (thrombosis) or DC 8009 (hemorrhage); the vascular conditions are rated 100 percent for six months and residuals thereafter with a minimum of 10 percent
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Mechanical and neurovascular sequence: a service-connected stroke can be followed within weeks to months by complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) of the paretic upper limb — the phenotype historically called shoulder-hand syndrome. Pertoldi and Di Benedetto (PMID 16474282) review that CRPS can arise as the consequence of a distant process such as a stroke, spinal lesion or myocardial infarction, and describe onset and severity as related to stroke etiology, the severity and recovery of the motor deficit, spasticity, sensory disturbances and glenohumeral subluxation. The proposed cascade combines lesion-driven central disinhibition and autonomic dysfunction with a localized exaggerated inflammatory response (neurogenic inflammation) and peripheral sensitization around affected joints and tendon sheaths; the authors state expressly that the pathophysiology is still not known, so this is an evidence-supported mechanistic proposal rather than a proven molecular pathway. Kim et al. (PMID 27495051) found ultrasonographic extensor-digitoris-communis tendon abnormalities with response to local steroid injection in 23 clinically diagnosed post-stroke CRPS patients, supporting a peripheral soft-tissue/tendon component. Katsura et al. (PMID 36281309) documented severely reduced affected-upper-limb activity (Fugl-Meyer Assessment, Action Research Arm Test, Motor Activity Log) in post-stroke CRPS among 102 first-ever stroke patients. Immobilization and disuse are themselves recognized contributors to pain, edema and regional bone change, so the stroke-specific contribution cannot be fully separated from disuse in these designs; the CRPS catalog identity's own governance already records this immobilization-confounder guard.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: document the stroke and its residual deficit, pain onset in a compatible distribution (shoulder and wrist with relative elbow sparing), vasomotor/sudomotor/trophic findings, and response to guideline-directed therapy. Exclude fracture, glenohumeral subluxation or rotator-cuff pathology, adhesive capsulitis, spasticity-related pain, infection and gout, which are competing causes; clinical guidance requires considering post-stroke CRPS only after typical shoulder/hand pain causes such as acute trauma or bony fracture are ruled out. A CRPS diagnosis recorded long after onset without serial findings weakens attribution; an ipsilateral presentation beginning during early rehabilitation with typical features and no alternative structural explanation favors the stroke-related route.

Legal and rating analysis: this is direct secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a) when the service-connected stroke and its residual deficit produce the CRPS. If CRPS is asserted to have worsened a pre-existing pain syndrome, an independent § 3.310(b) aggravation analysis must identify the qualifying baseline and the attributable increase beyond natural progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion requires reasoned balancing of the positive and negative evidence — lesion-to-symptom concordance, onset timing, and exclusion of competing causes — because population reports alone do not establish an individual probability. No individual probability is asserted here. CRPS has no dedicated diagnostic code; §§ 4.20 and 4.27 require a clinically justified analogous evaluation selected from the documented distribution and functional loss. The stroke primary is rated under § 4.124a DC 8007-8009. Do not duplicate the same pain, weakness or limitation under both the CRPS evaluation and the stroke residual codes; apply § 4.14. Landing this incoming route requires host-file review: the stroke residuals identity carries an association-only depression edge and a lesion-location note, and the CRPS identity already holds immobilization-confounder guardrails for its outgoing edges.

medicalEvidence.title: Shoulder-hand syndrome after stroke. A complex regional pain syndrome
medicalEvidence.authors: S Pertoldi; P Di Benedetto
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of CRPS/shoulder-hand syndrome after stroke. States CRPS may develop as the consequence of a distant process such as a stroke, and relates onset and severity to stroke etiology, motor deficit severity and recovery, spasticity, sensory disturbances and glenohumeral subluxation. Expressly notes pathophysiology is still not known and hypothesizes an exaggerated neurogenic inflammatory response. Review-level support only; does not establish individual causation.

medicalEvidence.title: Is poststroke complex regional pain syndrome the combination of shoulder pain and soft tissue injury of the wrist?: A prospective observational study: STROBE of ultrasonographic findings in complex regional pain syndrome
medicalEvidence.authors: Yong Wook Kim; Yoon Kim; Jong Moon Kim; Ji Seong Hong; Hyun Sun Lim; Hyoung Seop Kim
medicalEvidence.summary: Prospective observational STROBE study of 23 patients with clinically diagnosed poststroke CRPS; three-phase bone scans and ultrasonographic extensor-digitoris-communis tendon measurements before and after local steroid injection. Findings support a peripheral soft-tissue/tendon contribution in poststroke CRPS. Small selected cohort; provides no incidence or causal estimate.

medicalEvidence.title: Post-Stroke Complex Regional Pain Syndrome and Upper Limb Inactivity in Hemiplegic Patients: A Cross-Sectional Study
medicalEvidence.authors: Yuichi Katsura; Satoshi Ohga; Kazuhiro Shimo; Takafumi Hattori; Tsukasa Yamada; Takako Matsubara
medicalEvidence.summary: Cross-sectional study of 102 first-ever stroke patients examining prevalence of post-stroke CRPS and affected-upper-limb inactivity using Fugl-Meyer Assessment, Action Research Arm Test and Motor Activity Log. Documented severely decreased upper-limb activity in post-stroke CRPS patients. Cross-sectional design cannot separate disuse from lesion-specific mechanisms; no individual nexus estimate.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Adrenal insufficiency (secondary/tertiary, glucocorticoid-induced)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7911 (Addison's disease — adrenocortical insufficiency), using its crisis-count, episode-count and corticosteroid-therapy-required-for-control tiers; primary adrenal disease must be excluded because the code title does not limit the etiology
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected rheumatoid arthritis requiring chronic systemic corticosteroid therapy
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5002 (multi-joint arthritis as an active process, with rheumatoid arthritis expressly named among its examples) and DC 5003 for chronic residuals
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Pharmacological sequence: chronic systemic glucocorticoid therapy prescribed for service-connected rheumatoid arthritis suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis through negative feedback, reducing corticotropin (ACTH) secretion and adrenal cortisol output; secondary (tertiary) adrenal insufficiency may become clinically apparent during tapering or after withdrawal and may persist long after the drug stops. Younes and Younes (PMID 29184808) describe this mechanism directly and note that HPA-axis recovery after cessation is variable and can take 6-12 months. Broersen et al. (PMID 25844620) pooled 74 articles and 3,753 adult corticosteroid users tested for adrenal insufficiency: pooled percentages varied by route from 4.2 percent (nasal) to 52.2 percent (intra-articular) and by disease from 6.8 percent (inhaled-only asthma) to 60.0 percent (hematologic malignancy), with a dose gradient; oral therapy falls within this range. Bowley et al. (PMID 41521083) systematically reviewed only studies using protocolised systemic glucocorticoid regimens and ACTH-stimulation testing, reporting that adrenal insufficiency is a common complication of systemic glucocorticoid therapy with considerable variability; the retrieved abstract excerpt did not expose a pooled estimate, so none is claimed here. These sources establish treatment-mediated causation at the mechanism level while showing that individual risk depends on route, dose, duration, potency, tapering and host factors; no single percentage can be applied to a veteran.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: obtain the exact corticosteroid agent(s), route, dose, cumulative duration, taper schedule and stop dates; concurrent topical, inhaled or intra-articular exposure; morning cortisol or ACTH-stimulation results; symptoms such as fatigue, orthostasis, nausea, hyponatremia; and any adrenal-crisis or continued-steroid-dependence events. Document whether insufficiency predated steroid therapy — primary adrenal disease, pituitary pathology, prior pituitary surgery or radiation, opioid effects, checkpoint-inhibitor effects — as competing causes; a pre-existing or independently caused insufficiency changes the theory from § 3.310(a) causation to § 3.310(b) aggravation of a baseline. Recovery testing after withdrawal informs severity and permanence but is not a prerequisite to attributing the insufficiency to treatment.

Legal and rating analysis: 'Medication Side Effect' is treatment-mediated secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a): service-connected rheumatoid arthritis leads through documented corticosteroid exposure to HPA suppression and adrenal insufficiency. If pre-existing adrenal insufficiency was worsened by necessary steroid therapy, analyze aggravation under § 3.310(b) with a documented baseline and attributable decrement beyond the natural course. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion needs the individual's exposure and endocrine chronology plus competing-cause exclusion placing the evidence at least in approximate balance; pooled prevalence does not itself meet that standard. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: § 4.119 DC 7911 supplies tiers including corticosteroid therapy required for control (20 percent), one or two crises, or two to four episodes per year; use the actual event counts and treatment requirements. Do not duplicate the same endocrine manifestations under another code (§ 4.14). The rheumatoid arthritis host file is published and currently points only to depressive disorder and GERD; this new incoming route requires host-side review before any landing.

medicalEvidence.title: Adrenal Insufficiency in Corticosteroids Use: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
medicalEvidence.authors: Leonie H A Broersen; Alberto M Pereira; Jens Otto L Jørgensen; Olaf M Dekkers
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review/meta-analysis of 74 articles and 3,753 adult corticosteroid users tested for adrenal insufficiency. Pooled percentages varied by route (4.2 percent nasal to 52.2 percent intra-articular) and by disease (6.8 percent inhaled-only asthma to 60.0 percent hematologic malignancy), with a dose gradient. Establishes iatrogenic HPA-suppression risk across routes; heterogeneity and predominantly observational data limit individual prediction.

medicalEvidence.title: Adrenal insufficiency following systemic glucocorticoid therapy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
medicalEvidence.authors: Jonathan Bowley; Sophie Shallish; Natasha Smyth; Stephanie Lax; Fiona Pearce
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review/meta-analysis restricted to adults receiving protocolised systemic glucocorticoid regimens and assessed with ACTH-stimulation testing, addressing imprecise dose/duration reporting in earlier reviews. Reports adrenal insufficiency as a common complication of systemic glucocorticoid therapy with considerable variability. The retrieved PubMed abstract excerpt did not expose a pooled estimate; none is claimed here.

medicalEvidence.title: Recovery of steroid induced adrenal insufficiency
medicalEvidence.authors: Areej K Younes; Noor K Younes
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of steroid-induced secondary adrenal insufficiency: chronic glucocorticoid use suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis through negative feedback; recovery after cessation typically occurs but timing is variable and can take 6-12 months. Mechanism and time-course support at review level, not a cohort effect estimate.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Tardive dyskinesia associated with metoclopramide (medication-induced movement disorder)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated tardive-dyskinesia DC is listed in 38 CFR § 4.124a. A clinically justified analogous code under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 is required based on affected muscle groups and severity; DC 8103 (convulsive tic) and DC 8004 (paralysis agitans) are candidate comparators only and are not automatically applicable. Qualified-human rating review required
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected gastroesophageal reflux disease treated with metoclopramide (prokinetic/antiemetic therapy; verify the actual documented indication, because long-term use is restricted)
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7206 (gastroesophageal reflux disease)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Pharmacological sequence: metoclopramide is a dopamine-receptor antagonist (with 5-HT3 antagonism and 5-HT4 agonism) used as an antiemetic and gastroprokinetic; prolonged blockade of nigrostriatal and mesolimbic dopamine pathways can produce persistent involuntary choreoathetoid movements of the tongue, face, jaw and extremities — tardive dyskinesia — after prolonged exposure. Al-Saffar et al. (PMID 31050085) review this pharmacology, the regulatory restrictions introduced for long-term or high-dose oral use, and estimate the risk of tardive dyskinesia from metoclopramide at roughly 0.1 percent per 1,000 patient-years. Rao and Camilleri (PMID 19886950), reviewing the literature after the FDA's 2009 black-box warning, concluded the risk is likely below 1 percent — materially lower than the 1-10 percent previously suggested in national guidelines — and note that risk may be modified by age, dose, duration and pharmacokinetic/pharmacogenetic factors such as DRD3 and cytochrome P450 variation. Kenney et al. (PMID 18223146) identify metoclopramide as an increasingly recognized cause of tardive dyskinesia. These sources establish a recognized iatrogenic cause with a low absolute incidence; they do not quantify any particular veteran's risk, and the literature cannot identify in advance which exposed patients will develop persistent movements.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: document the service-connected upper-gastrointestinal indication and the actual metoclopramide prescription (dose, duration, refills, any history of exceeding 12 weeks of therapy), and obtain the movement-disorder examination with onset timing relative to exposure, persistence after discontinuation where safely observed, and functional impact. Distinguish tardive dyskinesia from acute dystonia or akathisia, drug-induced parkinsonism (the repository already carries a separate schizophrenia/antipsychotic parkinsonism proposal), essential tremor, and primary psychiatric or dental/oral causes. Competing causes include other dopamine-blocking agents (antipsychotics, promethazine, prochlorperazine), prior neuroleptic exposure, and underlying neurodegenerative disease. Because the same movement may be codable through several neurologic analogs, findings must be attributed once.

Legal and rating analysis: 'Medication Side Effect' is treatment-mediated secondary causation under § 3.310(a): service-connected GERD, through documented metoclopramide exposure, causes tardive dyskinesia. The GERD host file is published and does not currently propose this, and the tardive-dyskinesia identity already receives one association-only edge from bipolar disorder in which an antipsychotic is named as the proximate agent; this proposal is a distinct non-antipsychotic agent route and must be reconciled for duplicate scope rather than assumed additive. If a pre-existing movement disorder was worsened by therapy, analyze § 3.310(b) aggravation separately with a baseline and natural-course description. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion must weigh exposure chronology, persistence after withdrawal where safely documented, and competing causes against the low population incidence; a low base rate does not preclude an individual causal opinion, but it raises the evidentiary bar. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: there is no dedicated tardive-dyskinesia DC; §§ 4.20 and 4.27 require a justified analogous code selected from affected muscle groups and severity, with DC 8103 and DC 8004 as candidates only. Apply § 4.14 to avoid duplication with any mental-disorder or neurologic evaluation of the same movements.

medicalEvidence.title: Review article: metoclopramide and tardive dyskinesia
medicalEvidence.authors: A S Rao; M Camilleri
medicalEvidence.summary: Review published after the FDA's 2009 black-box warning. Available data suggest the risk of tardive dyskinesia from metoclopramide is likely below 1 percent, much lower than the previously suggested 1-10 percent national-guideline estimate; discusses mechanism, pharmacokinetics, risk modifiers and appropriate use. Counterweight against overstating the magnitude of risk.

medicalEvidence.title: Gastroparesis, metoclopramide, and tardive dyskinesia: Risk revisited
medicalEvidence.authors: Ahmad Al-Saffar; Hans Lennernäs; Per M Hellström
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of metoclopramide pharmacology, regulatory restrictions on long-term/high-dose oral use, and risk of tardive dyskinesia, estimated at approximately 0.1 percent per 1,000 patient-years. Frames the clinical context for appropriate prescribing and exposure-modifying factors.

medicalEvidence.authors: Christopher Kenney; Christine Hunter; Anthony Davidson; Joseph Jankovic
medicalEvidence.summary: Clinical review identifying metoclopramide as an increasingly recognized cause of tardive dyskinesia. The PubMed record carried no indexed abstract at verification time; cited only for the recognition claim, not for numeric risk.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Osteoradionecrosis of the jaw (maxilla or mandible)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.150, DC 9900 (maxilla or mandible, chronic osteomyelitis, osteonecrosis or osteoradionecrosis) — rated as chronic osteomyelitis under DC 5000 (§ 4.71a), subject to DC 5000's activity, recurrence and post-resection notes
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected oral cavity or oropharyngeal malignancy treated with therapeutic radiation
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.150, DC 9918 (neoplasm, hard and soft tissue, malignant), including its continuation of the 100 percent rating beyond treatment and its mandatory post-treatment residual evaluation
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Treatment-effect sequence: therapeutic ionizing radiation for a service-connected oral cavity or oropharyngeal malignancy injures bone, vascular and soft tissue within the radiation field; the resulting hypocellular, hypovascular, hypoxic tissue fails to repair, and exposed necrotic maxillary or mandibular bone — osteoradionecrosis (ORN) — may emerge months to years later, often after dental extraction or mucosal trauma. Singh et al. (PMID 35967463) describe ORN as one of the most dreaded complications of head and neck radiation therapy, characterize it as exposed necrotic bone within the radiation field, note that etiopathogenesis remains unclear, and review definitions, staging, incidence and management. Owosho et al. (PMID 28024723) reviewed 1,023 patients treated with intensity-modulated radiation therapy for oral cavity or oropharyngeal cancer and found 44 (4.3 percent) developed ORN, with case-control analysis of radiation dose, periodontal status, alcohol and smoking. Pereira et al. (PMID 30341256) examined 413 head-and-neck radiotherapy records over ten years and assessed prevalence and associated factors, consistent with multifactorial risk beyond dose alone. The 4.3 percent figure is from one high-volume center and is not a universal incidence. The proximate agent is radiation therapy, not the malignancy itself; the packet's 'Medication Side Effect' label functions here as the user-provided medication/treatment side-effect arm and should be read as treatment-mediated iatrogenic causation.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: obtain the cancer diagnosis, radiation fields, total dose and fractionation to the affected jaw, dates, dental extraction or trauma history, clinical examination (exposed bone persisting beyond expected healing), and serial imaging; obtain tissue sampling when infection or malignancy is suspected. Distinguish ORN from chronic osteomyelitis of another origin, bisphosphonate or antiresorptive-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (a competing cause already represented by the catalog's osteoporosis-to-osteonecrosis association), tumor recurrence, and dental abscess; periodontal disease, smoking, alcohol use and poor dental status are contributing factors that must not be misread as the sole cause. Pain with exposed bone is typical; fever or purulence suggests superimposed infection rather than excluding ORN.

Legal and rating analysis: this is a treatment complication of service-connected cancer care analyzed as secondary causation under § 3.310(a) (treatment-mediated), not as a new disease contracted from the tumor. If pre-existing osteonecrosis or dental disease was worsened by radiation, analyze § 3.310(b) aggravation with qualifying baseline records and an attributable increase beyond natural progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion needs the veteran's dose-field-to-defect concordance, latency, examination findings and competing-cause analysis placing the evidence at least in approximate balance; a population incidence does not itself establish the individual nexus. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: § 4.150 DC 9900 expressly covers osteoradionecrosis and directs rating as chronic osteomyelitis under DC 5000 with its notes; the malignant primary is recognized under DC 9918. Do not rate the same exposed-bone defect, pain or loss of jaw substance under both codes (§ 4.14). The oral-cancer host identity is draft and governed with six association-only outgoing edges; this new incoming treatment route requires host-side scope and governance review before any landing.

medicalEvidence.title: The Prevalence and Risk factors associated with Osteoradionecrosis of the Jaw in Oral and Oropharyngeal Cancer Patients treated with Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy (IMRT): The Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center Experience
medicalEvidence.authors: Adepitan A Owosho; C Jillian Tsai; Ryan S Lee; Haley Freymiller; Arvin Kadempour; Spyridon Varthis; Adi Z Sax; Evan B Rosen
medicalEvidence.summary: Retrospective single-institution review of 1,023 patients treated with intensity-modulated radiation therapy for oral cavity or oropharyngeal cancer (2004-2013); 44 (4.3 percent) developed osteoradionecrosis, with case-control analysis of radiation dose, periodontal status, alcohol and smoking. Quantifies occurrence in a modern technique era; single-center retrospective design limits generalization.

medicalEvidence.title: Osteoradionecrosis of the jaw: A mini review
medicalEvidence.authors: Annu Singh; Joseph M Huryn; Kenneth L Kronstadt; SaeHee K Yom; Joseph R Randazzo; Cherry L Estilo
medicalEvidence.summary: Mini-review describing ORN as a most-dreaded complication of head and neck radiation therapy, clinically characterized by exposed necrotic bone within the radiation field, with etiopathogenesis still unclear. Summarizes definitions, staging, incidence, etiology and institutional management/risk-mitigation strategies.

medicalEvidence.title: Osteoradionecrosis prevalence and associated factors: A ten years retrospective study
medicalEvidence.authors: Igor-Figueiredo Pereira; Ramon-Targino Firmino; Henrique-Côrtes Meira; Belmiro-Cavalcanti-Do Egito Vasconcelos; Vladimir-Reimar-Augusto-de Souza Noronha; Vagner-Rodrigues Santos
medicalEvidence.summary: Cross-sectional retrospective study of 413 medical records over ten years of head and neck radiotherapy; determined ORN prevalence and associated factors using multivariate Poisson regression. Supports population-level occurrence and multifactorial risk assessment; retrospective single-region design.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Heterotopic ossification (neurogenic) complicating traumatic brain injury
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5023 (heterotopic ossification); the Note to DCs 5013-5024 directs evaluation as degenerative arthritis based on limitation of motion of affected parts
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected residual deficits of traumatic brain injury (TBI)
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8045 (residuals of traumatic brain injury), with its cognitive, emotional/behavioral and physical facets and its note on overlapping manifestations
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Neurogenic sequence: severe traumatic brain injury is associated with neurogenic heterotopic ossification (NHO), aberrant lamellar bone forming in periarticular soft tissues — characteristically around the hips, elbows and shoulders — causing pain and loss of joint motion. Sullivan et al. (PMID 23610702) review that NHO affects approximately one in five patients sustaining spinal cord injury or traumatic brain injury, and describe pathophysiology coupling basic bone-formation mechanisms with systemic circulating humoral factors and likely neurological influences; clinical sequelae include pressure injuries, urinary tract infection and pneumonia, making early recognition important. Simonsen et al. (PMID 17572418) studied 114 consecutive adults with very severe TBI (post-traumatic amnesia at least 28 days) and found clinically significant HO in 7.9 percent, noting literature incidence from 11 to 73.3 percent depending on ascertainment. Aubut et al. (PMID 21447915) systematically reviewed 26 treatment studies (12 TBI, 14 SCI) and found the TBI evidence base dominated by surgical case series with limited randomized evidence. Collectively these sources establish TBI as a recognized cause of heterotopic ossification while showing that incidence estimates are highly method-dependent and the causal mechanism is incompletely understood. HO frequently coexists with long-bone fractures and spasticity; the TBI-related contribution must be separated from fracture callus and immobilization effects.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: obtain the TBI history and severity, timing relative to HO onset, joint examination with range-of-motion loss, serial radiographs/CT or bone scan, alkaline phosphatase and laboratory context, and operative pathology when resected. The differential includes fracture callus or nonunion, post-traumatic arthritis, infection, deep venous thrombosis and tumor; competing causes also include heterotopic bone arising from associated long-bone trauma or burns rather than the brain injury. HO is not caused by TBI in isolation: immobilization, spasticity and associated fractures modify risk, and a veteran with ossification at a fracture site may have the fracture as a co-cause. Early diagnosis before joint ankylosis is clinically important.

Legal and rating analysis: direct secondary causation under § 3.310(a) applies when the service-connected TBI and its clinical course produce the heterotopic ossification. If a pre-existing ossification or joint condition was worsened, analyze § 3.310(b) aggravation with qualifying baseline imaging/function and an attributable increase beyond natural progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion needs the veteran-specific TBI-to-HO chronology, location concordance with typical periarticular distributions, and competing-cause assessment; population incidence ranges cannot substitute for that balancing. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: § 4.71a DC 5023 is a dedicated code for heterotopic ossification, evaluated on limitation of motion under the Note to DCs 5013-5024. The TBI primary is rated under § 4.124a DC 8045; do not use the same limitation of motion to support both the DC 8045 physical-residual evaluation and the DC 5023 rating (§ 4.14). The heterotopic-ossification identity's existing governance authors only an association-only outgoing edge to peripheral neuropathy; this new incoming route from TBI residuals should be reviewed against that conservative posture.

medicalEvidence.title: Symptomatic heterotopic ossification after very severe traumatic brain injury in 114 patients: incidence and risk factors
medicalEvidence.authors: Louise Lau Simonsen; Stig Sonne-Holm; Michael Krasheninnikoff; Aase W Engberg
medicalEvidence.summary: Retrospective database and X-ray study of 114 consecutive adults with very severe TBI (post-traumatic amnesia at least 28 days): clinically significant heterotopic ossification in 7.9 percent, with the literature range noted as 11-73.3 percent; logistic regression identified independent risk-predicting features. Quantifies occurrence in a defined severe-TBI cohort.

medicalEvidence.title: Heterotopic ossification after central nervous system trauma: A current review
medicalEvidence.authors: M P Sullivan; S J Torres; S Mehta; J Ahn
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of neurogenic heterotopic ossification after central nervous system trauma: affects approximately one in five patients with spinal cord injury or traumatic brain injury; ectopic bone forms around joints such as the hip and elbow causing pain and movement limitation; pathophysiology links bone-formation mechanisms with systemic humoral and neurological influences; sequelae include pressure injuries and infection. Mechanism and clinical anchor.

medicalEvidence.title: A comparison of heterotopic ossification treatment within the traumatic brain and spinal cord injured population: An evidence based systematic review
medicalEvidence.authors: Jo-Anne L Aubut; Swati Mehta; Nora Cullen; Robert W Teasell; ERABI Group; Scire Research Team
medicalEvidence.summary: Evidence-based systematic review comparing heterotopic-ossification treatment in TBI versus spinal cord injury populations: 26 studies met inclusion criteria (12 TBI, 14 SCI); the majority of TBI studies were surgical, and formal quality/level-of-evidence assessment was applied. Demonstrates an evidence base dominated by non-randomized surgical series.
