originalRow.secondaryCondition: Dental erosion (tooth-surface loss: erosion, abrasion and abfraction) with progression to tooth loss
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated diagnostic code for enamel or dentin erosion is listed in 38 CFR § 4.150. Where acid-mediated loss has progressed to loss of teeth, evaluate under § 4.150, DC 9913 (teeth, loss of, due to loss of substance of body of maxilla or mandible), noting that DC 9913's note excludes alveolar loss from periodontal disease but does not address chemical tooth-substance loss; where erosion is documented without qualifying loss, a clinically justified analogous evaluation under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 is required. Qualified-human rating review required
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) with documented acid regurgitation reaching the oral cavity
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7206 (gastroesophageal reflux disease)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Acid-mediated dissolution sequence: in service-connected gastroesophageal reflux disease, gastroduodenal contents — hydrochloric acid at a pH frequently below 2 and the proteolytic enzyme pepsin — are regurgitated to the oropharynx, where they contact the palatal and occlusal surfaces of the teeth. Dental apatite dissolves once the local pH falls below its critical value (approximately 5.5 for hydroxyapatite), so repeated acid exposure produces irreversible, cumulative loss of enamel and then dentin rather than the reversible demineralization seen with dietary acid alone; the absence of normal salivary buffering and clearance during sleep amplifies overnight regurgitation, and reduced salivary flow can further slow re-hardening. Picos et al. (PMID 30564013), a systematic review of dental erosion in GERD, report erosive-lesion prevalence in GERD patients of about 48.81 percent versus 20.48 percent in non-GERD comparators, with a median prevalence near 25.5 percent and a reported range of 10.6 to 42 percent, and describe dental erosion as an extraesophageal complication of GERD. Ortiz et al. (PMID 33571021) systematically reviewed the association and prevalence of erosive wear in GERD and conclude that GERD can be considered a risk factor, while Alavi et al. (PMID 24738088) compared patients with and without GERD and found a higher risk of dental erosion in the GERD group in a sample of 140 adults aged 30 to 50. These sources establish reflux acid as a recognized cause of erosive tooth-surface loss at the mechanism and population level; they are observational, they do not quantify any individual veteran's exposure, and the literature cannot identify in advance which reflux patients will lose tooth substance.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: obtain the reflux diagnosis and its objective confirmation (endoscopy, ambulatory pH or impedance testing, or a documented reflux regimen), the onset date of reflux relative to the dental changes, and a dental examination with intraoral photographs or casts describing lesion location and depth. Erosion attributable to reflux characteristically affects palatal surfaces of the maxillary anterior teeth and, in more advanced disease, occlusal surfaces and posterior teeth; dietary acid (citrus, carbonated drinks, vinegar, acidic sports or vitamin-C products), occupational acid exposure, bruxism/attrition, abrasive toothpaste technique, reduced salivary flow from anticholinergic or other xerogenic medication, and eating disorders with self-induced vomiting are competing causes that must be excluded or apportioned. An intrinsic-acid route from an eating disorder is an already-recognized alternative route into this same dental identity, which the catalog records as an association-only incoming edge from bulimia nervosa; a reflux attribution requires the acid source to be the documented reflux rather than covert vomiting. Chronology (reflux preceding the erosion), an anatomically consistent palatal distribution, absence of a competing dietary or occupational acid source, and objective reflux findings favor the reflux-related route; erosion that predates the reflux or tracks a dietary pattern weakens it.

Legal and rating analysis: this is direct secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a) when the service-connected GERD and its acid regurgitation produce the tooth-surface loss and any resulting tooth loss; the theory is causation rather than aggravation because a new erosive process is being produced by the service-connected reflux. If a pre-existing erosive or abrasive lesion is asserted to have been worsened by reflux acid, a separate § 3.310(b) aggravation analysis must identify the qualifying baseline (pre-reflux dental status or imaging) and the attributable increment beyond natural progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion requires reasoned balancing of the objective reflux findings, the palatal distribution, the exposure chronology and the exclusion of competing causes, because observational prevalence data alone do not establish an individual probability. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: § 4.150 contains no diagnostic code for enamel or dentin erosion; DC 9913 covers loss of teeth due to loss of substance of the maxilla or mandible and expressly does not extend to alveolar loss from periodontal disease, so an erosion-only presentation requires a justified analogous code under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 and, when tooth loss has occurred, DC 9913 subject to its own note. Apply § 4.14 so that the same lost tooth surface or masticatory impairment is not rated twice, and do not duplicate the GERD evaluation. Landing this incoming route requires host-file review: the GERD host identity is published and currently points only to pulmonary targets (asthma, bronchiectasis, COPD, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary fibrosis, respiratory cancer and tuberculosis), and the dental-erosion identity already carries an association-only intrinsic-acid edge from bulimia nervosa that this reflux route must be reconciled against before any landing.

medicalEvidence.title: Dental erosion in gastro-esophageal reflux disease. A systematic review
medicalEvidence.authors: Andrei Picos; Mândra Eugenia Badea; Dan Lucian Dumitrascu
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review of dental erosion in GERD. Reports erosive-lesion prevalence of approximately 48.81 percent in GERD patients versus 20.48 percent in non-GERD comparators, with a median near 25.5 percent and a range of 10.6 to 42 percent, and frames dental erosion as an extraesophageal complication of GERD. Establishes population-level association and mechanism; observational designs cannot establish individual causation.

medicalEvidence.title: Updates in association of gastroesophageal reflux disease and dental erosion: systematic review
medicalEvidence.authors: Adriana De Cássia Ortiz; Simone Ortiz Moura Fideles; Karina Torres Pomini; Rogério Leone Buchaim
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review evaluating the association and prevalence of erosive tooth wear in patients with GERD. Describes dental erosion as dissolution of dental apatite by non-bacterial acid and concludes that GERD can be considered a risk factor. Supports the reflux-acid mechanism; review-level evidence without individual risk quantification.

medicalEvidence.title: Dental Erosion in Patients with Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) in a Sample of Patients Referred to the Motahari Clinic, Shiraz, Iran
medicalEvidence.authors: G Alavi; S Adib; A Bahrami; F Nikkhah
medicalEvidence.summary: Comparative clinical study of 140 adults aged 30 to 50 evaluating the association of GERD with dental erosion relative to non-GERD comparators; concluded that GERD patients are at higher risk of developing dental erosion. Provides primary clinical support for the association; single-region sample limits generalization.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Stress urinary incontinence (cough-induced urine leakage)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated diagnostic code designates stress urinary incontinence as a diagnosis in 38 CFR § 4.115b. The § 4.115a voiding-dysfunction schedule supplies severity tiers for 'Continual Urine Leakage, Post Surgical Urinary Diversion, Urinary Incontinence, or Stress Incontinence' (20, 40 or 60 percent by absorbent-material requirement), but it must be reached through a listed diagnostic code, so a clinically justified analogous evaluation under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 is required (DC 7542 neurogenic bladder and DC 7517 bladder injury are candidate comparators only and are not asserted automatically). Qualified-human rating review required
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with a documented chronic cough
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.97, DC 6604 (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Mechanical pressure-transmission sequence: in service-connected chronic obstructive pulmonary disease the chronic cough produces repeated, abrupt rises in intra-abdominal pressure. That pressure is transmitted to the bladder and to the pelvic floor, and when the generated force exceeds urethral closure pressure the result is involuntary urine leakage on coughing, sneezing or exertion — stress urinary incontinence. Repetitive loading of the pelvic connective tissue (endopelvic and pubocervical fascia and the urethral support mechanism) promotes urethral hypermobility and intrinsic sphincter deficiency; hyperinflation with diaphragmatic flattening and chronic smoking-related connective-tissue degradation are recognized co-factors. Zhu et al. (PMID 37226650), analyzing 2015 to 2020 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data in 9,059 women, found that 42.13 percent reported a stress-incontinence episode in the past year and 6.29 percent had a COPD diagnosis, and identified a logical association between COPD or asthma and stress urinary incontinence through coughing-related increases in intra-abdominal pressure. Dicpinigaitis (PMID 33644221) documented stress urinary incontinence in 63.3 percent of women presenting for evaluation of chronic cough, noting that this frequency greatly exceeds ordinary population estimates. Haukeland-Parker et al. (PMID 34895285) randomized women with COPD and urinary incontinence to pelvic floor muscle training, cough-suppression techniques or written information, demonstrating that the incontinence is treatable through pelvic-floor and cough-directed measures and thereby supporting a cough-driven mechanical mechanism. These sources establish a recognized mechanical pathway at the population level; they are observational or interventional rather than etiologic, and they cannot quantify any individual veteran's risk.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: document the COPD by spirometry and a longitudinal cough history, obtain a focused urinary history with a cough stress test or urodynamic confirmation, and record leakage onset relative to the cough. Vaginal delivery and parity, obesity, prior pelvic surgery (including hysterectomy and anti-incontinence or prostate surgery), pelvic radiation, chronic constipation, connective-tissue disorders, neurological disease, and medications such as diuretics or alpha-blockers are competing causes that must be assessed and apportioned. Men may develop post-prostatectomy stress incontinence, a competing mechanism that must not be attributed to cough without specific evidence, and mixed urinary incontinence combining urgency with stress leakage is common and requires urodynamic discrimination. A temporal link between the chronic cough and the onset of leakage, a positive cough stress test, and a plausible alternative-cause analysis favor the COPD-related route; leakage preceding the COPD or occurring only after pelvic surgery weakens it.

Legal and rating analysis: this is direct secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a) when the service-connected COPD and its chronic cough produce the stress urinary incontinence; the theory is causation because a distinct new leakage disability is generated, not merely a pre-existing pattern that is made worse. If a pre-existing continence problem first documented before service-connected COPD is asserted to have been aggravated, a separate § 3.310(b) aggravation analysis must identify the qualifying baseline and the attributable increment beyond natural progression, such as a documented change in pad use. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion requires the veteran-specific cough history, urodynamic or cough-stress findings, chronology and competing-cause apportionment to be balanced, because population prevalence and randomized treatment data do not themselves establish an individual probability. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: § 4.115a provides the stress-incontinence severity tiers but no free-standing diagnostic code, so the evaluation must pass through a listed genitourinary code analogized under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 (DC 7542 or DC 7517 as candidates only), with the 20/40/60 percent tiers keyed to absorbent-material requirement. Apply § 4.14 so that the same leakage is not also rated as part of the COPD evaluation, and combine § 4.25 consistently. Landing this incoming route requires host-file review: the COPD host identity is published and currently points only to sleep apnea and pulmonary hypertension, and the stress-urinary-incontinence identity is draft with no incoming edges.

medicalEvidence.title: Association between respiratory disease and stress urinary incontinence: An analysis of the 2015-2020 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
medicalEvidence.authors: Michael Zhu; Jasper Sim; Chihiro Okada; Joseph Kim; Nitya Abraham
medicalEvidence.summary: Analysis of 2015-2020 NHANES data in 9,059 women: 42.13 percent reported a stress-incontinence episode in the prior year and 6.29 percent had a COPD diagnosis. Identifies a logical association between COPD or asthma and stress urinary incontinence driven by coughing-related increases in intra-abdominal pressure. Cross-sectional design cannot establish individual causation.

medicalEvidence.title: Prevalence of stress urinary incontinence in women presenting for evaluation of chronic cough
medicalEvidence.authors: Peter V Dicpinigaitis
medicalEvidence.summary: Research letter reporting that 63.3 percent of women presenting for evaluation of chronic cough had stress urinary incontinence, a frequency well above ordinary population estimates, and framing cough as the mechanical driver. Supports the cough-to-incontinence mechanism; single-site series without causal inference.

medicalEvidence.title: Treatment of urinary incontinence in women with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease—a randomised controlled study
medicalEvidence.authors: Stacey Haukeland-Parker; Anne Edvardsen; Anja Bye; Sigurd L Steinshamn; Inger L Skaug; Kari Bø; Jorunn Helbostad; Hege H Clemm
medicalEvidence.summary: Three-armed single-blinded randomized controlled trial in women with COPD and urinary incontinence comparing 16 weeks of pelvic floor muscle training, cough-suppression techniques or written information. Demonstrates that the incontinence is modifiable by pelvic-floor and cough-directed interventions, supporting a cough-driven mechanical mechanism; a treatment trial, not an etiologic cohort.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Urge urinary incontinence (overactive bladder from diabetic neurogenic bladder dysfunction)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.115b, DC 7542 (neurogenic bladder) — rated as voiding dysfunction under § 4.115a, using its urgency, frequency and urine-leakage tiers
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus with documented autonomic neuropathy
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7913 (diabetes mellitus), with Note (1) requiring that compensable complications be evaluated separately unless they are part of the 100-percent criteria
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Microvascular and autonomic-neuropathy sequence: chronic hyperglycemia in service-connected type 2 diabetes damages the small vessels and autonomic nerve fibers supplying the lower urinary tract, impairing afferent bladder sensation and the coordinated detrusor-sphincter reflex. Golbidi et al. (PMID 21833175) describe diabetic cystopathy as a well-recognized complication that develops in patients with long-standing, poorly controlled diabetes and present a clinical spectrum that ranges from overactive bladder and urge incontinence to decreased bladder sensation and overflow incontinence, with pathophysiology driven by urologic complications of diabetes. Liu and Daneshgari (PMID 24709194) review diabetic bladder dysfunction as a common and bothersome complication and summarize the altered detrusor contractility, urothelial dysfunction and neural changes that underlie storage and emptying symptoms. Agochukwu-Mmonu et al. (PMID 33197694) document that diabetic autonomic neuropathy affects the genitourinary system and produces diabetic bladder dysfunction alongside sexual and other autonomic complications. Collectively these sources establish diabetes-related autonomic neuropathy as an accepted cause of bladder storage dysfunction, while the phenotype is heterogeneous — detrusor overactivity with urgency and urge leakage in some patients, impaired contractility with incomplete emptying in others — so individual attribution depends on urodynamic characterization rather than the diagnosis of diabetes alone.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: obtain the diabetes history with duration, glycemic control and documented autonomic neuropathy (gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension, resting tachycardia or heart-rate-variability testing), and urodynamic study documenting detrusor overactivity, impaired sensation or impaired contractility as appropriate; record urgency, frequency and leakage patterns and pad use. Benign prostatic hyperplasia or other bladder outlet obstruction, urinary tract infection, bladder stones, pelvic surgery or radiation, spinal cord or cauda-equina disease, multiple sclerosis, medication effects (diuretics, antimuscarinics, alpha-blockers, opioids) and idiopathic overactive bladder are competing causes that must be excluded or apportioned. Because diabetes also causes polyuria through osmotic diuresis, frequency alone is not evidence of neurogenic bladder; urge leakage with urodynamic detrusor overactivity in the setting of established diabetic autonomic neuropathy favors the diabetes-related route, whereas symptoms that begin with a competing urologic or neurologic disorder, or that persist unchanged with good glycemic control and no neuropathy findings, weaken it.

Legal and rating analysis: this is direct secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a) when the service-connected diabetes and its autonomic neuropathy produce the bladder storage dysfunction and urge leakage. If pre-existing urgency or incontinence is asserted to have been worsened, a separate § 3.310(b) aggravation analysis must identify the qualifying baseline urodynamic or symptom record and the attributable increment beyond natural progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion requires the individual's diabetes duration, neuropathy findings, urodynamic pattern and competing-cause analysis to be in approximate balance rather than resting on population reports, which do not establish an individual probability. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: § 4.115b DC 7542 (neurogenic bladder) directs rating as voiding dysfunction or urinary tract infection, whichever predominates, and § 4.115a supplies the urgency, frequency and urine-leakage tiers. DC 7913 Note (1) requires compensable complications to be evaluated separately unless they support the 100-percent diabetes criteria; apply § 4.14 so the same frequency, urgency or leakage is not also used to support a duplicate genitourinary rating. Landing this incoming route requires host-file review: the type-2-diabetes host identity is published and currently points to GERD, chronic kidney disease, diabetic retinopathy and depressive disorder, and the urge-urinary-incontinence identity is draft with no incoming edges.

medicalEvidence.title: Bladder Dysfunction in Diabetes Mellitus
medicalEvidence.authors: Saeid Golbidi; Ismail Laher
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of diabetic cystopathy as a well-recognized complication of long-standing, poorly controlled diabetes, describing a clinical spectrum from overactive bladder and urge incontinence to decreased bladder sensation and overflow incontinence, with discussion of the underlying pathophysiologic mechanisms. Establishes the mechanism; review-level evidence without individual risk estimates.

medicalEvidence.title: Diabetic Bladder Dysfunction
medicalEvidence.authors: Guiming Liu; Firouz Daneshgari
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of diabetic bladder dysfunction as a common and bothersome complication of diabetes, summarizing altered detrusor contractility, urothelial and neural changes and reporting the authors' own experimental data. Supports a diabetes-driven storage and emptying disorder; narrative review without an individual causation estimate.

medicalEvidence.title: Autonomic Neuropathy and Urologic Complications in Diabetes
medicalEvidence.authors: Nnenaya Agochukwu-Mmonu; Priyanka Merali; H Henry Lai; Claire S Yang; Aruna V Sarma; Hunter Wessells
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of diabetic autonomic neuropathy and its genitourinary complications, including diabetic bladder dysfunction, sexual dysfunction and recurrent urinary tract infection, drawing on urologic epidemiologic data. Documents the autonomic-neuropathy route to bladder dysfunction; review-level evidence.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Pleural effusion (transudative, heart-failure-associated)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.97, DC 6845 (chronic pleural effusion or fibrosis) under the Restrictive Lung Disease general rating formula, or rate the primary disorder; when the effusion is a manifestation of the service-connected cardiac disease it is generally evaluated with that condition rather than separately, subject to § 4.14
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected congestive heart failure (left or biventricular), rated under the heart-disease general rating formula
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.104, General Rating Formula for Diseases of the Heart, reached through the etiologic code such as DC 7005 (arteriosclerotic heart disease) or DC 7007 (hypertensive heart disease) as the documented cause requires
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Hydrostatic pressure sequence: in service-connected congestive heart failure, elevated left-heart filling pressures raise pulmonary capillary pressure and drive fluid across the pleural membrane faster than pleural lymphatics can resorb it, while systemic venous hypertension from right-heart failure further impairs lymphatic drainage; the result is a transudative pleural effusion, characteristically bilateral or right-sided and a marker of decompensation. Elgwairi et al. (PMID 36576376) describe pleural effusions as common in cardiac disease (approximately 500,000 cases per year in the United States), explain their pathogenesis and diagnostic evaluation, and note that although most heart-failure effusions are transudates, some 20 to 25 percent show increased protein and lactate dehydrogenase suggesting an exudative picture. Natanzon and Kronzon (PMID 19574887) analyze the anatomical and pathophysiologic basis of pleural and pericardial effusions in heart failure and emphasize that right-sided filling-pressure elevation is required. Korczynski et al. (PMID 30406935), reviewing 2,835 consecutive admissions with radiographic pleural effusion in 195 of 1,936 evaluated patients, found congestive heart failure responsible for 37.4 percent of all pleural effusions and identified it as the leading cause. Together these sources establish heart failure as a recognized and frequently dominant cause of pleural effusion at the mechanism and population level; they do not quantify any individual veteran's risk, and the effusion may coexist with other causes.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: obtain the heart-failure diagnosis with echocardiographic ejection fraction and filling-pressure assessment, natriuretic-peptide levels, chest imaging documenting the effusion and any change with diuresis, and, when tapped, pleural-fluid analysis with Light's criteria. Pneumonia or parapneumonic effusion, pulmonary embolism, malignancy (including mesothelioma and metastatic disease), tuberculosis, rheumatoid and other autoimmune pleuritis, pancreatitis, hepatic hydrothorax, nephrotic syndrome, and post-cardiac-surgery effusions are competing causes that must be excluded or apportioned; the fact that up to a quarter of heart-failure effusions meet exudative criteria means exudative chemistry does not by itself exclude heart failure. A temporal relationship between worsening cardiac function and the effusion, bilateral or right-predominant distribution, transudative chemistry where available, and resolution with heart-failure treatment favor the cardiac route; an effusion that predates the cardiac diagnosis, is left-sided or loculated, or persists despite adequate decongestion suggests another cause.

Legal and rating analysis: this is direct secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a) when the service-connected heart failure produces the pleural effusion. If a pre-existing pleural process is asserted to have been worsened, a separate § 3.310(b) aggravation analysis must identify the qualifying baseline imaging and the attributable increment beyond natural progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion requires reasoned balancing of the cardiac findings, the fluid characteristics, the response to heart-failure treatment and the exclusion of competing causes; population frequency data do not establish an individual probability. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: § 4.97 DC 6845 (chronic pleural effusion or fibrosis) sits within the Restrictive Lung Disease general rating formula and expressly allows rating the primary disorder instead; § 4.104 states that cor pulmonale is evaluated as part of the pulmonary condition that causes it, and the general instructions for secondary heart disease reflect the same non-duplication principle. Apply § 4.14 so that the same breathlessness or exercise limitation is not rated under both the cardiac general formula and a separate pleural-effusion evaluation. Landing this incoming route requires host-file review: the congestive-heart-failure identity is published and currently points only to depressive disorder, and the pleural-effusion identity is draft with incoming association-only edges from abscess, malignant and pleuritic sources but none cardiac.

medicalEvidence.title: Pleural Effusions in Patients With Congestive Heart Failure: Frequency, Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Implications
medicalEvidence.authors: Emadeldeen Elgwairi; Amira Abdalla; Ahmed Elkheshen; Zeyad Elharabi; Kenneth Nugent
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of pleural effusion in congestive heart failure, reporting approximately 500,000 cardiac-related cases per year in the United States, describing transudative pathogenesis and noting that 20 to 25 percent of heart-failure effusions show exudative protein and lactate dehydrogenase levels. Establishes mechanism and scale; review-level evidence.

medicalEvidence.title: Pericardial and pleural effusions in congestive heart failure-anatomical, pathophysiologic, and clinical considerations
medicalEvidence.authors: Alex Natanzon; Itzhak Kronzon
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of the anatomical and pathophysiologic basis of pleural and pericardial effusions in congestive heart failure, emphasizing that elevation of right-sided filling pressure is required for effusion formation. Provides the hemodynamic mechanism linking heart failure to transudative effusion; not a cohort risk estimate.

medicalEvidence.title: Significance of congestive heart failure as a cause of pleural effusion: Pilot data from a large multidisciplinary teaching hospital
medicalEvidence.authors: Piotr Korczyński; Katarzyna Górska; Adam Bialas; Renata Langfort; Elzbieta Wiatr; Jan Zielinski; Rafal Krenke
medicalEvidence.summary: Retrospective analysis of radiographs and records for 2,835 consecutive admissions: pleural effusion was found in 195 of 1,936 evaluated patients (10.1 percent), and congestive heart failure was responsible for 37.4 percent of all cases, making it the leading cause. Quantifies the population contribution of heart failure; retrospective single-center pilot design.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Rotator cuff tear with residual shoulder impairment (degenerative, diabetes-associated)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5201 (arm, limitation of motion) for limitation produced by the tear, and/or § 4.73, DC 5304 (Muscle Group IV — supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor, subscapularis, coracobrachialis), rated by the § 4.56 severity criteria when motion is relatively preserved; § 4.59 governs evaluation of painful motion. Qualified-human rating review required
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7913 (diabetes mellitus), with Note (1) on separately evaluating compensable complications
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Metabolic-tendinopathy sequence: chronic hyperglycemia in service-connected type 2 diabetes promotes formation of advanced glycation end-products that cross-link tendon collagen, increases oxidative stress and produces microangiopathic impairment of the tendon-bone insertion, a region already relatively hypovascular; the resulting degenerative tendinopathy weakens the rotator cuff so that a full- or partial-thickness tear may develop with ordinary loading or minor trauma. Giri et al. (PMID 35257948), a systematic review and meta-analysis, found diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidemia associated with rotator cuff disease and attributed the association at least in part to mechanisms related to vascular insufficiency. Xu et al. (PMID 36299460) established a type 2 diabetic rat model and documented glycation and oxidative changes in the rotator cuff tendon over 12 weeks, providing direct experimental support for diabetes-induced tendinopathy. Smith et al. (PMID 34223408) found that diabetic patients were at higher risk of undergoing rotator cuff repair surgery in a large retrospective cohort. These sources establish diabetes as a recognized contributor to rotator cuff pathology at the epidemiologic and experimental level while the tear itself remains multifactorial; the literature cannot identify which individual diabetic patient's tear is diabetes-attributable, and age-related degeneration is a competing process.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: obtain imaging that characterizes the tear (ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging documenting full- or partial-thickness involvement, retraction and fatty infiltration), the diabetes history with duration and glycemic control, and an examination of active and passive range of motion, strength and painful arc. Acute traumatic tears after a fall or lifting event, age-related degenerative tearing, shoulder instability or prior dislocation, subacromial impingement, inflammatory and crystal arthropathy, infection, and cervical radiculopathy referred to the shoulder are competing causes or contributors that must be assessed; smoking, overhead occupational loading and contralateral cuff disease are additional risk modifiers. A degenerative-tear pattern in a long-standing diabetic with impaired glycemic control, bilateral or attritional findings, and absence of a discrete traumatic event favors the diabetes-related route; a single high-energy injury, or a tear in a well-controlled diabetic with no other diabetic complications, weakens the metabolic attribution and points to trauma or age as the cause.

Legal and rating analysis: this is direct secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a) when the service-connected diabetes and its metabolic effects produce or materially accelerate the degenerative rotator cuff tear. If a pre-existing cuff tear or shoulder degeneration is asserted to have been worsened, a § 3.310(b) aggravation analysis must identify the qualifying baseline imaging or examination and the attributable increment beyond natural progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion requires the individual's glycemic history, tear morphology, absence of a discrete traumatic cause and competing-cause assessment to be balanced, because population association and animal-model data do not establish an individual probability. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: § 4.71a DC 5201 supplies the arm/shoulder limitation evaluation and § 4.73 DC 5304 covers the rotator cuff muscle group using § 4.56 severity criteria, with § 4.59 requiring that painful motion be considered; DC 7913 Note (1) governs separate evaluation of the diabetic complication. Apply § 4.14 so that the same limitation of motion or weakness is not rated under both the shoulder codes and any other orthopedic evaluation, and apply § 4.25 for combination. Landing this incoming route requires host-file review: the type-2-diabetes host identity is published and currently points to GERD, chronic kidney disease, diabetic retinopathy and depressive disorder, and the rotator-cuff-tear identity is draft with no incoming edges, while the separate rotator-cuff-injury identity already receives associations from bicipital tendinitis and SLAP tear.

medicalEvidence.title: Risk factors for rotator cuff disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis of diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia
medicalEvidence.authors: Ayush Giri; Deirdre O'Hanlon; Nitin B Jain
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis finding diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidemia associated with rotator cuff disease, with suggested mechanisms related to vascular insufficiency. Establishes a population-level metabolic association; heterogeneity and observational data limit individual inference.

medicalEvidence.title: Evaluating the role of type 2 diabetes mellitus in rotator cuff tendinopathy: Development and analysis of a novel rat model
medicalEvidence.authors: Kuishuai Xu; Chen Chen; Peng Zhang; Zhaoxu Wang; Hongxing Zhang; Xiaoyu Wang; Liang Zhang; Junfei Wang
medicalEvidence.summary: Experimental study establishing an intact rotator cuff rat model of type 2 diabetes and analyzing tendon changes over 12 weeks, demonstrating glycation and oxidative stress in diabetic rotator cuff tissue. Provides direct mechanistic support for diabetes-induced tendinopathy; animal model does not establish human individual causation.

medicalEvidence.title: Does diabetes mellitus predispose to both rotator cuff surgery and subsequent failure?
medicalEvidence.authors: Karch M Smith; Angela P Presson; Chong Zhang; Joshua J Horns; James M Hotaling; Robert Z Tashjian; Peter N Chalmers
medicalEvidence.summary: Large retrospective cohort analyzing whether diabetes mellitus predisposes to rotator cuff repair surgery and to subsequent revision surgery, finding diabetic patients at higher risk of undergoing rotator cuff repair. Supports a diabetes-to-cuff-pathology pathway at population level; retrospective design and confounding by indication limit causal inference.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Aortic aneurysm (ascending, thoracic or abdominal) aggravated by chronic hypertension
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.104, DC 7110 (aortic aneurysm: ascending, thoracic, or abdominal) — evaluated at 100 percent only when the aneurysm is 5 centimeters or larger, symptomatic, or requires surgery, and otherwise at 0 percent
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected hypertensive vascular disease (hypertension), with documented chronic blood-pressure elevation
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.104, DC 7101 (hypertensive vascular disease; hypertension and isolated systolic hypertension), confirmed by readings taken on at least three different days
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Hemodynamic wall-stress sequence: in service-connected hypertension, chronically elevated aortic wall tension and shear increase cyclic strain on an already age-degenerate media, promoting elastin fragmentation, collagen remodeling, matrix-metalloproteinase activation and smooth-muscle apoptosis; the resulting loss of tensile strength allows progressive dilatation. That mechanism superimposes on a pre-existing degenerative and atherosclerotic aortopathy, so the medically coherent theory is aggravation of a baseline process rather than creation of an aneurysm de novo. Kobeissi et al. (PMID 30903463), a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies of blood pressure and abdominal aortic aneurysm, found that hypertension increased the risk of developing abdominal aortic aneurysm by about 66 percent, with a dose relationship across blood-pressure categories. Altobelli et al. (PMID 30544688), meta-analyzing population-based risk-factor studies, reported hypertension with an effect size of approximately 1.55 for abdominal aortic aneurysm alongside age, male sex and smoking. Takagi et al. (PMID 27521823) found hypertension positively associated with aneurysm presence but not with aneurysm expansion rate, which is an important internal counterweight: the literature supports an association with the existence of aneurysm disease while the evidence that hypertension drives growth of an already-measured aneurysm is weaker. These sources are observational, and smoking, age, male sex, family history and genetic syndromes are established competing drivers, so no individual probability follows from them.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: obtain the serial imaging record showing aneurysm dimensions, the rate of change and the site (ascending, thoracic, abdominal), contemporaneous blood-pressure records documenting chronic elevation and control, and the full vascular-risk profile. Cigarette smoking, advanced age, male sex, family history of aneurysm, connective-tissue disorders such as Marfan or Loeys-Dietz syndrome, bicuspid aortic valve, prior dissection, vasculitis and other atherosclerotic disease are competing causes that must be documented and apportioned; distinguishing a discrete fusiform aneurysm from aortic ectasia matters because the diagnostic code turns on measured diameter, symptoms and operative need. A temporal pattern in which elevated pressures predate documented dilatation, together with a measured increment beyond the expected age-related rate of change, favors the hypertensive-aggravation route; an aneurysm that is stable over years of documented hypertension, or that occurs in a heavy smoker with a strong family history, weakens the attribution to hypertension.

Legal and rating analysis: because the theory asserted here is aggravation, the governing provision is 38 CFR § 3.310(b), which requires a qualifying baseline (the pre-existing degenerative aortic wall condition, documented by earlier imaging or the natural history of the disease) and an attributable increase beyond the natural progression of that baseline; if the evidence instead supports the aneurysm as an outgrowth of the hypertension itself, the same facts may be analyzed as direct causation under § 3.310(a). An 'at least as likely as not' opinion requires the blood-pressure record, the imaging trajectory, and the competing causes — especially smoking — to be weighed so that the evidence is at least in approximate balance; population relative risks such as the 66 percent meta-analytic estimate describe groups and do not establish an individual probability. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: § 4.104 DC 7110 provides a 100-percent evaluation only for an aneurysm that is 5 centimeters or larger, symptomatic, or requires surgery, and otherwise assigns 0 percent, so a small asymptomatic aneurysm is generally not compensable despite being service-connected secondary; DC 7101 governs the hypertension primary. Apply § 4.14 so that the same blood-pressure elevation and any cardiac or renal consequences are not rated twice, and note that § 4.104 directs that hypertension be evaluated separately from hypertensive heart disease. Landing this incoming route requires host-file review: the hypertension host identity is published and currently points to chronic kidney disease, ischemic heart disease, congestive heart failure and erectile dysfunction, and the aortic-aneurysm identity is draft with existing gout and tuberculosis inbound associations and outbound suggestions to valvular heart disease and hydronephrosis, so this hypertension route must be reconciled against that existing posture.

medicalEvidence.title: Blood pressure, hypertension and the risk of abdominal aortic aneurysms: a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies
medicalEvidence.authors: Elsa Kobeissi; Matthew Hibberd; Peter Collins; Jonathan Rees; Sarah Lewington
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies of blood pressure and abdominal aortic aneurysm. Found that hypertension increased the risk of developing abdominal aortic aneurysm by about 66 percent, with dose-response across blood-pressure categories. Establishes a population-level association; observational design cannot establish individual causation.

medicalEvidence.title: Risk Factors for Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm in Population-Based Studies: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
medicalEvidence.authors: Emma Altobelli; Roberto Rapacchietta; Valerio Fabiani Proto; Giovanni Paolo Di Girolamo
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of population-based studies of abdominal aortic aneurysm risk factors, reporting an effect size of approximately 1.55 for hypertension (alongside age, male sex and smoking). Supports hypertension as a risk factor; heterogeneous observational data limit individual inference.

medicalEvidence.title: Association of Hypertension with Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Expansion
medicalEvidence.authors: Hisato Takagi; Takuya Umemoto; ALICE (All-Literature Investigation of Cardiovascular Evidence) Group
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis finding hypertension positively associated with abdominal aortic aneurysm presence but not with aneurysm expansion rate. Serves as an internal counterweight that limits the claim: presence is supported, growth acceleration is not.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Trigger finger (stenosing flexor tenosynovitis, flexor-tendon triggering) associated with diabetes mellitus
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5024 (tenosynovitis, tendinitis, tendinosis or tendinopathy), evaluated under the Note to DCs 5013-5024 as degenerative arthritis based on limitation of motion, and/or DC 5229 (index or long finger, limitation of motion) or DC 5230 (ring or little finger, limitation of motion) depending on the digit involved. Qualified-human rating review required
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus (with or without documented peripheral neuropathy and with the duration and control of record)
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7913 (diabetes mellitus), with Note (1) requiring that compensable complications be evaluated separately unless used to support the 100-percent criteria
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Metabolic tenosynovial sequence: chronic hyperglycemia in service-connected diabetes drives non-enzymatic glycation of collagen and connective-tissue matrix in the flexor tendon sheath, with fibrocartilaginous metaplasia and thickening of the A1 pulley and the flexor tendon itself; the resulting size mismatch produces a mechanical block to tendon gliding and the painful catching or locking called trigger finger. Tissue deposition of advanced glycation end-products and associated microangiopathic change is the same process implicated in diabetic cheiroarthropathy and Dupuytren diathesis, which commonly co-occur with triggering. Lofgren et al. (PMID 36994346) conducted a population-based longitudinal cohort study over more than 20 years in 30,446 individuals and found diabetes mellitus to be an important independent risk factor for developing trigger finger after adjustment for sex, age, body-mass index, manual work and statin use. Koh et al. (PMID 19687073) surveyed 544 patients with diabetes and found that 10 percent had a history of trigger digits with 4 percent having multiple-digit involvement, that risk was significantly higher in insulin-dependent patients, and that mean diabetes duration was significantly longer in those with multiple involved digits. Junot et al. (PMID 31456430) reviewed 75 patients with trigger finger and found that 80 percent met criteria for metabolic syndrome, framing trigger finger as a metabolic-associated disorder rather than a purely mechanical overuse injury. These sources establish diabetes as a recognized contributor to stenosing flexor tenosynovitis; they are observational and cannot determine which individual diabetic patient's triggering is diabetes-attributable.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: document the diabetes history with duration, glycemic control and any other diabetic connective-tissue or neuropathic manifestations, and obtain a hand examination localizing the affected digit(s) with the classic nodular thickening, pain and mechanical locking. Repetitive or forceful manual work, rheumatoid and other inflammatory arthritis, hypothyroidism, amyloid deposition (including dialysis-related amyloid), gout and other crystal arthropathy, local trauma, prior steroid injection, and de Quervain or other discrete tendon disorders are competing causes that must be assessed; multiple-digit involvement, bilateral disease or recurrence after release favors a systemic metabolic contribution, whereas a single digit after a discrete overuse or traumatic episode favors a local mechanical cause. Because the same structural change can be coded through the tendinopathy code or through digit-specific limitation of motion, the findings must be attributed once.

Legal and rating analysis: this is direct secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a) when the service-connected diabetes and its metabolic effects produce the stenosing tenosynovitis; the theory is causation because a new tendon-gliding disability is generated. If a pre-existing trigger finger or flexor tenosynovitis is asserted to have been worsened, a separate § 3.310(b) aggravation analysis must identify the qualifying baseline (prior examination or surgical record) and the attributable increment beyond natural progression, such as new digits involved or increasing recurrence. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion requires the diabetes duration and control, the digit pattern, the recurrence and the competing-cause assessment to be weighed so that the evidence is at least in approximate balance; cohort risk estimates do not establish an individual probability. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: § 4.71a DC 5024 covers tenosynovitis/tendinopathy and the Note to DCs 5013-5024 directs evaluation as degenerative arthritis on limitation of motion, while DC 5229 and DC 5230 rate digit-specific limitation; DC 7913 Note (1) governs separate evaluation of the diabetic complication. Apply § 4.14 so that the same triggering and loss of finger motion are not rated under both the tendinopathy code and a digit-limitation code, and apply § 4.25 where a separate digit is genuinely and separately impaired. Landing this incoming route requires host-file review: the type-2-diabetes host identity is published and currently points to GERD, chronic kidney disease, diabetic retinopathy and depressive disorder, and the trigger-finger identity is draft with no outgoing edges and one inbound association-only edge from Dupuytren contracture.

medicalEvidence.title: Diabetes Mellitus as a Risk Factor for Trigger Finger -a Longitudinal Cohort Study Over More Than 20 Years
medicalEvidence.authors: Jin Persson Löfgren; Malin Zimmerman; Lars B Dahlin; Peter M Nilsson; Mattias Rydberg
medicalEvidence.summary: Population-based cohort of 30,446 individuals followed more than 20 years, finding diabetes mellitus an important independent risk factor for developing trigger finger after adjustment for sex, age, body-mass index, manual work and statin use. Strongest available longitudinal support; observational and not an individual causation estimate.

medicalEvidence.title: Trigger digits in diabetes: their incidence and characteristics
medicalEvidence.authors: S Koh; S Nakamura; T Hattori; H Hirata
medicalEvidence.summary: Questionnaire survey of 544 patients with diabetes: 10 percent had a history of trigger digits and 4 percent had multiple-digit involvement, with significantly higher risk in insulin-dependent patients and significantly longer mean diabetes duration in those with multiple involved digits. Supports an incidence and severity gradient with diabetes; single-center questionnaire design.

medicalEvidence.title: Epidemiology of Trigger Finger: Metabolic Syndrome as a New Perspective of Associated Disease
medicalEvidence.authors: H S N Junot; A S M D Santos; C E S Ramos; B C da Silva; A C C F Bruin; V M P de Araújo; P F de Vasconcelos; L F M F de Moraes
medicalEvidence.summary: Retrospective observational study of 75 patients with trigger finger in which 80 percent met criteria for metabolic syndrome, framing trigger finger as an associated metabolic disorder. Supports the metabolic route; single-center retrospective design.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Xerostomia (persistent dry mouth with salivary hypofunction) from inhaled anticholinergic therapy
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated diagnostic code for xerostomia or salivary hypofunction is listed in 38 CFR Part 4. A clinically justified analogous evaluation under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 is required based on demonstrated oral dryness, salivary measurement where available and functional impact; where the dryness is an inseparable burden of the service-connected respiratory treatment it may instead be evaluated with the respiratory condition. Qualified-human rating review required
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected chronic obstructive pulmonary disease treated with a maintenance inhaled anticholinergic agent (for example tiotropium or ipratropium)
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.97, DC 6604 (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease)
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Pharmacological sequence: maintenance inhaled antimuscarinic bronchodilators block muscarinic M1 and M3 receptors in the airway to relieve bronchospasm, but the same M3 blockade at salivary and mucosal receptors reduces serous and mucous salivary secretion; because the drug is deposited in the oropharynx during inhalation, the local concentration there is high, and systemic absorption (greater for ipratropium given its quaternary-ammonium pharmacokinetics) adds a systemic anticholinergic contribution. The result is persistent xerostomia, sometimes with soreness, altered taste, difficulty swallowing dry foods and increased dental caries. Kesten et al. (PMID 17166984), pooling adverse-event data from 19 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled tiotropium trials, found a higher relative risk of dry mouth in the tiotropium group (relative risk 3.60; 95 percent confidence interval 2.56 to 5.05). Casaburi et al. (PMID 11083677), a 13-week randomized multicenter trial of tiotropium versus placebo in 470 patients with stable COPD, reported dry mouth as the most common adverse event after tiotropium (9.3 percent versus 1.6 percent; p less than 0.05). Xu et al. (PMID 39403528) analyzed the United States Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System database for drug-induced dry mouth and found tiotropium bromide monohydrate the single most frequently reported drug (2,080 cases) among 75,899 dry-mouth reports. These sources establish an exposure-linked pharmacological effect with a clear dose-and-drug gradient; they describe group-level reporting and do not quantify any individual veteran's symptom burden.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: document the exact inhaled anticholinergic agent, dose, start date and duration; the temporal relationship between starting the inhaler and the onset or worsening of dryness; objective findings such as clinical oral examination, salivary flow or sialometry when available, and evidence of oral sequelae (candidiasis, caries, mucosal changes). Other xerogenic medications (tricyclic and other antidepressants, antihistamines, diuretics, opioids, antipsychotics, antispasmodics), Sjogren syndrome and other autoimmune disease, diabetes and its polyuria-related oral dryness, head and neck radiation, smoking, mouth-breathing from nasal obstruction, dehydration and anxiety are competing causes that must be documented and apportioned. Dryness that begins or escalates after the inhaler is started, improves with mouth rinsing or a change of agent, and lacks another xerogenic exposure favors the medication route; pre-existing oral dryness or a strong non-medication cause weakens it. The same anticholinergic exposure may also be coincidental to an unrelated sicca syndrome, so objective sicca testing should be considered when features suggest autoimmune disease.

Legal and rating analysis: this is treatment-mediated secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a): the service-connected COPD is treated with an inhaled anticholinergic and that pharmacological exposure produces the xerostomia, so the theory is a medication side effect rather than a separate coexisting disease. If pre-existing oral dryness is asserted to have been worsened, a separate § 3.310(b) aggravation analysis must identify the qualifying baseline (prior dental or sicca assessment) and the attributable increment beyond natural progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion requires the exposure chronology, the drug-specific adverse-event evidence and the competing-cause analysis to be weighed so that the evidence is at least in approximate balance; trial incidence and pharmacovigilance reporting rates describe groups and do not establish an individual probability. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: Part 4 contains no diagnostic code for xerostomia, so a clinically justified analogous evaluation under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 is required and must not invent a rated value; alternatively, where the dryness cannot be separated from the respiratory treatment, evaluate it with the service-connected respiratory condition. Apply § 4.14 so that the same dryness, mucosal injury or dental consequence is not rated twice, and coordinate any separate dental or oral evaluation. Landing this incoming route requires host-file review: the COPD host identity is published and currently points to sleep apnea and pulmonary hypertension, and the xerostomia identity is draft with inbound association-only edges from salivary-gland cancer, sialadenitis and sialolithiasis but no medication route.

medicalEvidence.title: Pooled clinical trial analysis of tiotropium safety
medicalEvidence.authors: Steven Kesten; Michele Jara; Charles Wentworth; Stephan Lanes
medicalEvidence.summary: Pooled analysis of adverse-event data from 19 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled tiotropium trials in obstructive lung disease; found a higher relative risk of dry mouth in the tiotropium group (relative risk 3.60; 95 percent CI 2.56 to 5.05). Strongest trial-level support for the anticholinergic route; pooled group data only.

medicalEvidence.title: The spirometric efficacy of once-daily dosing with tiotropium in stable COPD: a 13-week multicenter trial. The US Tiotropium Study Group
medicalEvidence.authors: R Casaburi; D D Briggs Jr; J F Donohue; C W Serby; S S Menjoge; T J Witek Jr
medicalEvidence.summary: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicenter trial (470 patients with stable COPD; tiotropium 18 micrograms once daily versus placebo) reporting dry mouth as the most common adverse event after tiotropium (9.3 percent versus 1.6 percent; p less than 0.05). Provides randomized incidence support; single trial population.

medicalEvidence.title: Disproportionality analysis of drug-induced dry mouth using data from the United States food and drug administration adverse event reporting system database
medicalEvidence.authors: Dan Xu; Qiong Zhang; Xiaoyan Hu; Chuanfeng Liu; Mengna Wu; Yanan Yu; Xue Wang; Yixin Zhang
medicalEvidence.summary: Pharmacovigilance disproportionality analysis of 75,899 dry-mouth reports in the FAERS database identifying tiotropium bromide monohydrate as the drug most frequently associated with dry mouth (2,080 cases). Supports the drug-specific signal; spontaneous reporting is subject to reporting bias.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Acquired flatfoot (pes planus with hindfoot valgus) due to rheumatoid arthritis
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5276 (flatfoot, acquired) — pronounced, marked pronation and severe symptom criteria
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected rheumatoid arthritis (multi-joint, active or with chronic residuals)
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5002 (multi-joint arthritis as an active process, with rheumatoid arthritis expressly named among its examples) and DC 5003 for chronic residuals
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Inflammatory-structural sequence: in service-connected rheumatoid arthritis, chronic synovitis erodes the midfoot and hindfoot joints (talonavicular, subtalar and naviculocuneiform) and attacks the tibialis posterior tendon sheath, weakening the dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch; the combination of joint destruction and posterior tibial tendon dysfunction allows progressive valgus collapse of the hindfoot and midfoot — acquired flatfoot. Bouysset et al. (PMID 12022347) obtained weight-bearing radiographs of 308 feet in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and 202 control feet, and found that flat foot increased markedly after three to four years of disease duration, with forefoot deformity progression tracked alongside. Zhao et al. (PMID 39421746), applying bidirectional Mendelian randomization and mediation analysis in European populations, found genetic evidence consistent with rheumatoid arthritis causally contributing to postural deformities including flat foot, and their review of the literature reported flat-foot prevalence of roughly 11.0 to 42.1 percent in rheumatoid arthritis. Mizuki et al. (PMID 41053714) analyzed rheumatoid foot deformity patterns and reported flat foot and hindfoot valgus deformities in the range of 19 to 43 percent, emphasizing that coronal hindfoot alignment drives forefoot deformity. These sources establish rheumatoid arthritis as a recognized cause of acquired flatfoot at population and genetic-instrumental levels; observational and genetic designs cannot determine whether any individual veteran's arch collapse is attributable to the arthritis rather than to an independent cause.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: document the rheumatoid arthritis by diagnosis and disease duration with inflammatory activity, and characterize the flatfoot with weight-bearing radiographs or clinical measurement of arch height, hindfoot valgus, tenderness and tibialis posterior function; note whether the deformity is flexible or fixed because that determines both mechanism and rating. Congenital or hereditary pes planus, posterior tibial tendon dysfunction unrelated to inflammatory disease, tarsal coalition, Charcot arthropathy (including diabetic Charcot), obesity and mechanical overload, prior trauma or fracture, and tibialis posterior rupture from other causes are competing causes that must be assessed. A temporal sequence in which a previously normal arch collapses after years of active seropositive rheumatoid disease, with radiographic joint erosion and tibialis posterior dysfunction, favors the rheumatoid route; a lifelong flatfoot or a deformity that develops without active inflammatory disease and without joint erosion points to another cause.

Legal and rating analysis: this is direct secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a) when the service-connected rheumatoid arthritis produces the acquired flatfoot; the theory is causation because a new structural foot disability is generated by the inflammatory disease. If a pre-existing flatfoot or arch insufficiency is asserted to have been worsened, a separate § 3.310(b) aggravation analysis must identify the qualifying baseline (earlier imaging or examination) and the attributable increment beyond natural progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion requires the disease duration and activity, the radiographic erosion pattern, the tibialis posterior findings and the competing-cause analysis to be weighed so that the evidence is at least in approximate balance; prevalence figures and Mendelian randomization do not establish an individual probability. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: § 4.71a DC 5276 is the dedicated acquired-flatfoot code, while the primary is rated under DC 5002 during active disease and DC 5003 for chronic residuals; the Note to DCs 5013-5024 is not the operative route for acquired flatfoot. Apply § 4.14 so that the same arch collapse, foot pain or weight-bearing limitation is not rated under both DC 5276 and a DC 5003 residual limitation for the same foot, and apply § 4.25 and the bilateral factor where both feet are separately impaired. Landing this incoming route requires host-file review: the rheumatoid-arthritis host identity is published and currently points to depressive disorder and GERD, and the flatfoot identity is draft with an outbound association-only suggestion to osteoarthritis and no inbound edges for this inflammatory route.

medicalEvidence.title: Rheumatoid flat foot and deformity of the first ray
medicalEvidence.authors: Maurice Bouysset; Jacques Tebib; Eric Noel; Thierry Tavernier; Pierre Miossec; Jean-Claude Vianey; Jean-Pierre Duivon; Michel Bonnin; Chantal Nemoz; Jocelyne Jalby
medicalEvidence.summary: Weight-bearing radiographic study of 308 feet in patients with rheumatoid arthritis versus 202 control feet; flat foot increased markedly after three to four years of disease duration, with forefoot deformity progression described. Direct clinical support for the rheumatoid-to-flatfoot sequence; cross-sectional radiographic design.

medicalEvidence.title: The causality between rheumatoid arthritis and postural deformities: bidirectional Mendelian randomization study and mediation analysis
medicalEvidence.authors: Piqian Zhao; Hongjun Chen; Zhihao Li; Tie Li; Shaokun Zhang
medicalEvidence.summary: Bidirectional Mendelian randomization and mediation analysis in European populations finding genetic evidence consistent with rheumatoid arthritis causally contributing to postural deformities including flat foot; reports literature prevalence of flat foot in rheumatoid arthritis of approximately 11.0 to 42.1 percent. Instrumental-variable design reduces confounding but cannot substitute for individual clinical attribution.

medicalEvidence.title: Impact of coronal and sagittal hindfoot alignment on metatarsus primus elevatus in patients with rheumatoid foot deformities
medicalEvidence.authors: Shinichi Mizuki; Yasuhiko Kubota; Takaaki Tanaka; Yuya Kawabata; Kiminori Yukata; Akira Furukawa; Toshihiro Matsui
medicalEvidence.summary: Analysis of rheumatoid foot deformity patterns reporting flat foot and hindfoot valgus deformities in approximately 19 to 43 percent of patients and emphasizing coronal hindfoot alignment as a driver of forefoot deformity. Supports the structural collapse sequence; cross-sectional clinical series.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Femoral neuropathy (diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy / diabetic amyotrophy)
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8526 (anterior crural nerve (femoral): complete paralysis 40 percent; incomplete severe 30, moderate 20, mild 10 percent), with DC 8626 (neuritis) as the alternative when the presentation is inflammatory-painful rather than paralytic. Qualified-human rating review required
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus with documented diabetic neuropathy
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7913 (diabetes mellitus), with Note (1) requiring that compensable complications be evaluated separately unless used to support the 100-percent criteria
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism:
Immune-ischemic microvasculitic sequence: diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy (diabetic amyotrophy) is a subacute, painful, asymmetric lower-limb neuropathy that involves the lumbosacral roots and plexus and therefore commonly the femoral territory, producing quadriceps weakness, wasting and knee-extensor impairment. The prevailing pathophysiologic explanation is an ischemic microvasculitis with epineurial inflammatory infiltrates affecting nerve roots and plexus, rather than the simple length-dependent metabolic axonopathy of classic diabetic polyneuropathy; weight loss and poor glycemic control are typical antecedents. Ng et al. (PMID 30760636) used the Rochester Epidemiology Project to determine the previously unknown incidence of lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy in Olmsted County over 16 years, identifying 59 patients and reporting an incidence of approximately 4.16 per 100,000 person-years with a strong association with diabetes mellitus. Dyck and Windebank (PMID 11932965) compared large diabetic and nondiabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy cohorts and described the pathophysiology and treatment implications, noting that age at onset, course and distribution of symptoms partially overlap between the diabetic and nondiabetic forms. Pinto et al. (PMID 33653898) characterized neurologic outcomes and survival in the population-based cohort and reported that recovery is often prolonged and incomplete. These sources establish diabetes as a recognized major association of the syndrome while acknowledging that a clinically similar nondiabetic form exists, so the individual attribution rests on the documented diabetic context and exclusion of alternatives.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: document the diabetes history with duration, control and coexisting neuropathy; obtain the neurologic examination and electrodiagnostic study localizing the lesion to the lumbosacral roots, plexus or femoral nerve, with imaging used to exclude structural causes; record the tempo (subacute, painful, asymmetric), weight loss and functional deficit such as knee-extension weakness and gait impairment. Lumbar spinal stenosis or disc-related radiculopathy, compressive femoral neuropathy from retroperitoneal hematoma, tumor or surgery, other plexopathies (malignant infiltration, radiation, vasculitis, hereditary), inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, statin or other toxic myopathy, and the recently reported association with GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy are competing causes that must be excluded or apportioned; distinguishing diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy from diabetic distal symmetric polyneuropathy matters because the repository already carries a separate distal-polyneuropathy proposal and the two must not be double-counted. A subacute painful asymmetric proximal leg syndrome with electrodiagnostic root/plexus localization in a person with poorly controlled diabetes and no structural alternative favors the diabetes-related route; a slowly symmetric distal sensory neuropathy pattern points to a different diabetic mechanism with different rating consequences.

Legal and rating analysis: this is direct secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a) when the service-connected diabetes and its immune-ischemic microvasculitis produce the femoral/radiculoplexus neuropathy; the theory is causation because a distinct new focal motor and sensory disability is generated. If a pre-existing neuropathy is asserted to have been worsened, a separate § 3.310(b) aggravation analysis must identify the qualifying baseline (prior electrodiagnostic or examination findings) and the attributable increment beyond natural progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion requires the diabetic context, the electrodiagnostic localization, the subacute tempo, and the exclusion of structural and other competing causes to be weighed so that the evidence is at least in approximate balance; incidence figures describe populations and do not establish an individual probability. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: § 4.124a DC 8526 rates femoral-nerve paralysis (complete 40 percent; incomplete severe 30, moderate 20, mild 10), with DC 8626 for neuritis where the presentation is predominantly painful-inflammatory; DC 7913 Note (1) governs separate evaluation of the diabetic complication. Apply § 4.14 so that the same quadriceps weakness, sensory loss and gait impairment are not rated under both the focal femoral/plexus code and a separate diabetic peripheral-neuropathy or lumbar-spine code, and combine only genuinely distinct impairments under § 4.25. Landing this incoming route requires host-file review: the type-2-diabetes host identity is published and currently points to GERD, chronic kidney disease, diabetic retinopathy and depressive disorder, and the femoral-neuropathy identity is draft with an outbound suggestion to unexplained chronic pain and no inbound edges.

medicalEvidence.title: Lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy: Incidence and the association with diabetes mellitus
medicalEvidence.authors: Peng Soon Ng; Peter J Dyck; Ruple S Laughlin; Prabin Thapa; Marcus V Pinto; P James B Dyck
medicalEvidence.summary: Population-based study using the Rochester Epidemiology Project over 16 years identifying 59 patients with lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy and determining its previously unknown incidence (approximately 4.16 per 100,000 person-years) along with its association with diabetes mellitus. Establishes incidence and the diabetes association; population-level data.

medicalEvidence.title: Diabetic and nondiabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathies: new insights into pathophysiology and treatment
medicalEvidence.authors: P James B Dyck; Anthony J Windebank
medicalEvidence.summary: Comparison of large diabetic and nondiabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy cohorts describing the subacute painful asymmetric lower-limb syndrome, its association with weight loss and type 2 diabetes, and the proposed ischemic microvasculitic pathophysiology with treatment implications. Mechanistic support; a clinically similar nondiabetic form exists, so individual attribution requires context.

medicalEvidence.title: Lumbosacral Radiculoplexus Neuropathy: Neurologic Outcomes and Survival in a Population-Based Study
medicalEvidence.authors: Marcus V Pinto; Peng-Soon Ng; Benjamin M Howe; Ruple S Laughlin; Prabin Thapa; Peter J Dyck; P James B Dyck
medicalEvidence.summary: Population-based characterization of neurologic outcomes and survival in 59 patients with lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy over 16 years, reporting prolonged and often incomplete recovery. Supports the clinical significance and natural history; population-based observational design.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Cholelithiasis (chronic gallstone disease, predominantly pigment stones) complicating service-connected cirrhosis of the liver
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7315 (cholelithiasis, chronic) — evaluated by reference to DC 7314 (chronic biliary tract disease): 30 percent with three or more clinically documented attacks of right-upper-quadrant pain with nausea and vomiting in the past 12 months or requiring biliary stricture dilatation at least once in the past 12 months; 10 percent with one or two such documented attacks; 0 percent if asymptomatic with no documented attack in the past 12 months. Qualified-human rating review required; where stones are asymptomatic the schedule yields 0 percent, and where cholecystectomy complications dominate, DC 7318 applies instead
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected cirrhosis of the liver (hepatic cirrhosis) with documented hepatic synthetic dysfunction or portal hypertension
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7312 (cirrhosis of the liver), assigned on Model for End-Stage Liver Disease score or on continuous daily debilitating symptoms with ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatic encephalopathy, variceal hemorrhage, coagulopathy, portal gastropathy, or hepatopulmonary/hepatorenal syndrome, with Note (3) allowing rating on symptomatology where no Model for End-Stage Liver Disease score exists in the record
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Bile-composition and gallbladder-motility sequence: in service-connected cirrhosis of the liver, three convergent derangements shift bile from cholesterol-saturated toward pigment-stone lithogenicity. First, hepatocyte dysfunction reduces bile-salt synthesis and canalicular bile-salt secretion, lowering the bile-salt pool and with it the capacity to keep cholesterol and unconjugated bilirubin in micellar solution. Second, portal hypertension with hypersplenism accelerates erythrocyte sequestration and turnover, while impaired hepatic glucuronidation reduces conjugation of bilirubin, so the biliary load of unconjugated, water-insoluble pigment rises. Third, gallbladder motor function is impaired in cirrhosis — reduced cholecystokinin responsiveness, gallbladder wall thickening, and elevated circulating estrogens from reduced hepatic clearance all promote stasis and crystal nucleation; the resulting stones in cirrhosis are most often pigment stones and are frequently asymptomatic. Del Olmo et al. (PMID 9361181), a controlled cohort of 313 histologically or laparoscopically confirmed cirrhosis patients against 357 liver-disease-free comparison patients, reported higher prevalence and incidence of gallstone disease in cirrhosis and concluded that cirrhosis of the liver may be considered a risk factor for cholecystolithiasis. Mallick and Anand (PMID 35535063) review the pathogenesis and management of gallstone disease in cirrhosis, reporting a prevalence of gallstone disease in cirrhosis of roughly 25 to 30 percent, substantially above general-population estimates, and attributing it to the altered bile composition and gallbladder dysmotility described above. Wang et al. (PMID 38382725), a systematic review and meta-analysis pooling 115 studies and more than 32 million participants, place pooled global gallstone prevalence at approximately 6.1 percent, which supplies the population-level comparator against which the cirrhosis-specific prevalence is contrasted. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory — the service-connected cirrhosis is asserted to have produced a new pathological entity, symptomatic chronic cholelithiasis, rather than merely to have worsened a baseline lithogenic tendency. A § 3.310(b) aggravation theory is not the theory offered here, because the literature describes stone formation in a previously stone-free biliary tree rather than measurable worsening of documented pre-existing stones; if the record shows gallstones documented before the cirrhosis-associated derangement, the case must be re-pleaded as aggravation of a baseline condition in which the cirrhosis-attributable increment is separated from the natural progression of age- and obesity-related stone disease, and § 3.310(b) then governs. Chronology is decisive: the corresponding § 3.310(a) and § 3.310(b) analysis requires imaging evidence of cholecystolithiasis after the clinical onset of cirrhosis, together with the cirrhosis diagnosis itself, so that the nexus opinion can state that the gallstone disease is at least as likely as not causally related to the service-connected cirrhosis — a conclusion that requires documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence, consistent with § 3.102 and with the requirement that the opinion rest on evidence of record rather than on speculation. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include advancing age, female sex, obesity and metabolic syndrome, rapid weight loss or bariatric surgery, pregnancy, hemolytic disorders independent of portal hypertension, hepatitis C infection and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease as separate hepatic drivers within the same liver, ileal disease or resection, prolonged fasting or total parenteral nutrition, and fibrate or somatostatin-analog medication, as well as genetic lithogenic predisposition; none of these operates to defeat the theory, but each must be addressed in the individual case because population-level relative risks do not transfer to the individual claimant. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating caution under § 4.14: cholelithiasis symptoms may be rated only once, and where the same abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting supports an evaluation of the cirrhosis or of a residual gastropathy, the rating schedule's own anti-pyramiding instruction for DCs 7301 through 7329 requires a single evaluation under the diagnostic code reflecting the predominant disability picture, so § 4.14 bars duplicative compensation for the same manifestations.

medicalEvidence.title: Prevalence and incidence of gallstones in liver cirrhosis
medicalEvidence.authors: J A Del Olmo; F García; M A Serra; L Maldonado; J M Rodrigo
medicalEvidence.summary: Controlled study of 313 patients with cirrhosis confirmed by histology and/or laparoscopy and 357 liver-disease-free comparison patients undergoing ultrasonographic examination: prevalence and incidence of gallstone disease were higher in cirrhosis, and the authors concluded that cirrhosis of the liver may be considered a risk factor for cholecystolithiasis — the primary human evidence that cirrhosis precedes and predicts gallstone formation.

medicalEvidence.title: Gallstone Disease in Cirrhosis-Pathogenesis and Management
medicalEvidence.authors: Bipadabhanjan Mallick; Anil C Anand
medicalEvidence.summary: Review reporting that gallstones are more common in patients with cirrhosis and that incidence rises with severity of liver disease, that pigment stones predominate in cirrhosis and usually remain asymptomatic, and that the mechanism involves altered bile composition and gallbladder dysmotility — the mechanistic source for the lithogenic pathway asserted in this row.

medicalEvidence.title: Global Epidemiology of Gallstones in the 21st Century: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
medicalEvidence.authors: Xin Wang; Wenqian Yu; Guoheng Jiang; Hongyu Li; Shiyi Li; Linjun Xie; Xuan Bai; Ping Cui; Qi Chen; Yanmei Lou; Li Zou; Sulian Li; Zhongfang Zhou; Chi Zhang; Peng Sun; Min Mao
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 115 studies and more than 32 million participants estimating pooled global gallstone prevalence at approximately 6.1 percent with geographic and sex variation — the general-population denominator against which the higher cirrhosis-specific prevalence is compared.
