originalRow.secondaryCondition: Fibromyalgia (primary fibromyalgia syndrome with widespread musculoskeletal pain) in a veteran with service-connected hypothyroidism
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5025 (fibromyalgia (fibrositis, primary fibromyalgia syndrome)): 40 percent for widespread musculoskeletal pain and tender points that are constant or nearly so and refractory to therapy; 20 percent for episodic pain present more than one-third of the time, often precipitated by environmental or emotional stress or overexertion; 10 percent when continuous medication is required for control. Note to DC 5025 defines widespread pain as pain on both sides of the body, above and below the waist, affecting both the axial skeleton and the extremities. Qualified-human rating review required
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected hypothyroidism, biochemically documented by elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone with low or low-normal free thyroxine
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7903 (hypothyroidism): 100 percent for hypothyroidism manifesting as myxedema; 30 percent for hypothyroidism without myxedema; with Notes (1) and (2) directing that after the initial diagnostic period the residual effects of hypothyroidism be rated under the appropriate diagnostic codes within the appropriate body systems
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Endocrine-myopathic and central-sensitization sequence: thyroid hormone deficiency slows skeletal-muscle relaxation and mitochondrial oxidative metabolism, producing a hypothyroid myopathy with aching, stiffness, cramps, and exercise intolerance, and it alters peripheral and central nociceptive processing so that a chronic widespread-pain phenotype can emerge. In parallel, the autoimmune thyroiditis that is the leading cause of hypothyroidism in the United States shares inflammatory and neuroimmune pathways with fibromyalgia, so affected individuals can carry both the endocrine deficiency and a centrally amplified pain state. Haliloglu et al. (PMID 28176037) examined fibromyalgia in patients with thyroid autoimmunity and reported a fibromyalgia prevalence of approximately 30 to 40 percent in Hashimoto thyroiditis with structural pathology against roughly 2 to 7 percent in the general population, alongside a relationship with disease activity. Park et al. (PMID 34369360) performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of the relationship between fibromyalgia and thyroid autoimmunity, finding an association with widespread chronic pain together with correlated clinical symptoms and depression. Nishioka et al. (PMID 27905199) measured thyroid autoantibodies in 207 patients with clinically defined fibromyalgia syndrome and found a high prevalence of anti-thyroid-stimulating-hormone-receptor antibody, indicating a substantial autoimmune-thyroid overlap population. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory, in which the service-connected hypothyroidism is asserted to have produced a new and separately diagnosable condition, fibromyalgia, with its own rating criteria under DC 5025. It is not offered as a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; an aggravation theory would be required only where the record documents fibromyalgia predating the hypothyroidism and the claim is that the endocrine disease measurably worsened a pre-existing baseline pain disorder, in which case the hypothyroidism-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing fibromyalgia and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a)/(b) require the hypothyroidism diagnosis and its laboratory confirmation to precede or coincide with the fibromyalgia diagnosis, so that the clinician can state that the fibromyalgia is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected hypothyroidism — an opinion that must rest on a documented temporal sequence, a rule-out of competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102, and not on the population associations cited here. Competing causes that must be weighed include primary sleep disturbance and obstructive sleep apnea, major depressive and anxiety disorders, physical deconditioning after injury, other autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis or Sjögren's syndrome, statin and other medication-related myalgia, vitamin D deficiency, hepatitis C, and small-fiber neuropathy, all of which can independently produce widespread pain and fatigue. Reporting caution is required in the individual case: the cited studies define their populations by thyroid autoimmunity rather than by biochemically confirmed hypothyroidism alone, so a nexus opinion must document hypothyroidism by laboratory testing and must not treat the autoimmune-thyroid association as proof that hypothyroidism itself caused the pain. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14: fibromyalgia fatigue, sleep disturbance, and depression may not be compensated twice, and where the same manifestations support a mental-disorder evaluation under § 4.130, the higher single evaluation principle applies so that § 4.14 bars duplicative ratings for one symptom picture.

medicalEvidence.title: Fibromyalgia in patients with thyroid autoimmunity: prevalence and relationship with disease activity
medicalEvidence.authors: Sema Haliloglu; Bilge Ekinci; Hulya Uzkeser; Hakan Sevimli; Ayse Carlioglu; Pinar Mazlum Macit
medicalEvidence.summary: Reported a fibromyalgia prevalence of approximately 30 to 40 percent in patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis with structural pathology compared with roughly 2 to 7 percent in the general population, and described a relationship with thyroid disease activity — the primary prevalence evidence linking thyroid autoimmunity to fibromyalgia.

medicalEvidence.title: Is thyroid autoimmunity a predisposing factor for fibromyalgia? A systematic review and meta-analysis
medicalEvidence.authors: Seoeun Park; Jeong-Seung Kwon; Yong-Beom Park; Ji Woon Park
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis concluding that autoimmune thyroid disease and elevated thyroid autoantibodies are associated with fibromyalgia and widespread chronic pain, with correlated clinical symptoms and depression — pooled evidence for the endocrine-to-central-pain pathway.

medicalEvidence.title: High prevalence of anti-TSH receptor antibody in fibromyalgia syndrome
medicalEvidence.authors: Kenya Nishioka; Toyoyoshi Uchida; Chie Usui; Ryota Tanaka; Takashi Matsushima; Yoshifuji Matsumoto; Ikuro Nakamura; Kusuki Nishioka; Nobutaka Hattori
medicalEvidence.summary: In 207 patients with clinically defined fibromyalgia syndrome, thyroid function testing and antibody assays found a high prevalence of anti-thyroid-stimulating-hormone-receptor antibody, especially prominent in that population — direct human evidence of a substantial thyroid-autoimmune overlap in fibromyalgia.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Meniere's disease (secondary endolymphatic hydrops) following service-connected traumatic brain injury residuals
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.87, DC 6205 (Meniere's syndrome (endolymphatic hydrops)): 100 percent for hearing impairment with attacks of vertigo and cerebellar gait occurring more than once weekly; 60 percent for one to four attacks a month; 30 percent for vertigo less than once a month; with the note that the condition may instead be evaluated by separately rating vertigo as a peripheral vestibular disorder (DC 6204), hearing impairment, and tinnitus (DC 6260), whichever method yields the higher overall evaluation, but with no combining of those separate evaluations with an evaluation under DC 6205. Qualified-human rating review required
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected residuals of traumatic brain injury, with a documented closed-head or blast injury and persistent physical residuals including balance or vestibular dysfunction
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8045 (residuals of traumatic brain injury) — evaluated on the cognitive-impairment and subjective-symptoms table with separate evaluation of physical dysfunction under the appropriate diagnostic code; DC 8045 expressly directs that any residual with a distinct diagnosis that may be evaluated under another diagnostic code, such as migraine headache or Meniere's disease, be evaluated separately rather than under the table
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Post-traumatic inner-ear fluid-homeostasis sequence: a blow to the head or a blast overpressure event delivers shearing and hydraulic force to the labyrinth, to the temporal bone, and to the endolymphatic sac and duct. Mechanical disruption of the membranous labyrinth allows potassium-rich endolymph to contaminate perilymph, depolarizing hair cells and producing episodic vertigo; injury or obstruction of the endolymphatic duct and sac impairs longitudinal flow and resorption of endolymph, so endolymphatic volume rises and secondary endolymphatic hydrops develops with fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and recurrent vertigo — the clinical profile of Meniere's disease. Ferster et al. (PMID 28306649) review secondary endolymphatic hydrops and identify it as a pathologic finding of the inner ear producing episodic vertigo and intermittent hearing loss, with post-mortem temporal-bone histopathology demonstrating hydrops in a post-traumatic case. Chung et al. (PMID 24782951) report a case of post-traumatic Meniere's disease in which the patient developed tinnitus, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, and recurrent vertigo, with symptom improvement only after endolymphatic sac decompression surgery, documenting a trauma-triggered hydrops that behaved as Meniere's disease. DiBiase and Arriaga (PMID 9386247) state that post-traumatic Meniere's disease is a true clinical entity based on clinical observation and histopathologic study, and that the traumatic insult may be a blow to the head or a temporal bone fracture, while they also record that many cases of Meniere's disease have no identifiable etiologic agent — an important limitation that the individual nexus opinion must confront rather than ignore. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory, in which the service-connected traumatic brain injury residuals are asserted to have caused a distinct inner-ear disease rated separately under DC 6205. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would be the correct theory only where the record shows idiopathic Meniere's disease or pre-existing vestibular disease before the head injury and the claim is that the trauma measurably worsened a baseline disorder, in which case the trauma-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing disease and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the corresponding individual analysis require documentation that the head injury preceded the onset of the vertiginous and fluctuating hearing symptoms, that vestibular and audiologic testing supports endolymphatic hydrops (for example, fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss with episodic vertigo), and that the examiner can state that the Meniere's disease is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected traumatic brain injury — an opinion that requires a documented temporal sequence, an accounting for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include idiopathic Meniere's disease without any traumatic trigger, viral labyrinthitis, vestibular neuritis, otosclerosis, autoimmune inner ear disease, syphilis, noise-induced cochlear injury, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, migraine-associated vertigo, and acoustic trauma, together with a positive family history of Meniere's disease; the discrimination is clinically demanding because most head injuries do not cause hydrops and because Meniere's disease is itself usually idiopathic. No individual probability is asserted here. Two rating cautions apply. First, DC 8045 itself forbids rating the same manifestation twice: vertigo, tinnitus, and hearing loss routed to DC 6205 may not simultaneously be used in the traumatic-brain-injury subjective-symptoms facet, consistent with § 4.14 non-pyramiding. Second, the note to DC 6205 bars combining an evaluation under DC 6205 with separate evaluations of hearing impairment, tinnitus, or vertigo, so only one coherent rating construct may be used.

medicalEvidence.title: Secondary Endolymphatic Hydrops
medicalEvidence.authors: Ashley P O'Connell Ferster; Sebahattin Cureoglu; Nevra Keskin; Michael M Paparella; Huseyin Isildak
medicalEvidence.summary: Review establishing secondary endolymphatic hydrops as an inner-ear pathologic finding that produces episodic vertigo and intermittent hearing loss, with post-mortem temporal-bone histopathology demonstrating hydrops plus necrotic organ of Corti in a post-traumatic case — the mechanistic source linking head trauma to hydrops.

medicalEvidence.title: A Case of Post-Traumatic Meniere's Disease
medicalEvidence.authors: Juyong Chung; Hahn Jin Jung; Chong Sun Kim; Young Ho Kim
medicalEvidence.summary: Case report of post-traumatic Meniere's disease following head trauma, with tinnitus, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, and recurrent vertigo that failed symptomatic medical treatment and improved markedly only after endolymphatic sac decompression — documented human example of the trauma-to-Meniere's sequence.

medicalEvidence.title: Post-traumatic hydrops
medicalEvidence.authors: P DiBiase; M A Arriaga
medicalEvidence.summary: Clinical and histopathologic analysis stating that post-traumatic Meniere's disease is a true clinical entity, that the traumatic insult may be a blow to the head or a temporal bone fracture, and simultaneously recording that many Meniere's disease cases have no identifiable etiologic agent — the etiologic-affirmation evidence together with its candid limitation.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Dry eye syndrome (keratoconjunctivitis sicca and thyroid-eye-disease-associated ocular surface disease) in a veteran with service-connected hyperthyroidism
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.79, DC 6025 (disorders of the lacrimal apparatus (epiphora, dacryocystitis, etc.)): 20 percent bilateral and 10 percent unilateral; where punctate corneal epithelial disease is documented, DC 6001 (keratopathy) is also available and is evaluated under the General Rating Formula for Diseases of the Eye, subject to the prohibition on pyramiding the same visual impairment under § 4.14. Qualified-human rating review required; a clinically justified analogous evaluation under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 may be required where the predominant disability picture is tear-film failure without a lacrimal-apparatus diagnosis
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected hyperthyroidism, including Graves' disease, with documented thyroid-stimulating-hormone-receptor antibody positivity or clinical thyrotoxicosis
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7900 (hyperthyroidism, including, but not limited to, Graves' disease): 30 percent for six months after initial diagnosis, with residuals of disease or complications of medical treatment thereafter rated within the appropriate diagnostic code in the appropriate body system; Note (2) expressly directs that eye involvement occurring as a manifestation of Graves' disease be separately evaluated as diplopia (DC 6090), impairment of central visual acuity (DCs 6061 through 6066), or under the most appropriate diagnostic codes in § 4.79
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Orbitopathy and tear-film sequence: in service-connected hyperthyroidism due to Graves' disease, thyroid-stimulating-hormone-receptor autoantibodies activate orbital fibroblasts, driving glycosaminoglycan and hyaluronan deposition, adipogenesis, and cytokine-mediated orbital inflammation. The resulting proptosis, eyelid retraction, restrictive myopathy, and widened palpebral fissure increase the exposed ocular surface area and reduce the completeness of eyelid closure, so the tear film destabilizes and evaporates faster than the lacrimal system can replace it; lymphocytic infiltration and dysfunction of the lacrimal and accessory glands further reduce aqueous secretion, and the consequent ocular surface inflammation perpetuates tear-film instability and punctate epithelial damage. Selter et al. (PMID 25584018) reviewed the relationship between Graves' ophthalmopathy and dry eye syndrome and concluded that an increased risk of dry eye syndrome exists in patients with thyroid disease, describing a complex and bidirectional clinical relationship. Rana et al. (PMID 35167950) reviewed ocular surface disease in thyroid eye disease and reported that the prevalence of ocular surface disease among thyroid eye disease patients is estimated to range from about 65 to 95 percent, and that ocular surface inflammation and multifactorial changes to ocular surface homeostasis contribute substantially alongside the anatomical proptosis and corneal exposure mechanism. McAlinden (PMID 26605355) provides the epidemiologic linkage in his overview of thyroid eye disease, reporting that approximately 60 percent of patients with hyperthyroidism develop thyroid eye disease and that among thyroid eye disease patients roughly 85 percent are hyperthyroid, 10 percent hypothyroid, and 5 percent euthyroid — the last figure being the critical limitation for this theory. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory, in which the service-connected hyperthyroidism is asserted to have caused dry eye syndrome as an orbital and ocular-surface manifestation of the same autoimmune process. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would be the correct theory only where the record documents dry eye syndrome predating the thyroid disease and the claim is that the thyroid orbitopathy worsened a baseline tear-film disorder, in which case the attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of that baseline condition and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require that the hyperthyroidism or Graves' disease diagnosis, and ideally thyroid-stimulating-hormone-receptor antibody status, precede or coincide with the onset of dry eye symptoms and objective ocular surface signs such as reduced tear break-up time, positive ocular surface staining, or Schirmer testing, so that the examiner can state that the dry eye syndrome is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected hyperthyroidism — an opinion requiring a documented temporal sequence, an accounting for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be weighed include age-related tear deficiency, meibomian gland dysfunction and blepharitis, contact-lens wear, environmental exposure and screen-related tear evaporation, systemic medications such as antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, and isotretinoin, Sjögren's syndrome and other autoimmune sicca disease, diabetes mellitus, and prior ocular surgery or radiation. A further individualized caution: because thyroid eye disease and dry eye can occur in euthyroid and hypothyroid patients, the presence of dry eye in a veteran with treated thyroid disease does not by itself establish causation, and the nexus opinion must tie the ocular surface disease to the Graves' autoimmune process rather than to thyroid hormone levels alone. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14: where dry eye has produced visual impairment that is separately rated under DCs 6061 through 6066 or under another § 4.79 code, the same impairment may not be rated a second time, and DC 7900 Note (2) and DC 7903 Note (3) both contemplate a single coordinate evaluation under § 4.79 for the eye involvement.

medicalEvidence.title: The relationship between Graves' ophthalmopathy and dry eye syndrome
medicalEvidence.authors: Jessica H Selter; Anisa I Gire; Shameema Sikder
medicalEvidence.summary: Literature review concluding that a complex relationship exists between Graves' ophthalmopathy and dry eye syndrome and that patients with thyroid disease carry an increased risk of dry eye syndrome — direct human evidence of the thyroid-eye-to-ocular-surface pathway.

medicalEvidence.title: Ocular Surface Disease in Thyroid Eye Disease: A Narrative Review
medicalEvidence.authors: Harkaran S Rana; Sruti S Akella; Carson E Clabeaux; Zachary P Skurski; Vinay K Aakalu
medicalEvidence.summary: Narrative review reporting that the prevalence of ocular surface disease among thyroid eye disease patients is estimated at roughly 65 to 95 percent, and that ocular surface inflammation and multifactorial disruption of ocular surface homeostasis contribute substantially alongside proptosis and corneal exposure — the quantitative and mechanistic link.

medicalEvidence.title: An overview of thyroid eye disease
medicalEvidence.authors: Colm McAlinden
medicalEvidence.summary: Overview of thyroid eye disease epidemiology, risk factors, and pathogenesis reporting that approximately 60 percent of patients with hyperthyroidism develop thyroid eye disease and that among thyroid eye disease patients about 85 percent are hyperthyroid, 10 percent hypothyroid, and 5 percent euthyroid — the epidemiologic linkage together with its individualized limitation.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Meralgia paresthetica (lateral femoral cutaneous neuropathy with painful anterolateral thigh dysesthesia) in a veteran with service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8529 (external cutaneous nerve of thigh): 10 percent for severe to complete paralysis, 0 percent for mild or moderate paralysis; where the presentation is inflammatory rather than paralytic, the corresponding neuritis code DC 8629 (external cutaneous nerve of thigh neuritis) applies, and where the presentation is purely sensory pain, DC 8729 (neuralgia) applies. Qualified-human rating review required — the maximum 10 percent evaluation under DC 8529 means the benefit of this mapping is frequently a 10 percent rating plus establishment of secondary service connection
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus, with documented diagnostic laboratory criteria and duration of disease
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7913 (diabetes mellitus), assigned on the insulin, dietary, activity-regulation, and complication tiers, including the 20 percent tier for diabetes managed by regulation of diet or oral medication, with the note to DC 7913 addressing the relationship between diabetes and its separately evaluated complications
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Metabolic-and-entrapment sequence: in service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic hyperglycemia drives nerve injury through polyol-pathway flux with sorbitol accumulation, formation of advanced glycation end products, oxidative stress, and impairment of the endoneurial microvasculature, so axons become more susceptible to mechanical deformation. The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is anatomically vulnerable where it angulates as it passes beneath or through the inguinal ligament, and in the diabetic phenotype co-existing central adiposity and increased intra-abdominal pressure add extrinsic compression and further elevate intraneural pressure at that site. The combination converts a tolerable anatomic narrowing into a symptomatic mononeuropathy, producing burning, numbness, and painful dysesthesia over the anterolateral thigh that spare strength and deep tendon reflexes. Parisi et al. (PMID 21975198) conducted a population-based study in Olmsted County, Minnesota, identifying 262 patients with meralgia paresthetica against 262 normal controls and concluded that diabetes mellitus appears to be an independent risk factor for the development of meralgia paresthetica, while also recording the important observation that patients who have both meralgia paresthetica and diabetes mellitus tend to develop meralgia paresthetica before the diabetes is diagnosed. Weng et al. (PMID 28511974) analyzed etiologies in a hospital-based referral series of patients with electrodiagnostically confirmed meralgia paresthetica in Taiwan and found that obesity and certain occupations carried increased risk while only a small minority (approximately 2 percent) of their cases had diabetes mellitus, which is a direct internal counterweight to the diabetes-specific theory and must be disclosed. Chalk and Namiranian (PMID 38697741) review meralgia paresthetica and list diabetes mellitus among the recognized risk factors along with obesity, tight clothing, and prior hip or lumbar spine surgery. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory, in which the service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus is asserted to have caused a new mononeuropathy affecting the external cutaneous nerve of the thigh. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would be the correct theory only where the record documents meralgia paresthetica predating the diabetes and the claim is that the metabolic disease worsened a baseline entrapment neuropathy, in which case the diabetes-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of a pre-existing compression neuropathy and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require a documented diagnosis of type 2 diabetes with its laboratory confirmation, documentation of meralgia paresthetica by clinical description and ideally by sensory nerve conduction study or somatosensory evoked potentials with normal strength and reflexes, and a temporal sequence in which the diabetic metabolic derangement precedes or coincides with the onset of the thigh dysesthesia, so that the examiner can state that the meralgia paresthetica is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected diabetes — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence, consistent with § 3.102. A specific evidentiary caution follows from the Parisi finding that meralgia paresthetica often precedes the clinical diagnosis of diabetes: in such cases the examiner must address whether undiagnosed glucose intolerance was already operative, or the nexus opinion should be framed as aggravation or left unestablished. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include obesity and rapid weight change, tight belts, garments, or body armor, prolonged sitting or standing postures with hip flexion, pregnancy, prior hip or lumbosacral spine surgery or iliac crest bone graft harvest, direct groin trauma, pelvic tumors or retroperitoneal mass, lead toxicity, hypothyroidism, and other metabolic neuropathies. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14: sensory loss and pain in the anterolateral thigh may be rated only once — DC 8529, DC 8629, or DC 8729 — and the same sensory deficit may not simultaneously support an evaluation of diabetic peripheral neuropathy on the same extremity, consistent with § 4.14 non-pyramiding and with the note to DC 7913 requiring complications to be evaluated under the appropriate diagnostic code.

medicalEvidence.title: Meralgia paresthetica: relation to obesity, advanced age, and diabetes mellitus
medicalEvidence.authors: Thomas J Parisi; Jay Mandrekar; P James B Dyck; Christopher J Klein
medicalEvidence.summary: Population-based study in Olmsted County, Minnesota, identifying 262 patients with meralgia paresthetica and 262 normal controls, concluding that diabetes mellitus appears to be an independent risk factor for meralgia paresthetica while also noting that patients with both conditions often develop the neuropathy before the diabetes is diagnosed — the primary diabetes-to-neuropathy evidence and its caveat.

medicalEvidence.title: Risk factor analysis for meralgia paresthetica: A hospital-based study in Taiwan
medicalEvidence.authors: Wei-Chieh Weng; Yi-Chia Wei; Wen-Yi Huang; Yu-Yi Chien; Tsung-I Peng; Chia-Lun Wu
medicalEvidence.summary: Retrospective etiologic analysis of electromyographically confirmed meralgia paresthetica referral patients finding that male middle-aged patients with higher body mass index and certain occupations were at increased risk while only a small minority (about 2 percent) had diabetes mellitus — the counterweight showing that diabetes is neither necessary nor sufficient for this neuropathy.

medicalEvidence.title: Meralgia paresthetica
medicalEvidence.authors: Colin Chalk; Dina Namiranian
medicalEvidence.summary: Clinical review of meralgia paresthetica describing its diagnosis by history of painful sensory disturbance on the anterolateral thigh with normal strength and reflexes, and listing obesity, tight clothing, and diabetes mellitus among its risk factors — the diagnostic-criteria and risk-factor source for the mapping.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Osteomalacia (defective bone mineralization, renal osteodystrophy spectrum) in a veteran with service-connected chronic kidney disease
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5014 (osteomalacia, residuals of) — evaluated as degenerative arthritis based on limitation of motion of affected parts under the note to DCs 5013 through 5024; because osteomalacia often presents with bone pain, proximal myopathy, and fractures rather than joint limitation, a clinically justified analogous evaluation under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 may be required, and residual fractures are separately rated under the fracture codes. Qualified-human rating review required
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected chronic kidney disease (chronic renal failure) with documented reduction in glomerular filtration rate and laboratory evidence of disordered mineral metabolism
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.115b, DC 7530 (chronic renal disease requiring regular dialysis) and DC 7502 (nephritis, chronic), each rated as renal dysfunction under the criteria of § 4.115a; DC 7537 (interstitial nephritis, including disorders of calcium metabolism) is the alternative code where that is the documented renal pathology. Note that the schedule provides no free-standing chronic-kidney-disease code, so the renal dysfunction evaluation in § 4.115a supplies the rating level
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Renal mineral-metabolism sequence: as glomerular filtration falls in service-connected chronic kidney disease, phosphate retention and reduced renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation of vitamin D produce hypocalcemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism. The resulting chronic parathyroid hormone excess drives high bone turnover (osteitis fibrosa), while the deficiency of active vitamin D and the accumulation of uremic toxins impair osteoblast-mediated deposition of mineral into osteoid, so newly formed bone matrix remains unmineralized — the histologic definition of osteomalacia. In dialysis-treated and advanced disease, additional contributors include aluminum or iron accumulation and hypophosphatemia after aggressive phosphate control, and the mixed uremic osteodystrophy picture in which osteomalacia coexists with hyperparathyroid bone disease. Pazianas and Miller (PMID 33774081) situate osteoporosis, osteomalacia, and the forms of renal osteodystrophy within the single spectrum of chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD), which is the framing that makes an osteomalacia claim in kidney disease medically coherent. Hou et al. (PMID 30298663) review mineral bone disorders in chronic kidney disease and define CKD-MBD as abnormal metabolism of calcium, phosphorus, parathyroid hormone, or vitamin D together with abnormalities in bone turnover, mineralization, volume, linear growth, or strength — the mineralization-abnormality limb of that definition being the osteomalacia mechanism asserted here. Patel and Hashmi (PMID 32809577) describe the CKD-MBD syndrome as encompassing disordered calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, and fibroblast growth factor-23 metabolism leading to altered bone morphology (renal osteodystrophy) and vascular calcification. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory — the service-connected renal failure is asserted to have produced a distinct metabolic bone disease, osteomalacia, and not merely to have aggravated an existing skeletal disorder. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would be the correct theory only where the record documents pre-existing osteomalacia or osteoporosis from another cause (for example, malabsorption, prior gastric surgery, or anticonvulsant therapy) and the claim is that the renal disease measurably worsened that baseline mineralization defect, in which case the renal-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing bone disease and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require a documented sequence in which the decline in renal function precedes the metabolic bone disease, and they require objective evidence of osteomalacia rather than of osteoporosis alone: elevated alkaline phosphatase, low or low-normal serum phosphate, appropriate parathyroid hormone levels, and ideally bone biopsy showing increased osteoid volume and mineralization lag time, or imaging and dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry findings interpreted with the knowledge that bone mineral density is unreliable in advanced kidney disease. Only with that evidence can an examiner state that the osteomalacia is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected chronic kidney disease — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102, not a transfer of the population association to the individual claimant. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include vitamin D deficiency from inadequate sun exposure or diet, malabsorption from celiac disease, bariatric surgery, or pancreatic insufficiency, anticonvulsant and tenofovir therapy, hypophosphatemic and other inherited phosphate-wasting disorders, primary hyperparathyroidism, liver disease, prior gastrectomy, and coexisting age-related or glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, which is a separate disease and should not be relabeled as osteomalacia. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14: osteomalacia cannot be compensated simultaneously under DC 5014 and again as the same limitation of motion or fracture through another code, and the note to DCs 5013 through 5024 requires a single evaluation as degenerative arthritis on limitation of motion where that is the predominant disability picture.

medicalEvidence.title: Osteoporosis and Chronic Kidney Disease-Mineral and Bone Disorder (CKD-MBD): Back to Basics
medicalEvidence.authors: Michael Pazianas; Paul D Miller
medicalEvidence.summary: Review article stating that, on the basis of bone histology, osteoporosis is only one part of a spectrum of skeletal complications that includes osteomalacia and the various forms of renal osteodystrophy of chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder — the framing evidence that osteomalacia is a kidney-disease skeletal complication.

medicalEvidence.title: Mineral bone disorders in chronic kidney disease
medicalEvidence.authors: Yi-Chou Hou; Chien-Lin Lu; Kuo-Cheng Lu
medicalEvidence.summary: Review documenting that as glomerular filtration loss aggravates, disturbed mineral metabolism worsens bone microstructure and remodeling in what is termed CKD-mineral bone disease, characterized by abnormal calcium, phosphorus, parathyroid hormone, or vitamin D metabolism and by abnormalities in bone turnover, mineralization, volume, linear growth, or strength — the mineralization-defect mechanism.

medicalEvidence.title: Chronic Kidney Disease-Mineral Bone Disorder (CKD-MBD)
medicalEvidence.authors: Preeti Patel; Muhammad F. Hashmi
medicalEvidence.summary: StatPearls review of the CKD-MBD syndrome, tracing the term to the recognition that disorders of calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, and fibroblast growth factor-23 metabolism produce altered bone morphology (renal osteodystrophy) and vascular calcification in kidney disease — corroborating the mineral-metabolism derangement asserted in this row.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Vocal cord paralysis (recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy with hoarseness or aphonia) following thyroidectomy performed for service-connected thyroid enlargement
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.97, DC 6516 (laryngitis, chronic): 30 percent for hoarseness with thickening or nodules of cords, polyps, submucous infiltration, or pre-malignant changes on biopsy; 10 percent for hoarseness with inflammation of cords or mucous membrane. Where the injury is complete, DC 6519 (aphonia, complete organic) pays 100 percent for constant inability to communicate by speech and 60 percent for constant inability to speak above a whisper, and its note directs that incomplete aphonia be evaluated as laryngitis, chronic (DC 6516). DC 6520 (larynx, stenosis of, including residuals of laryngeal trauma) may apply where stenosis or flow-volume-loop-confirmed upper airway obstruction follows. Qualified-human rating review required
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected nontoxic thyroid enlargement (goiter) severe enough to require thyroidectomy
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7902 (thyroid enlargement, nontoxic), with Note (1) requiring symptoms due to pressure on adjacent organs such as the trachea, larynx, or esophagus to be evaluated under the appropriate diagnostic code within the appropriate body system and Note (2) permitting separate evaluation of neck disfigurement under DC 7800
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Surgical-nerve-injury sequence: the recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove and passes in intimate proximity to the thyroid gland's inferior pole before entering the larynx, where it supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid. Thyroidectomy performed to treat service-connected goiter therefore places the nerve at direct risk: traction, thermal spread from electrocautery, ligature entrapment, or transection produces neurapraxia or axonal loss, and the resulting loss of adductor and abductor innervation leaves the vocal fold immobile in a paramedian or intermediate position with hoarseness, breathy dysphonia, impaired cough, and — when the insult is bilateral or severe — inspiratory stridor or aphonia. Jeannon et al. (PMID 19335706), a systematic review of reported incidence after thyroid surgery, found an average temporary recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy rate of 9.8 percent and a permanent palsy rate of 2.3 percent, with rates varying by extent of surgery and case mix. Hayward et al. (PMID 22989215) reviewed recurrent laryngeal nerve injury in thyroid surgery and reported permanent palsy in 0.3 to 3 percent of cases with transient palsies in 5 to 8 percent, emphasizing identification of high-risk patients. Alkaf et al. (PMID 41047809) retrospectively assessed vocal cord palsy after thyroidectomy and reported an overall permanent vocal cord palsy incidence of approximately 2.9 percent with left and right cord involvement of 1 percent and 1.9 percent respectively, and analyzed associated risk factors. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-causation theory. The theory is that a disability resulting from treatment of a service-connected condition is itself proximately due to that service-connected condition, so the service-connected goiter that necessitated the thyroidectomy is the legal and medical predicate for a nerve injury caused by the operation undertaken to treat it; the theory is not that the goiter mechanically paralyzed the cord, unless compressive or retrosternal goiter with documented preoperative cord palsy is separately shown. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would govern only where the record shows pre-existing vocal cord dysfunction (for example, from a prior thyroid or cervical spine operation, intubation trauma, or idiopathic palsy) and the claim is that the goiter-directed surgery worsened a baseline deficit, in which case the surgical increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing palsy and § 3.310(b) applies. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require documentation that the goiter and its surgical indication precede the onset of dysphonia, that the surgery was actually performed for the service-connected goiter, and that the postoperative course records hoarseness or dysphonia with laryngoscopic confirmation of vocal fold immobility; where the record lacks a preoperative laryngoscopy, the examiner must address whether the palsy was pre-existing. With that evidence an examiner can state that the vocal cord paralysis is at least as likely as not caused by the thyroidectomy performed for the service-connected thyroid enlargement — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include anesthetic or intubation-related cord trauma, pre-existing idiopathic or compressive palsy, superior laryngeal nerve injury (a different nerve with a different functional deficit), viral neuritis, stroke or other central causes, laryngeal malignancy, prior neck surgery or radiation, and coincidental presbylaryngis; the rates published in the cited series are population incidences and do not establish the cause in a given veteran. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14: the same dysphonia and airway findings may not be rated simultaneously under DC 6516 and DC 6519, and where a laryngectomy or partial laryngectomy has been performed, the schedule requires residuals to be rated under DC 6516, DC 6519, or DC 6520 rather than duplicated.

medicalEvidence.title: Diagnosis of recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy after thyroidectomy: a systematic review
medicalEvidence.authors: J-P Jeannon; A A Orabi; G A Bruch; H A Abdalsalam; R Simo
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review of the reported incidence of recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy after thyroid surgery, finding an average temporary palsy rate of 9.8 percent and a permanent palsy rate of 2.3 percent, with variation by extent of surgery — the primary incidence evidence for the surgical-injury pathway.

medicalEvidence.title: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury in thyroid surgery: a review
medicalEvidence.authors: Nathan James Hayward; Simon Grodski; Meei Yeung; William R Johnson; Jonathan Serpell
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy in thyroid surgery reporting permanent palsy in 0.3 to 3 percent of cases and transient palsies in 5 to 8 percent, with attention to high-risk patients and intraoperative nerve identification — corroborating the mechanism and magnitude of the surgical risk.

medicalEvidence.title: Incidence of recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and associated risk factors after thyroidectomy: a retrospective study
medicalEvidence.authors: Hussein Alkaf; Sarah Abuduruk; Sara Bayounos; Sherif Kamel Abdelmonim; Jabir Alharbi; Mohammad Ali Alessa; Haddad Alkaff; Ameen Alherabid
medicalEvidence.summary: Retrospective cohort assessing permanent vocal cord palsy after thyroidectomy, reporting overall permanent vocal cord palsy in about 2.9 percent of cases with laterality data and risk-factor analysis — a contemporary incidence estimate for the specific outcome asserted here.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Tendinopathy (fluoroquinolone-associated tendinitis, tendinosis, or tendon rupture) in a veteran treated with a fluoroquinolone for service-connected chronic prostatitis
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5024 (tenosynovitis, tendinitis, tendinosis or tendinopathy) — evaluated as degenerative arthritis based on limitation of motion of affected parts under the note to DCs 5013 through 5024, with the ankle and foot joint codes (for example DC 5271, ankle limited motion) supplying the limitation-of-motion evaluation where the Achilles tendon is involved. Qualified-human rating review required; where the schedule's analogue produces an inappropriately low result for a documented tendon rupture with functional loss, the analogous-rating rule of §§ 4.20 and 4.27 must be considered
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected chronic prostatitis (chronic bacterial prostatitis) for which systemic fluoroquinolone therapy was prescribed
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.115b, DC 7525 (prostatitis, urethritis, epididymitis, orchitis (unilateral or bilateral), chronic only) — rated as urinary tract infection, with tubercular infections rated under §§ 4.88b or 4.89
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Pharmacological iatrogenic sequence: fluoroquinolones chelate divalent cations and inhibit tenocyte proliferation and collagen synthesis, induce matrix metalloproteinase activity and extracellular-matrix degradation, generate reactive oxygen species and mitochondrial toxicity in tenocytes, and impair tendon stem-cell differentiation, so the tendon loses tensile strength and becomes prone to microtearing. Because the Achilles tendon is subject to the highest repetitive tensile loads in the body and has a relatively poor vascular supply in its mid-substance, it is the archetypal site, and the risk rises with age, with corticosteroid co-administration, with renal impairment, and with longer or repeated courses — which is directly relevant to chronic prostatitis, where fluoroquinolones are used in prolonged regimens. Alves et al. (PMID 31270563), a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies, quantified the elevated risk of tendon injury associated with fluoroquinolone exposure, establishing the association at pooled-analytic strength rather than as anecdote. Shu et al. (PMID 36147351) analyzed the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System for 2016 to 2021 and found that a majority of reported fluoroquinolone-associated suspected tendinitis and tendon rupture cases resulted in serious outcomes, with disproportionality signals for ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and moxifloxacin. Duman et al. (PMID 40005998) review fluoroquinolone-mediated tendinopathy and tendon rupture and note that although several effects on tendon tissue are identified — changes in gene expression, metabolism, and function of tendon-resident cells — the exact molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood, which is a limitation the individual nexus opinion must disclose rather than overstate. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-causation theory pleaded as a medication side effect, in which a disability caused by treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected because the treatment was undertaken for the service-connected chronic prostatitis. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would govern only where the record shows pre-existing tendon disease or degenerative tendinopathy and the claim is that the antibiotic exposure worsened a baseline tendon condition, in which case the drug-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of that baseline tendinopathy and § 3.310(b) applies. Chronology is the decisive element and the corresponding § 3.310(a) or (b) analysis requires: an actual prescription record identifying the fluoroquinolone, dose, and dates; onset of tendon pain during or within the recognized post-exposure window after the course; imaging or examination findings of tendinopathy or rupture; and identification of the prescriber's indication as the service-connected chronic prostatitis. Only then can an examiner state that the tendinopathy is at least as likely as not caused by the fluoroquinolone therapy — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include degenerative Achilles tendinopathy, prior ankle trauma or surgery, systemic corticosteroid use (an independent and synergistic risk factor), diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, hyperlipidemia and statin therapy, inflammatory arthropathy and enthesitis, gout, and repetitive occupational loading; because the reporting systems cited capture suspected associations rather than adjudicated causes, none of them converts into an individual probability. No individual probability is asserted here. No intentional rechallenge, unsupervised discontinuation of a prescribed antibiotic, or patient-specific prescribing recommendation is made. Rating discipline under § 4.14: the same tendon limitation of motion and pain may not be compensated twice, and where the affected joint also carries a separate service-connected arthritic or traumatic rating, the schedule's note to DCs 5013 through 5024 requires a single evaluation for the limitation of motion.

medicalEvidence.title: Fluoroquinolones and the risk of tendon injury: a systematic review and meta-analysis
medicalEvidence.authors: Carlos Alves; Diogo Mendes; Francisco Batel Marques
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies quantifying the risk of tendon injury associated with fluoroquinolone exposure, noting that tendinopathy is a recognized adverse reaction and providing pooled-analytic support for the drug-to-tendon pathway.

medicalEvidence.title: Fluoroquinolone-associated suspected tendonitis and tendon rupture: A pharmacovigilance analysis from 2016 to 2021 based on the FAERS database
medicalEvidence.authors: Yamin Shu; Qilin Zhang; Xucheng He; Yanxin Liu; Pan Wu; Li Chen
medicalEvidence.summary: Pharmacovigilance disproportionality analysis of the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System finding signals for tendonitis and tendon rupture with ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and moxifloxacin and reporting that most reported cases resulted in serious outcomes — the contemporary safety-signal evidence.

medicalEvidence.title: Fluoroquinolone-Mediated Tendinopathy and Tendon Rupture
medicalEvidence.authors: Ezgi Duman; Sigrid Müller-Deubert; Girish Pattappa; Ioannis Stratos; Stephan A Sieber; Hauke Clausen-Schaumann; Victoria Sarafian; Chisa Shukunami; Maximilian Rudert; Denitsa Docheva
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of fluoroquinolone-mediated tendinopathy and tendon rupture describing the drug class's potential to trigger severe side effects including tendinopathy and tendon rupture and detailing effects on tendon-resident cell gene expression, metabolism, and function, while candidly recording that the exact molecular mechanisms remain unclear — the mechanistic source together with its stated uncertainty.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Raynaud's syndrome (secondary Raynaud's phenomenon with digital vasospasm, and its digital ulcer and auto-amputation sequelae) in a veteran with service-connected systemic sclerosis
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.104, DC 7117 (Raynaud's syndrome (also known as secondary Raynaud's phenomenon or secondary Raynaud's)): 100 percent with two or more digital ulcers plus auto-amputation of one or more digits and a history of characteristic attacks; 60 percent with two or more digital ulcers and history of characteristic attacks; 40 percent for characteristic attacks occurring at least daily; 20 percent for attacks four to six times a week; 10 percent for attacks one to three times a week; with the note that these evaluations are for Raynaud's syndrome as a whole regardless of the number of extremities involved. DC 7124 governs primary Raynaud's disease only and must not be used here. Qualified-human rating review required
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), with documented cutaneous or visceral involvement
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.118, DC 7821 (cutaneous manifestations of collagen-vascular diseases not listed elsewhere (including scleroderma, calcinosis cutis, subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus, and dermatomyositis)) — evaluated under the General Rating Formula for the Skin; visceral involvement is separately rated in the affected body system, for example esophageal disease under § 4.114
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Microvascular and fibrotic vascular sequence: in service-connected systemic sclerosis, endothelial injury with intimal proliferation and progressive obliterative vasculopathy narrows the digital arteries and arterioles, while platelet activation, increased endothelin-1 and reduced nitric oxide and prostacyclin signaling shift the digital vascular bed toward vasoconstriction and impaired vasodilation. The consequence is an exaggerated, reversible digital vasospasm in response to cold or emotional stress — Raynaud's phenomenon — which in systemic sclerosis is not a benign primary disorder but a marker and driver of progressive digital ischemia; when the vasospasm and fixed structural narrowing coexist, persistent hypoperfusion produces digital pitting scars, ischemic ulcers, and auto-amputation of fingertips. Hughes et al. (PMID 32099191) state that Raynaud phenomenon occurs in virtually all patients with systemic sclerosis and is often the earliest clinical manifestation, and that it is caused by impaired digital perfusion requiring careful assessment. Sunderkötter and Riemekasten (PMID 16987831) describe Raynaud's phenomenon in systemic sclerosis as an initial event in the pathophysiological cascade leading to sclerosis, characterized by recurrent reversible spasms of small arterioles and digital arteries triggered by cold and emotional stress and producing the characteristic sudden pallor of the digits. Maciejewska et al. (PMID 35566614) review Raynaud's phenomenon with a focus on systemic sclerosis and state that systemic sclerosis is one of the most frequent causes of secondary Raynaud's phenomenon and that its appearance may occur long before other signs and symptoms, emphasizing the treatment distinction between primary and secondary forms. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory — the service-connected systemic sclerosis is asserted to have produced a separate, separately rated vascular condition, secondary Raynaud's phenomenon, with its own diagnostic code at DC 7117 rather than being folded into the skin or musculoskeletal evaluation of the scleroderma itself. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; an aggravation theory would be required only where the record shows pre-existing primary Raynaud's disease (DC 7124) or cold-injury-related vasospasm and the claim is that the systemic sclerosis measurably worsened a baseline vasospastic disorder, in which case the attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of the primary disease and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require documented systemic sclerosis with American College of Rheumatology or EULAR classification features (for example, sclerodactyly, specific autoantibodies, nailfold capillary abnormalities, or internal-organ involvement), a clinical description of characteristic attacks meeting the DC 7117 note definition — sequential digital color change lasting minutes to hours, precipitated by cold or emotional stress — and a temporal relationship in which the vasospastic attacks begin with or after disease onset. Where digital ulcers or auto-amputation are asserted for the 60 or 100 percent tiers, the ulcer history and imaging or photographic documentation must be of record. Only then can an examiner state that the Raynaud's syndrome is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected systemic sclerosis — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include primary Raynaud's disease (which is the schedule's separate DC 7124 entity), cold-injury residuals under DC 7122 (whose note directs separate evaluation of Raynaud's syndrome unless those findings already support an evaluation there), cigarette smoking and other vasoconstrictor exposure, beta-blocker, ergotamine, or stimulant medication, hypothyroidism, carpal tunnel syndrome and thoracic outlet syndrome, vibration-tool exposure, cryoglobulinemia, and other connective tissue diseases such as mixed connective tissue disease or systemic lupus erythematosus, which are distinct service-connected or non-service-connected identities and must not be merged with systemic sclerosis. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14: DC 7117 evaluations are for Raynaud's syndrome as a whole, so the same digital attacks, ulcers, or amputations may not be compensated a second time under the cold-injury code or as residuals of the scleroderma skin evaluation, and separate amputation ratings follow only the amputation rule and the schedule's own provisions.

medicalEvidence.title: Raynaud phenomenon and digital ulcers in systemic sclerosis
medicalEvidence.authors: Michael Hughes; Yannick Allanore; Lorinda Chung; John D Pauling; Christopher P Denton; Marco Matucci-Cerinic
medicalEvidence.summary: Review stating that Raynaud phenomenon occurs in virtually all patients with systemic sclerosis and is often the earliest clinical manifestation, that it results from impaired digital perfusion, and that careful assessment is required — the primary evidence that the vasospastic disorder is a manifestation of the sclerosis rather than an unrelated condition.

medicalEvidence.title: Pathophysiology and clinical consequences of Raynaud's phenomenon related to systemic sclerosis
medicalEvidence.authors: C Sunderkötter; G Riemekasten
medicalEvidence.summary: Article describing Raynaud's phenomenon as an initial event in the pathophysiological cascade leading to sclerosis in systemic sclerosis, characterized by recurrent reversible spasms of small arterioles and digital arteries triggered by cold and emotional stress — the mechanistic account of the vascular pathway asserted in this row.

medicalEvidence.title: Raynaud's Phenomenon with Focus on Systemic Sclerosis
medicalEvidence.authors: Magdalena Maciejewska; Mariusz Sikora; Cezary Maciejewski; Rosanna Alda-Malicka; Joanna Czuwara; Lidia Rudnicka
medicalEvidence.summary: Review reporting that systemic sclerosis is one of the most frequent causes of secondary Raynaud's phenomenon, that its appearance may occur long before other signs and symptoms, and that treatment differs by underlying cause — the classification evidence distinguishing secondary from primary Raynaud's.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (drug-induced, with annular photosensitive lesions and Ro/SS-A autoantibodies) in a veteran receiving hydrochlorothiazide for service-connected hypertension
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.118, DC 7821 (cutaneous manifestations of collagen-vascular diseases not listed elsewhere (including scleroderma, calcinosis cutis, subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus, and dermatomyositis)) — evaluated under the General Rating Formula for the Skin at 0, 10, 30, or 60 percent depending on the percentage of body or exposed-area involvement and on the duration and constancy of required systemic therapy; DC 7809 (discoid lupus erythematosus) is the alternative code where the morphology is discoid rather than subacute. Qualified-human rating review required
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected hypertension (hypertensive vascular disease) treated with hydrochlorothiazide or a hydrochlorothiazide-containing combination product
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.104, DC 7101 (hypertensive vascular disease (hypertension and isolated systolic hypertension)): 10 percent at diastolic pressure predominantly 100 or more, or systolic predominantly 160 or more, or as the minimum evaluation for a history of diastolic pressure predominantly 100 or more requiring continuous medication for control, with Note (1) requiring confirmation by readings taken two or more times on at least three different days
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Photosensitization and autoantibody-induction sequence: hydrochlorothiazide and its metabolites absorb ultraviolet radiation in the UVA range and, on photoactivation, generate reactive species that damage keratinocytes and alter the presentation of nuclear antigens; in genetically susceptible individuals this drives an interface dermatitis with prominent epidermal photosensitivity and induces Ro/SS-A (anti-SSA) autoantibodies directed against a ribonucleoprotein that translocates to the keratinocyte surface after ultraviolet exposure, where antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity produces the characteristic annular, polycyclic, photodistributed lesions of subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus. The reaction spares the kidneys and central nervous system in typical cases, distinguishing it clinically from systemic drug-induced lupus, and it is characteristically reversible: lesions clear within weeks of withdrawing the offending drug, and recurrence after rechallenge has been documented. Reed et al. (PMID 3873891) reported five patients taking hydrochlorothiazide who developed photosensitive eruptions with the clinical and histologic features of subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus and antibodies to the SS-A(Ro) antigen; the eruptions cleared after the drug was discontinued, anti-SS-A antibodies disappeared in one patient after thiazide withdrawal, and rechallenge with hydrochlorothiazide reproduced the dermatitis — the original human evidence, including the rechallenge that supports a causal rather than coincidental relationship. Lowe et al. (PMID 21039412) systematically reviewed drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus, noting that the initial appearance of SCLE lesions with Ro/SS-A autoantibodies as an adverse reaction to hydrochlorothiazide was first reported in 1985, that an increasing number of drug classes has since been implicated, and that most cases resolved within weeks of drug withdrawal with Ro/SS-A autoantibodies present in about 80 percent of cases where such data were available. Callen (PMID 20693204) reviews drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus and records that the first description dates to 1985, when a series of five patients was found to have hydrochlorothiazide-induced SCLE, and that at least 40 other drugs have since been implicated. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-causation theory pleaded as a medication side effect, in which a disability caused by treatment of the service-connected hypertension is itself service-connected because the thiazide was prescribed for that service-connected condition. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would be the correct theory only where the record shows pre-existing cutaneous lupus or another photosensitive dermatosis and the claim is that the thiazide exposure measurably worsened a baseline skin disease, in which case the drug-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of that baseline dermatosis and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology is decisive and the corresponding § 3.310(a) or (b) analysis requires: a prescription record identifying hydrochlorothiazide or a thiazide-containing product with start and stop dates; onset of the eruption after the drug was started, in a photodistributed pattern; dermatologic or histologic confirmation of an interface dermatitis compatible with SCLE and, where available, positive Ro/SS-A antibody testing; and documented improvement or resolution after the drug was withdrawn, since the natural history of resolution on withdrawal is itself strong evidence of the drug's causal role. Only then can an examiner state that the subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus is at least as likely as not caused by the thiazide prescribed for the service-connected hypertension — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include idiopathic subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (which carries systemic associations and requires different prognostic counseling), systemic lupus erythematosus, discoid lupus, dermatomyositis, polymorphous light eruption, photosensitive drug reactions to other agents such as terbinafine, proton pump inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors, or tumor necrosis factor inhibitors, rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis, and tinea corporis; the fact that more than 40 drugs have been implicated means the prescriber's specific agent must be the one documented in the record. No individual probability is asserted here. No intentional rechallenge, unsupervised discontinuation of an antihypertensive, or patient-specific prescribing recommendation is made. Rating discipline under § 4.14: two or more skin conditions may be combined under § 4.25 only if separate areas of skin are involved, and where two conditions involve the same area the highest single evaluation applies, so an SCLE rating may not be pyramided with a dermatitis or scar rating for the same skin; the note to DC 7809 likewise bars combining that code with the systemic lupus code.

medicalEvidence.title: Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus associated with hydrochlorothiazide therapy
medicalEvidence.authors: B R Reed; J C Huff; S K Jones; P W Orton; L A Lee; D A Norris
medicalEvidence.summary: Report of five patients taking hydrochlorothiazide who developed photosensitive eruptions with the clinical and histologic features of subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus and antibodies to the SS-A(Ro) antigen; eruptions cleared after the drug was discontinued, anti-SS-A antibodies disappeared in one patient after thiazide withdrawal, and rechallenge reproduced the dermatitis — the founding human evidence of causal drug induction.

medicalEvidence.title: A systematic review of drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus
medicalEvidence.authors: G C Lowe; C L Henderson; R H Grau; C B Hansen; R D Sontheimer
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review of the drug-induced SCLE literature reporting that the first cases were hydrochlorothiazide-induced and that the number of implicated drugs has grown, that most cases resolve spontaneously within weeks of drug withdrawal, and that Ro/SS-A autoantibodies were present in about 80 percent of cases with such data — the pooled clinical picture applied in this row.

medicalEvidence.title: Drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus
medicalEvidence.authors: J P Callen
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of drug-induced SCLE recording that the first description dates to 1985, when a series of five patients were found to have hydrochlorothiazide-induced SCLE, and that at least 40 other drugs have since been implicated in inducing SCLE — the historical and differential-diagnosis context for attributing a given eruption to a specific prescribed agent.

originalRow.secondaryCondition: Myositis (statin-associated immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy with anti-HMGCR autoantibodies) in a veteran on statin therapy for service-connected hypertension
originalRow.secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5021 (myositis) — with the note to DCs 5013 through 5024 directing that group to be evaluated as degenerative arthritis based on limitation of motion; where the predominant disability is proximal muscle weakness and fatigue rather than joint limitation, the muscle-injury provisions of § 4.73 and the evaluation of muscle disability in § 4.56 govern, and an analogous evaluation under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 may be required. Qualified-human rating review required
originalRow.primaryCondition: Service-connected hypertensive vascular disease (hypertension) for which a statin was prescribed as part of cardiovascular risk management
originalRow.primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.104, DC 7101 (hypertensive vascular disease (hypertension and isolated systolic hypertension)): 10/20/40/60 percent on diastolic or systolic pressure thresholds, or as the minimum evaluation for a history of diastolic pressure predominantly 100 or more requiring continuous medication for control, with Note (1) requiring confirmation by readings taken two or more times on at least three different days
originalRow.etiologicalMechanism: Pharmacological iatrogenic sequence: statins inhibit 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis. In genetically susceptible patients the drug upregulates expression of the HMGCR protein in regenerating skeletal muscle, and that overexpressed enzyme becomes the target of a specific autoantibody response, producing an immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy characterized by symmetric proximal muscle weakness, markedly elevated creatine kinase, myofiber necrosis with minimal inflammation on biopsy, and — critically — persistence and even progression after the statin is withdrawn, which distinguishes it from the self-limited toxic myopathy that resolves on discontinuation. Because the disease is antibody-driven rather than simply dose-toxic, the ordinary temporal assumption that stopping the drug ends the illness does not hold. Mammen et al. (PMID 21360500) identified anti-HMGCR autoantibodies in 45 of 750 patients presenting to a myositis center, with the great majority of patients aged 50 and older having had statin exposure, and demonstrated the statin-dependent upregulation of the autoantigen. Nazir et al. (PMID 28277343) systematically reviewed 100 reported cases of statin-associated autoimmune myopathy and described a syndrome of symmetric proximal weakness with extreme creatine kinase elevation, occurring predominantly in males, and separate from the ordinary statin myalgia that resolves on drug cessation. Khoo et al. (PMID 40347460) calculated the incidence of anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy across four independent cohorts in the United Kingdom and Australia and described its clinical characteristics, treating it as a rare but definable complication of statin therapy — the contemporary denominator evidence for a rare-event claim. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-causation theory pleaded as a medication side effect, in which a disability caused by treatment of the service-connected hypertension is itself service-connected because the statin was prescribed for that service-connected condition. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would be the correct theory only where the record documents pre-existing myositis, inflammatory myopathy, or another myopathic process and the claim is that the statin exposure measurably worsened that baseline muscle disease, in which case the drug-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing myopathy and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require: a prescription record identifying the statin with start and stop dates and the indication of the service-connected hypertension or its cardiovascular risk profile; onset of proximal weakness during or after exposure; laboratory confirmation of markedly elevated creatine kinase; and, where available, positive anti-HMGCR antibody testing or muscle biopsy showing necrotizing myopathy, since the antibody and biopsy findings are what distinguish the immune-mediated disease from ordinary statin myalgia. Only then can an examiner state that the myositis is at least as likely as not caused by the statin prescribed for the service-connected hypertension — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include ordinary statin-associated myalgia and self-limited toxic myopathy, hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, inflammatory myopathies unrelated to statins (dermatomyositis, polymyositis, and other immune-mediated necrotizing myopathies), paraneoplastic myositis associated with an occult malignancy, viral myositis including influenza, HIV, and hepatitis, glucocorticoid or colchicine myopathy, alcohol-related muscle disease, and inherited metabolic myopathies. No individual probability is asserted here. No intentional rechallenge, unsupervised discontinuation of a prescribed statin, or patient-specific prescribing recommendation is made. Rating discipline under § 4.14: the same weakness, creatine kinase elevation, or limitation of motion may not be compensated more than once — a myositis rating under DC 5021 and a separate muscle-injury rating for the same proximal groups are not cumulative, and § 4.14 and the note to DCs 5013 through 5024 require a single evaluation for the same manifestation.

medicalEvidence.title: Autoantibodies against 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase in patients with statin-associated autoimmune myopathy
medicalEvidence.authors: Andrew L Mammen; Tae Chung; Lisa Christopher-Stine; Paul Rosen; Antony Rosen; Kimberly R Doering; Livia A Casciola-Rosen
medicalEvidence.summary: Identified anti-HMGCR autoantibodies in 45 of 750 patients presenting to a myositis center, with nearly all patients aged 50 and older having statin exposure, and showed statin-dependent upregulation of the autoantigen — the founding mechanistic evidence that statins can induce an antibody-mediated necrotizing myopathy.

medicalEvidence.title: Statin-Associated Autoimmune Myopathy: A Systematic Review of 100 Cases
medicalEvidence.authors: Salik Nazir; Saroj Lohani; Niranjan Tachamo; Dilliram Poudel; Anthony Donato
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review of 100 reported cases describing statin-associated necrotizing myopathy as symmetric proximal muscle weakness with extreme creatine kinase elevation, distinct from the ordinary toxic myopathies that resolve on statin discontinuation — the clinical picture evidence for the immune-mediated rather than dose-toxic mechanism.
